reviews.text: McG's "3 Days to Kill" is a strangely scatterbrained experience. On one hand, it is an action film led by a seasoned fighter, cleaner, or killer in the vein of "Taken." On the other hand, it is a film about a man coming to grips with both his family and his mortality. At the same time, however, it is a satirical take on the aformentioned action film and a light-toned, moderate camp and silliness-infused riff on parenthood: sort of the CIA operative as symbol for the minefield that is raising a teenage girl. Though these pieces and tones never find an ideal balance, "3 Days to Kill" still rates as an engaging, entertaining film.

This has neither, so what's left is a limp stage play with a brutally inert rhythm behind the camera, making the RIPE dialogue feel especially rote and frankly sounding embarrassing from the well-beloved thesps/hardmen trying a little too hard to give it some legitimacy. McShane knows what he's doing, but Winstone looks lost; reheated Sexy Beast is not a good look, and when this is the exact flipside of that deceptively wholesome film, the whole thing just reeks. It has some undeniably weapons-grade swearing though, can't deny that.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: 600 Miles is written as a thriller on weapons smuggling in the Mexico/USA border and directed by Arturo Ripstein’s son Gabriel in a naturalistic detailed oriented approach that couldn’t be further from genre. The tension can be compelling and Ripstein gets good performances from Krystian Ferrer and Tim Roth as the young smuggler and american agent that ends his hostage. Characters interactions are often trite and the initial points about how easy it is for Mexican cartels to legally buy guns in US end up getting lost in the middle of the road movie mechanics. Third act amps up the violence not always for the best. Ripstein is better known for producing Michel Franco’s vile movies and the connection is obvious (that awful final scene seem to come straight from a Franco movie), but this has a much better dramatic shape even if remains a limited experiment.

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: Split screens, frames melting into themselves, and aspect ratio changes all colour this highly experimental children's nihilist masterpiece, which, despite its often gorgeous imagery and formal control, is incredibly depressing. Charlie Brown stands there while three girls sing "Failure Face" to him, a song about how dumb he is and how he’s never going to accomplish anything. He gets picked apart by his therapist, who says he has a "tendency toward fatness." It’s a lot—too much, in the way only Charlie Brown manages to convey—taking a child's melancholy and grounding it so that it becomes both tender and extremely funny. We even have a five-minute section of Beethoven played over scenes that sooner belong in a Godard than a movie featuring a narcissistic dog. Just one of the best things ever made.

reviews.text: Released in 1956, A Day of Fury appeared early in the small cycle of westerns about small towns having their collective morality challenged by the arrival of bad men. The best — and best known — of these is probably 1959's No Name on the Bullet, which stars Audie Murphy as a hired gun whose presence in a town arouses violence, suspicion, and fear, but there are others as well, including 1965's unimpressive Black Spurs, a film very much built on the No Name on the Bullet template.

Jones was another who was lured to television, something that curtailed his career in terms of films he ended up directing for the likes of Universal, Allied Artists Pictures, and predominately 20th Century Fox. His filmography heavily features Westerns, mostly smaller budget affairs with slightly lesser stars, such as George Montgomery, Guy Madison, or my man Rory Calhoun. A Day of Fury might just be the finest of the films I've seen so far from Jones, and that's not just because it has former October 1958 Playboy Playmate Mara Corday as a love interest!

It's a moment befitting her character, a young socialite who winds up in all the papers, but also speaks to Taylor the star, hounded her whole life by flash photography and the salacious appetite of the public. reviews.text: There's a stark, corrosive sadness seeping through A Simple Plan like blood freezing in snow. Upper Midwestern Noir so black and so cold that it could take digits off extremities without any the wiser. The spectre looming above, behind it all is economic collapse: foreclosure, unemployment, neurological difficulty, isolation, loneliness. The people of A Simple Plan are presented directly, warmly, without irony or condescension, so that when the bad stuff starts going around, it hurts and it keeps hurting, a dull ache which sharpens to acuity now and again. Scott Smith adapted his novel into this screenplay, so its voice is both preserved and fluidly translated to the screen. Raimi's direction may be career-best to that point, pulled back behind…

Aquí lo que está en juego es la vida de ese intermedio entre el objeto y la vida que es el cine, sin ser exactamente ni objeto ni la vida. Los aparatos de proyección se rompen, las latas de película son pesadas y ocupan espacio, las butacas hace rato que dejaron de adaptarse a los cánones del confort. reviews.text: Every new movie that comes out as a "love letter to films" pales in comparison to this.This is an all too relatable glimpse at the preservation of cinephilia and what it means to try and keep a passion alive against all odds.When you have more passion for cinema, than your own sex life, you know what your purpose really is.Attempt to give yourself that same love and attention, and nurture your own life the same way and find yourself jaded. A useful life can be one where there's a balance. One where your love for cinema can be as much a part of your personality as your haircut, or who you choose to spend time with and take in a new movie with at the end of the day.

Una introspección reflexiva en la propia vida. Jorge es un hombre de casi 50 años que luego del cierre de la cinemateca en la que trabajó 25 años cierra, queda varado en el mundo, y empieza a verdaderamente vivir "La Vida Útil". reviews.author: Kevin Watson
reviews.text: If you want to know how not to market a cinema, watch 'A Useful Life.' It's the story of a 45 year old man who not only works in a cinema but has made it his entire life. He moves his head like he's a human camera trying to run a smooth tracking shot, and he repeatedly waits in the shadows for a woman he desires presumably because everyone looks better in film noir. Heck, he's even in black and white and (for English viewers) subtitled which reminds me of a phase I went through in my my teens when I wondered if I would come across as more sophisticated if I walked around with subtitles.

reviews.author: Mariana Dianela
reviews.text: Es un hecho que para el mundo instrumental el cine es inútil. En cambio, para algunos pocos significa más que solamente imágenes y sonidos; es algo que ayuda a desarticular las mentiras de los señores trajeados. ¿Qué puede ser más útil en nuestra vida que ver películas de Manoel de Oliveira en una Cinemateca? Aunque no hay duda que existe la precarización cultural, debemos intentar percibir la vida (y la cinefilia) con otros enfoques que nos acerquen más a lo que nos movió por primera vez. Una caminata puede cambiarlo todo.

reviews.author: Jo Brennan
reviews.text: «Uruguay no tiene cine», dice Manuel Martínez Carril en 1968, acorde a la introducción de La crítica uruguaya ante el cine nacional (1920-2001), «aunque tiene una fuerte cultura cinematográfica asentada en la difusión del cine de calidad y de las páginas de crítica a partir de 1952». Contra la irregularidad de la producción cinematográfica uruguaya del siglo XX —se bromea que el cine local tiene más nacimientos que cualquier otro país, y Álvaro Lema Mosca dedicó un libro a este fenómeno (Los nacimientos del cine uruguayo: una historia completa)—, hubo un período prolífico de crítica de cine, con ese auge de la creación de la primer revista Film, acompañado de la perseverancia de los cineclubes locales. Múltiples actores, séase participantes…

reviews.author: dmartsfilm
reviews.text: I thought this one would be the most fun out of the whole 28 film Abbott and Costello box set since the space setting had potential for campy fun. They don’t even go to Mars like the title suggests and the whole movie is filled with tired performances and an uninspired story. There’s still a few things here and there I did enjoy about this film due to Bud and Lou, but overall it was a bit disappointing. They really missed an opportunity to go full out sci-fi and commit to making a 50’s sci-fi B movie with the duo, but it literally isn’t any of that. It’s a watchable film though and some of the silliness worked, but it should’ve went full space camp and it would’ve been a massive amount of fun!

reviews.text: In Abbott And Costello Go To Mars, Bud Abbott and Lou Costello go to … <checks notes> … Venus. The incorrect title may be the funniest gag in the film. It’s notable for apparently being the first feature-length comedy about the Space Race. The 1946 Popeye cartoon Rocket To Mars and the 1948 and 1952 Bugs Bunny cartoons Haredevil Hare and The Hasty Hare beat A&C to the punch, but other comedians would quickly follow in their footsteps. The Three Stooges’ Have Rocket, Will Travel is a remake of this film in all but name. Like that Stooges film, this suffers from the fact that A&C were in the declining years of their partnership. By 1953, their routines had grown stale —…

reviews.text: Definitely one of A&C's sillier and more insubstantial movies, this one is still a reasonable amount of blithely inane fun despite being not as clever and witty as their earlier films. Alas, the sharp verbal banter that distinguishes their best work is noticeably absent here. In its place we get a lot of silly slapstick stuff that's strictly hit or miss, with the most amusing things occurring when the pair wind up on Venus which turns out to be populated by nothing but comely young women who make Lou their unlikely king. Mari Blanchard gives a delightful performance as the man-hating queen of Venus. Moreover, having the Venusian ladies played by a bunch of extremely fetching Miss Universe beauty pageant…

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Abbott and Costello Go to Mars is a shambles. They do not go to Mars. They go to Venus... and Mardi Gras in New Orleans. The plot is slapdash with unnecessary characters and haphazard subplots. The gags are dumb, the pace is all over the place. But damn, I enjoyed it. A lot. The Mardi Gras sequence that takes up most of the first half is fantastic with bizarre costumes (the extending neck woman is incredible) and a delightfully chaotic atmosphere. Then, when Abbott and Costello barrel into space and end up in a female-populated Venus, it reaches delirious heights of silliness. There's always something beautiful about this era of science fiction with its inventive, magical technology and weird props. And it's so much fun to see black-and-white 50s sci-fi with a dollop of Abbott and Costello mixed in. A mad, wonderful, stupid film.

reviews.text: When I saw that this was written by Errol Flynn, I assumed it would just be an excuse for him to canoodle with some woman half his age, like a Captain Blood's Midlife Crisis type of thing. Instead, it's a kind of Adventure/Film Noir hybrid that works pretty well thanks largely to the performance of Micheline Presle as a scheming Creole Femme Fatale who is determined to rise above her station and wreak revenge on the local gentry for their uppity ways. Vincent Price is the sniveling shit who is the main target of her ire and Agnes Moorhead is her witchy aunt, who looks like she is covered in soot. There is also a cameo by Jess Franco's pal Howard Vernon and he's not even playing a perv. This one definitely caught me by surprise; yet another film from Flynn's later period that is better than I anticipated. He was more than just a carousing chicken hawk after all.

reviews.text: This one wasn’t super great. It’s about a woman who wants to be rich so she manipulates men to get what she wants. There’s an interesting idea in there because at first she wants a man (Vincent price) but he rejects her and betrays her even though he lists after her. She finds another man (Errol Flynn, who also wrote the screenplay) who actually loves her for who she is but then she betrays him. Then Price ends up needing her so she blackmails him, which causes him to lose all interest in her even though she still wants him. It’s basically a love triangle romance film, but not a great one as none of the characters are that likable in my opinion. Probably the most disappointing part is that there are zero adventures gone on by Captain Fabian despite the title of the film. Directed in part by Robert Florey (Murders in the Rue Morgue).

For decades this was the definition of a superhero flick & even today modern films a modeled similarly in many respects. It hosts solid characters, mystery that holds up through the end, and even action on occasion that still entertains today. I'd say this is probably one of the best, if not the most famous serial of its' kind. If I could rate individual episodes, of course some would rank much higher, but in total this one is probably mildly entertaining at best by today's standards.

reviews.text: A&C RankedAfrica Screams is one of the small handful of Abbott & Costello films I hadn't seen (mostly because it was not made by Universal), and was made toward the latter half of their time in the spotlight, ten years before Costello would die from a heart attack. This film seems like it was made in the early to mid 50s though because their magic is not totally "there" regarding many of their typical scenarios and jokes. What makes this particular film lower than many of the others is the uninspired production design, the uninspired script, and the uninspired acting--not that any acting in an A&C film will win any awards--but it's a notch or three below the standard. There's another aspect others may appreciate more, which is the obvious lack of knowledge folks had regarding animals and African culture. Some of this is incidentally hysterical and quite the curio of the 1940s.

As a rule when watching the duo, you want the films written by John Grant, even better if Charles Lamont is directing - neither of whom are present. All are wildly different from each other and all pushing boundaries in their own way. Then there’s Agitator, which might be the most overlooked out of all of them. It doesn’t have the same immediate shock factor or recognition, but it might be one of his most devastating movies. What starts off feeling like a standard yakuza story slowly reveals itself to be something much more reflective and, honestly, kind of sad. reviews.author: James Grimmer
reviews.text: The first thing that comes to mind is that looks can be deceiving. This is alluded to throughout, and as such, the facade that John puts on is one of the more prominent aspects of the film. I wouldn't say that it is to the point where it yields a deep exploration of the subconscious, which you may find disappointing. The writing isn't the most polished, nor does the blending of fantasy and reality ever really come off as fully realized. On the other hand, the idea that there is more to John than meets the eye is conveyed well enough, and on top of that, it provides a solid foundation for the dream sequences. I can't knock that.

Because, if anyone thought about it for a half a second, they would see something was amiss with Nick. Perhaps not in a supernatural way, but in a way that is most definitely unsettling and malevolent. But the thing is, they don't think about it, because either they don't want to know, or they don't want to acknowledge what they do know.

reviews.text: I hadn’t rewatched this in some time. Alias Nick Beal is filled to the brim with great performances. Ray Milland leads in a deviously menacing performance as the titular Nick Beal. He’s joined by Audrey Trotter as the haunted femme fatal of the piece. Both are excellent as are Thomas Mitchel, George Macready and Frank Clark. It’s a solid cast. Director John Farrow and cinematographer Lionel Lindon make some very interesting choices both visually and in terms of dramatic pace. Overall it’s a high quality and very unique melodramatic/supernatural noir.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Noir really comes in all kind of different shapes and sub-genres. Here it presents itself in the form of a Faustian morality tale. Alias Nick Beal is about the dangers of excessive and misguided ambition and making a pact with the devil in the hope that the end will justify the means. It’s an age old theme and here it is wonderfully and uniquely presented in form of a “fantasy” Film Noir.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Slept on this one, but so did history, apparently. It's from that wonderful period in horror when fully formed adults who have emotions and know how to write people made movies for other adults. This will never turn up on Criterion Collection like Rosemary's Baby or Don't Look Now, but its intentions seem more humble and sincere: the Catholic Church is perverse and creates monsters, so let's make a slick, good-looking thriller about some creepy practitioners. Gold star for use of jaunty old-timey music as counterpoint to some pretty grisly murder scenes

reviews.text: "All That Money Can Buy" or "The Devil and Daniel Webster" is a 1941 supernatural drama directed by William Dieterle. Naturally the film is based on Stephen Vincent Benét 1936 story that published originally in the "The Saturday Evening Post". On a personal level, part of me wanted to place this film's (and overall story in general) discernment of theme in the folklorist category due to the application of fantasy and horror applied in such a fablistic manner. Being incepted in 1936 its far too modern to press that button, but I have no problem unofficially compartmentalizing the story as such as access to describing the theme. Either way, I hope one day way out yonder that mentality is compartmentalized…

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Jabez Stone is a hardworking farmer trying to make an honest living, but a streak of bad luck tempts him to do the unthink-able: bargain with the devil himself. In exchange for seven years of good fortune, Stone promises “Mr. Scratch” his soul. But when the troubled farmer begins to realize the error of his choice, he enlists the aid of the one man who might save him: the legendary orator and politician Daniel Webster. Directed with stylish flair by William Dieterle, All That Money Can Buy brings the classic short story by Stephen Vincent Benét to life with inspired visuals, an unforgettable, Oscar-winning score by Bernard Herrmann, and a truly diabolical performance from Walter Huston as the devil.

reviews.text: A Mystery Comedy if you can handle the whiplash as they change tone on a dime, especially in the first act. Bogart is "Gloves" Donahue, a "promoter" and gambler with a gang around him. He only eats one kind of cheesecake and when the cheesecake maker is killed, he, at the prompting of his mother, searches for the killer which leads him to Nazi spy ring. It's pretty entertaining, but drags a bit in the 3rd act as they get more serious about the evils of Nazi spies. I saw this perhaps 30 years ago, but now own it in a 4-movie Bogie set. It's perhaps the only Bogie I own my son hadn't seen. Lots of great character actors, Peter Lorre, William Demarest, Jackie Gleason in only his 3rd movie, Barton MacLane, Edward Brophy, Judith Anderson, Conrad Veidt, etc.

Much like Lucky McKee’s cult classic, this unexpected surprise by Jay Lee is a tour de force, one-woman showcase. Jade Dornfeld is Angela Bettis reborn—a deeply damaged, haggard-looking mental wreck who strangely enough deserves our empathy. Although Alyce Kills suffers from a not-so-original conceit, the film totally makes up for it with its unforgettable lead star, some real slick production, and of course great dark humor.

reviews.text: An elegant reimagining of the famous Lizzy Borden murders for a more modern audience. The dialogue wasn't stilted in the slightest. The cinematography was inventive and nuanced. My absolute favourite shot was when the director chose to film the back of....Some Bitch...'s head, for no reason, instead of showing us what she was actually looking at. Every scene has an almost "found footage" style. Not because they were going for that but because the director got his aunt with Parkinson's to hold the camera. Such a charitable man. If you're a fan of stable camera angles, this film is not for you. I, on the other hand, love it when the budget doesn't allow for a fucking tripod. This film proves that we have reached the apex of humanity. It's all downhill from here.

reviews.text: Pineapple Express without the laughs and The Bourne Ultimatum without the thrills, American Ultra is a stoner action comedy that riffs on the familiar story of a guy who can’t remember that he’s actually a government-trained killing machine. Artless and unpleasant, this is the kind of late-summer swill that gives August a bad name. Directed by Nima Nourizadeh (Project X), the film stars Jesse Eisenberg as Mike, a rural Virginia convenience-store attendant with stringy hair and a weed habit. The one good thing in his otherwise meaningless existence is his endlessly patient girlfriend, Phoebe (Kristen Stewart), whose unconditional love for Mike is as inexplicable to him as it is to us.

reviews.text: While this offers the people whose lives are at stake much more of a presence (and a literal voice) than LINCOLN, it's more interesting now as a bookend with that film, especially since both are largely concerned with political language and procedure. But I'm not sure it fully transcends being just well-meaning. There's a curious moment, when Cinque and his people are first released by a lower court, and while everyone is celebrating, one of the Mende, still in chains, clutches a Bible. It's a telling moment of both historical transition and of hypocrisy, that supposedly God-given freedom is almost always subject to some other system or power structure. This movie continues to grow on me.

reviews.author: Michael James
reviews.text: It is one skillfully crafted and disturbing historical drama, one that portrays an important tale of slave revolt and its legal consequences. Though there are some reservations on its historical accuracies, it does handle the sensitive subject matter sensibly enough. You get some intensely gripping and moving moments, however the cliched formulaic route does make it feel repetitive and slightly longer. It possesses an ensemble cast, however the ones who make the most impact are Djimon Hounsou and Matthew McConaughey. Anthony Hopkins scores with his big finale speech. Despite of the shortcomings, it definitely is worth the watch.

reviews.text: There's plenty going on in this movie that barely qualifies as a film noir (it was released in 1941, at the beginning of the cycle). Susan Hayward stars as a woman who constantly needles one of the twins about his masculinity. A mob forms to find the killer after a reward of $5,000 is offered, leading to some bizarre cultural commentary. Bonus: for Nirvana fans, the actress Frances Farmer has a small role. For Anthrax fans, well, you know what I'm talking about.

reviews.text: Soviet-era creature feature from the tail end of Krushchev's tenure as leader of the country's ruling party. In this case, it's sort of both, as she appears in flashbacks as a doomed ancestor and, as Harriet in the film's modern day, is compelled, every night at midnight, to hand her body over to her ancestor's malicious, "hideous" cousin, Belinda.

reviews.author: Bob McQueen
reviews.text: Pretty great little classic film starring the incredible Barbara Steele playing different roles as she becomes possessed as starts messing with the men of the town, turning them all against each other. It all revolves around a statue recovered from a lake and some sister jealousy from many years prior with the ugly sister putting a curse on that statue. All sorts of shenanigans ensue, it was fun watching Steele turn the town against one another. I don't think Satan was ever mentioned at all......

reviews.author: theironcupcake
reviews.text: Barbara Steele's last Italian Gothic is one of her best and long the least accessible. As her films often are, it's a rumination on her uncanny beauty, but this time it's a love/hate rumination as well as one that asks us to consider things from her side, as the bearer of that beauty. While it certainly takes the viewer to some horrific extremes of human nature and frailty, it seems less a horror film than a romantic tragedy, streaked not only with tears but with aspects of witchery, folk superstition, and hypnosis. The direction is by Camillo Mastrocinque (TERROR IN THE CRYPT aka CRYPT OF THE VAMPIRE) and the storyline - which involves the salvaging and restoration of a life-sized…

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: Gothic comfort food for the chilly autumn night soul. You know the drill; a large isolated mansion, family secrets, creepy portraits, sinister local weirdos, rape, disembodied ghost hands, Peter Cushing turning up half way through and a title that proves true when it starts about five minutes in and continues throughout. Directed by Roy Ward Baker, this is solidly atmospheric. Also, it manages to be a little creepy because, no matter how old-school the effects, no-eyes in a face is never something I want to see.

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: I’ve been digging into this Amicus boxset from Severin films and it’s been a real treat to watch the two I’ve yet to see, the werewolf murder mystery The Beast Must Die, and the 70’s gothic supernatural tale, And Now the Screaming Starts, as I make my way towards the classic of the set which I have seen, Asylum.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: A real cozy little period horror from Amicus! And Now the Screaming Starts has a real foreboding atmosphere, which really makes the best of the central location and drives through the narrative, which focuses on a deadly secret from the past presiding over the manor house at the centre of the film. The film gets going straight away - a hallway full of paintings that harks back to House of Usher precedes several sequences in which the lady of the house is menaced by axes, eyeless corpses and severed hands. The film constantly hints at a mystery that nobody in the house wants to talk about, and for good reason it seems as those that do uniformly end up dying…

reviews.author: Helen_S
reviews.text: I've never seen that much love for this one but I've always adored it. One of my favourite haunted house films. As much as I love Amicus' modern day horrors I do wish they'd done a few more period ones like this. The score is beautiful, the cast is fantastic as is and then just to top it all off Peter Cushing arrives midway through. The house is the stuff of dreams in all its gothic glory. Stephanie Beacham is marvelous, her final shot in this is incredible. It's creepy, atmospheric and the backstory is heartbreaking. But it's hard to have too much sympathy for Silas as his revenge sucks! Best scene in the graveyard with Charles bashing his relatives bones up, ha!

reviews.author: haley
reviews.text: a little slow at times, but extremely atmosphere throughout. the cinematography is stunning and the sets are outstanding. unfortunately, i did almost fall asleep multiple times due to boredom. despite that, i still think this is worth checking out, even if you don't finish it.

reviews.author: pirateneckbeard
reviews.text: "In my dreams I go back to the year 1795, to a time when I was happy. I was on my way to be married, I was going to the house in which I was to find my days filled with fear, my nights filled with horror." -Catherine Fengriffen

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: This one’s going out for Herbert Charles Angelo Kuchacevich ze Schluderpacheru (aka Herbert Lom), born September 11, 1917.

reviews.author: Flynch
reviews.text: „Embryo des Bösen“Schöner britischer Gothic-Horror aus der Amicus-Schmiede, inklusive Nebel, viel Regen und einer recht grausamen Story. Dass auch die Effekte, inklusive eiskaltem Händchen, erstaunlich krude geworden sind passt perfekt zum schaurigen Familienfluch. Herbert Lom, präsent in den Rückblenden, darf überzeugend brutal sein, während Peter Cushing eher durch seine Frisur als durch sein, stark storybedingt, Schauspiel auffällt. Roy Ward Baker liefert wiedermal gekonnt die gothische Schauermär ab, die vorallem mit einer dichten Atmosphäre, tollen Sets, einigen Grausamkeiten und mit einer tollen Garde an Mimen dem Hammer-Fan die gewünscht schaurig schöne Gruselkost liefert.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: I watched this believing it was going to be boring but it proved me wrong. It saved making the clues that don't make sense understandable until the end when it reached its most fervent pitch. And a gothic vibe of horse carriages at dusk and creepy family portraits and awesome wall paper welcomes you from the start. It's got the same kind of curse plot that Black Sunday had, which is vengeance on a past injustice never really goes away, but it's only fed to us in bits and pieces until it goes into a flashback of its nasty origins. Peter Cushing arrives midway through as a pioneer in the science of the mind which he carries off in classic fashion, but the significance of his role as someone you believe could figure this out logically, is really why it stands out so well because gothic horror films tend to beat down science and logic.

reviews.author: kat🕷
reviews.text: "And Now the Screaming Starts!" isn't too intense: an old family curse, a castle, a ghost, and a creepy, autonomous hand killing people. With Peter Cushing, always a joy to watch, there's a nice Gothic vibe, and a few good scenes that make the 91 minutes more or less enjoyable.

reviews.author: Demdike
reviews.text: Amicus are traditionally best known for their horror anthology films but they also made some cracking feature length movies as well such as The Skull (1965), The Beast Must Die (1974) and this. Peter Cushing, Ian Ogilvy, Stephanie Beacham and Herbert Lom star in this gory film about the Fengriffen family curse in which a disembodied hand avenges a Fengriffen ancestor's rape of a servants bride.

reviews.author: Bloodspiller🩸
reviews.text: One of Amicus' few feature lengths that's not an anthology. As consistent with a lot of their productions, you could mistake this for a Hammer film by the actors alone.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: And Soon the Darkness is a really effective and unsettling suspense thriller that makes the best of its simple premise. Taking place entirely in the daytime, we focus on two young women on a cycling holiday in rural France. They split up after an argument, but one soon goes missing - leaving the other to search for her. The language barrier is put to great use here. All the French dialogue is spoken without subtitles, really emphasising the vulnerable situation our lead finds herself in as she's not even able to communicate properly with the people around her. The French countryside is vast but somehow claustrophic at the same time - creating a real feel of isolation, which is realised…

reviews.author: Geesuss
reviews.text: Even if it doesn’t make me feel really hyped while watching, “As Soon The Darkness” is a truly entertaining 70s thriller, with an evocative atmosphere and an engaging main performance by Pamela Franklin who carries the film almost entirely.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Slow, but it builds to such a tense spiderweb of a finale that all is forgiven by the end. There's a special kind of horror here, one that most women are deeply familiar with, the phenomenon of being adrift in a world where you can never tell just which man in your vicinity is capable of guilty of the perpetrator of misogynist violence. It's exquisite once it gets around to it.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "And Soon the Darkness" is a 1970 thriller film directed by Robert Fuest. A small and tight thriller, the film follows two young British women as they take a bike holiday in the French countryside. Going along on an extended ride, the two get in a slight disagreement of schedule with one riding ahead and the other staying put. The stint of separation turned out to be far more dire as expected, as one of the women goes missing with the other traversing through the local townsfolk asking for help. As if the language barrier of French and English wasn't enough, the true dire circumstance is that the killer is most likely amongst the locals, turning the film into an…

reviews.author: The Horror of Marna Larsen
reviews.text: It's of course odd that Franklin suspects the one person she can actually communicate with out of the other suspects, all of which act really dodgy. It's frustrating how that character doesn't give her the least bit of useful information instead of acting dodgy and vaguely threatening so of course it can't possibly be him, right? But the actress's incredibly expressive face cautions us that maybe it isn't so - after all, imagine yourself completely alone, worried for your friend, you can't understand anyone. Plus, your friend was clearly attracted to that guy and look how well it ended up for her, right? The urge to flee is palpable throughout the entire film, a tightening, asphyxiating pressure. Franklin's performance in…

reviews.author: Ben Peterson
reviews.text: The quietness of 70s cinema. Let the camera talk. It’s always effective and sometimes it can be eerie - even in broad daylight. This is surely the story with 1970’s And Soon the Darkness.

I am a dumb man but just from assumption, the plot of “two pretty young British girls are bicycling across Europe and are currently in rural France” may sound terrifying to many women out there in 2023. The pair “having a row” and they separate, only for Michele Dotrice to go missing so Pamela Franklin has to try and find her when there are plenty of creepy people around and she barely speaks French”… that’s scary to me, so imagine if I was…

reviews.author: Jack Often
reviews.text: I'm finishing up my project (for now) of watching every adaptation of Christie's book that is available to me by going back to basics. The last time I watched this (in 2013 according to my offline journal,) I was underwhelmed both by the tamer ending of the stage play from which it is adapted, and by director René Clair's whimsical comic tone which doesn't fit the material, especially in the first half.But a funny thing happened this time around, maybe by having so many inferior versions to compare it with; it grew on me. The photography is nice at times. Judith Anderson is divine and gives a more witty performance than I remembered. She's easily the best Emily Brent,…

reviews.text: There's really nothing better than these AIP psychedelic flicks. This is probably one of the lesser examples, but it still manages to hold your interest all the way through. The music and carefree lifestyle is just so appealing, even when there's a sadistic Manson-esque guy running around fat shaming emotionally unstable girls and seducing her parents.

reviews.author: dantesring
reviews.text: As the studio system collapsed young filmmakers were getting their chance to flex their creative muscles. In many ways this led to to culture shaking entertainment with films like BONNIE AND CLYDE and EASY RIDER changing the way films were made and received. It also led to a lot of goofy experimentation that didn't really gel into a cohesive whole and this is where ANGEL ANGEL DOWN WE GO fits in.This film, about a cult leading rock singer that infiltrates a wealthy family to tear it apart, is a mess. It is a creative mess for sure but sloppy all the same. It is a variation on BONDU SAVED FROM DROWNING, but lacks that films sense of purpose and…

reviews.author: coles84
reviews.text: Certainly a trippy one that’s for sure. A rock band/cult do a bit of singing, a bit of kidnapping and a bit of drugs while the story drags along quite tediously. I am sure there is a misunderstood film that my eyes did not take in on this viewing but it all felt a bit messy despite me appreciating its attempts at being a cult film. Jennifer Jones gets star billing but doesn’t get near enough screen time and there are certainly some lines of dialogue you will be wondering if you really heard what you thought.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Pretty good AIP psychedelia, with a debutante taken in by a Manson-esque pop star and his band, who are also skydiving class warriors. At its best sort of like if TEOREMA got mashed up with PSYCH-OUT, trippy enough but mostly way too tame.

reviews.author: mrbalihai
reviews.text: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide was a magical substance in Hollywood during the 1960s; it had the ability to take an otherwise tepid exercise in cheap exploitation like Angel, Angel, Down We Go, and imbue it with a frothy head of pseudo-Freudian psychoanalytic symbolism that would embarrass a freshman philosophy major with its tawdry sexuality and "shocking" insights into society's failings...at least that's the way it must've appeared to its director, screenwriter, and cast. For those of us not under the influence of hallucinogenics, it just comes off like a Beyond the Valley of the Dolls knockoff.

The music is good and the visuals are nice, and Jennifer Jones serves up just the right amount of campiness. But ultimately I just couldn’t care less about any of the characters.

Of course that arrangement doesn’t go well. Don Stroud’s a great link between the biker and hippie worlds. Bill McKinney’s great pre-Clint Eastwood regular, pre-Deliverance even. This is the first Larry Bishop has really stood out to me. Wild to see Aldo Ray as the sheriff too. Big respect to Lee Madden highlighting a few key stunt performers like Bud Ekins right up the front of the end credits.

reviews.author: Henry Winkler
reviews.text: The first movie to be released by Roger Corman's revolutionary production company New World Pictures. But what a fucking mess. Shoddy in every regard. Shitty cinematography, shitty lighting (what little lighting there is, everything shot at night is completely unwatchable), shitty audio, shitty editing, shitty acting (even though the movie has two great actors in it, William Smith and R.G. Armstrong). It's practically not even a movie. There's no story. Things just happen. And none of the things just happening are interesting.

reviews.text: Biker movie notable for being the first movie released through Roger Corman's New World Pictures. It tries to have it both eays, but director Richard Compton matter of fact approach do give it strong sense of civil unrest. It is a contemporary western whose only certainty is its spiral towards violence.

It’s directed and written by Richard Compton, who also made Macon County Line and Return to Macon County. With a tagline that shouts right in your face, “CHOPPER OUTLAWS!..riding their hot throbbing machines to a brutal climax of violence!” you know exactly what this movie has to offer.

reviews.author: Ramon Villalobos
reviews.text: Watched this because I love biker pictures and I have a fascination with director Richard Compton's directorial style. He often overreaches his material and makes things more interesting than they have any right being and this was his second movie that he wrote so I was curious to see how that'd go and it went pretty well! Angels Die Hard is a wild little movie that is meandering and messy but man it's a lot of fun. Mostly it follows a group of bikers dealing with the passing of one of their brothers while being harrassed by a small town police force. Its dirty and grimy and a bit barbaric but Compton once again has a distinct eye for cinema.…

reviews.author: JacobMaxKelly
reviews.text: Nice editing choice. Do you have to do it for the whole movie? Shoddily put together but with the psych rock tunes and dumb dudes riding bikes and starting fights it has an undeniable dudes rock appeal. Normally can't hack all the edgy nazi imagery in these but this one isn't so annoying and in it they end up saving some people from a mine. Interestingly, they shoot at Lake Isabella, which was a popular location for westerns further cementing how the biker films were a modern version of those. Not the best NWP movie but I believe it is the first. First proper one anyway.

reviews.author: John Charles
reviews.text: There's even less story than usual for the genre in this, one of the very first releases from New World Pictures. It's a strange biker film that tries to have it both ways by presenting its antiheroes as the usual threats to society (they take over a restaurant and rape a waitress) and also as good guys at heart who are just misunderstood (helping to save a child from a mine cave-in). Cheap and crudely made, the movie occasionally benefits from that, but it's also lacking in coverage and wastes the iconic presence of William Smith (who does have one good scene at a funeral). The best aspect of the production is an enjoyable collection of obscure fuzz rock.

reviews.author: calum
reviews.text: "Angels Die Hard" was the first film to be produced by Roger Corman's New World Pictures, which is the only real point of note about the whole thing. It is badly written and directed by Richard Compton with the narrative meandering all over the place with great chunks of the run time given over to either the bike gang out on the road or the bikers being hassled by rednecks and the cops. The camera work is poor and the acting worse, but to be fair none of the actors have anything of worth to do. On the upside the film does have a decent soundtrack made up of unknown acid-folk and mellow psych-rock jams from a range of outfits but in the main from East-West Pipeline.

reviews.author: bulletproofQpid
reviews.text: "Y'know, the law wasn't designed just to protect the squares. It was designed to protect us too."

reviews.author: Chuck Dowling
reviews.text: Biker movies continue to be the worst genre of film, hands down.

reviews.author: Eltopo68
reviews.text: Biker movies tend to fall into two camps. On one side is the biker as anti-authoritarian, sticking it to the man, symbol of individual freedom (i.e. "Easy Rider".) The other side is biker as debauched, drug-fueled, sex-crazed animal who would do anything for a kick (i.e. "The Born Losers".) "Angels from Hell" tries to straddle the line between both sides and it's this ambiguity that keeps it from getting within smelling distance of any of the classics. It's also fairly tame for a biker film with the occasional bout of sex and violence, but it's pretty watered down. It does have a satisfying coda though and I've seen a lot worse that the genre has to offer.

reviews.author: Michael_Elliott
reviews.text: Mike (Tom Stern) gets back from Vietnam and heads to California to take over the motorcycle gang he left behind. Soon he's battling a local sheriff (Jack Starrett) who wants them to live by a certain code.

reviews.author: Marty McKee
reviews.text: It’s cops versus bikers in this exploitation picture about a disillusioned Vietnam vet who plans to organize America’s largest biker gang and really stick it to The Man. American International Pictures, jumping on the biker bandwagon created by its smash hit THE WILD ANGELS, rushed ANGELS FROM HELL into production for a spring 1968 release. Produced by Joe Solomon (THE LOSERS) and Kurt Neumann (ENTER LAUGHING) for Solomon’s Fanfare production company, it was a hit that played on double bills with other AIP films like THE MINI-SKIRT MOB and THE NAME OF THE GAME IS KILL. Despite its box office success, ANGELS FROM HELL isn’t very good, and its bubblegum soundtrack by The Peanut Butter Conspiracy and The Lollipop Shoppe…

reviews.author: NoSubculture
reviews.text: In anticipation of Jeff Nichols' new film The Bikeriders (2024), I've decided to do a deep dive into the biker film subgenre. I am currently on my fourth movie of this journey and I'm already starting to notice a lot of similarities. These films seem to share a lot of tropes. They all have similar sounding titles with "Angel," "Devil," or "Hell" being used. There's a lot of counterculture influence, there's usually a Vietnam vet somewhere in the mix, and the lead character is usually a guy who thinks he has all the answers, oh and it seems like a lot of these movies star Jack Starrett pretty much playing the same angry cop character. There's also a troubling amount…

reviews.text: The 2018 Cult Movie ChallengeWeek 23: Independent International Week--A deeply gonzo post-Easy Rider, post-Charles Manson biker film that tries to cash in on both while also getting a taste of the growing violent women/women in prison box office dollar too. But since at its heart Angels' Wild Women is an extremely shitty biker movie, of course it's starring Ross Hagen. Ol' Ross looks like he's been spending his time since Sidehackers/Hellcats living inside a whiskey flask stuffed inside an old shoe stuffed inside a trunk filled with demons stuffed inside a Hell's Angels' asshole. Okay, maybe that's a tad harsh, but damn Ross, just what exactly were you up to in the early 70s?

It starts out revving, but kind of runs out of gas halfway through but then Adamson siphons enough out of someone's tank to get this across the finish line with a biker vs. evil hippie commune brawl filmed at Spahn's Movie Ranch (a fact highlighted in the advertisements) just to add a little more tastelessness to an already unsavory genre. Regina Carrol has to have set a…

reviews.author: Nick FW
reviews.text: Angels' Wild Women isn't exactly about anything. It just has characters, and they get into predicaments. Badass biker mamas, rowdy pill poppers, a hippie love cult - yeah, you could call this a counterculture movie. We see Gary Kent as a rapist shitkicker, Al Adamson in a cameo as himself, and the Manson Family ranch as a prominent backdrop. There are as many memorable moments as there are aviator sunglasses. Top notch cult cinema.

reviews.author: b_noire
reviews.text: This had potential at the beginning--it starts off with a bunch of plotless biker scenes and a little rape revenge scene featuring the 'wild women.' All vibes and not much else, which is fine for what this is. Too bad this was yet another patchwork clickbait job because the aforementioned Wild Women don't appear nearly enough, and they aren't exactly wild. I was expecting something more akin to Faster Pussycat Kill Kill but instead everything gets bogged down by slow as molasses melodrama.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: I'm still an Adamson neophyte but if I had to define the "Adamson touch" based on the few movies of his I've seen it would be thus: Enough crazy and unpredictable shit thrown at the screen that the last thing on the viewer's mind is the fact that the plot and characters are nonexistent. His two movies with Jim Kelly are masterpieces of this formula, but Angels' Wild Women isn't quite there yet.

In an episodic manner that's being filtered through the vaguely hallucinatory perspective of an imaginative child (a style kinda reminiscent of the Bob Clark classic A Christmas Story), we're amusingly introduced to Anina's family and friends as well as the authority figures, intimidating rivals and random bystanders that she encounters each day as she tries to navigate the rocky existence of a girl with a palindrome name.

reviews.author: Brian Finch
reviews.text: The question I asked myself when watching this is, "Does hearing the other side of the conversation enhance the story in any way?" I am not sure. On one hand this short shows how two people can make a connection with one another having never even met. It makes her phone call even lonelier and filled with more despair. But on the other hand, when I re-watch Gravity, the phone call will be less enigmatic. I can no longer speculate what is happening on the other side of the radio, because the answer has already been given to me.

reviews.text: Short Drama - In the 2013 feature film "Gravity," there is a scene where astronaut Ryan Stone (Sandra Bullock) makes radio contact with someone on the ground named Angingaaq (Orto Ignatiussen), who speaks no English. In this short, writer-director Jonás Cuarón explores the scene from the other end, taking us to the Sikvivitsoq Fjord near Ilulissat, Greenland. There we see the Inuit fisherman Angingaaq make contact with Stone in the Soyuz space capsule, and he thinks her name is "Mayday."

reviews.author: JP Fournier
reviews.text: Based on the true story of two gay men trying to adopt a boy with down-syndrome during the 70s, “Any Day Now” does not present the promise of a happy story. However, this is a joy to watch. Alan Cumming is a tour de force as Rudy Donatello, a drag performer whose unfiltered smart mouth is his biggest asset as well has his worst enemy. While I knew where this story was heading, because of history, I was not expecting it to hit me as hard as this film did. Yes, it’s probably more manipulative than the average films, but this is a history lesson and message that could use a bit of skillful coloring and masterful crafting. Truly unforgettable.

reviews.author: Ian M
reviews.text: Italians and their virtuosic idea of what cinema lives and breathes. Directed by Giorgio Mariuzzo, with a great eye for the slow pace that envelops the entire film. Focusing first on the characters and second on the atmosphere that surrounds and almost destructs them. His use of widescreen framing and zooms is glorious—Italian cinema from this era perfects the art of the zoom, and particularly the close-up. Italian cinema is all about centralizing emotion, and Mariuzzo more than capably gets that across. The performances work on a great level of understated emotions; the romance bleeds within itself, both literally and figuratively, and at every turn, the emotions are detailed through silent glances and precise facial expressions, which tell the story…

The flying carpet and kaiju-like dragon totems are neat, the poorly rendered genie not so much. Christopher Lee is always a good get for your villain in a movie like this; you know he'll supply the gravitas that your wooden hero who looks…

reviews.author: Owen
reviews.text: Arabian Adventure feels like some lost chapter of a story, a distant, magical memory that you've nearly forgot. It draws you in during the very first few minutes and never lets go. The film pays homage to other previous Eastern adventure films like the Sinbad Cycle, or "The Thief of Bagdad", while still adding Kevin Connor's very unique adventure film touches to it. Everything from the set pieces to the performances scream classical adventure, it is the perfect cozy Sunday morning movie. Though it was likely a dated film, even for the time it was released, It has aged so well as a fan of fantasy movies.

Great cast of character actors, though it could really use a Vincent Price or Peter Cushing for the lead corpse. reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: Every era has an underappreciated horror-comedy that deserves a cult following. If the brightest gem of them all is 1985's Clue, then it's darling predecessor should be none other than Arnold. It's the heartwarming tale of a fresh corpse tormenting his gold-digging new bride from beyond the grave for cheating on him with Roddy Fucking McDowall, and the local constabulary are too busy pontificating on whether cemeteries come naturally foggy or if they're simply built where there's already fog. It might feel like a TV sitcom, but unlike Dark Shadows or The Munsters, Arnold doesn't shy away from the macabre. Just wait until that first kill.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Seeing this in 1956 on a big screen must have been an unreal experience. It isn’t perfect, but it is such an underrated, immersive epic that brilliantly spoke to the ambition and excitement around evolving mid-century technology (which is likely why it doesn’t speak to the voices of today). The Todd-AO 70mm format allows each shot to feel so FULL. I love the comedic theatrical staging, lavish production design, vibrant colors, creative panoramic compositions, diversity of costumes, very ‘50s cameos and, overall massive sense of scope and crowd size—yet all of that is undermined by our natural world’s most incomprehensible, staggering beauty, constantly emphasized above everything else. People nowadays should give this a fair shot and appreciate it more for what it represented.

The info those sensors gather will enable other scientists to monitor seismic activity and predict earthquakes and tidal waves more accurately. On Bridges’ team are loyal Brian Kelly, star of Flipper, and level-headed Marshall Thompson, star of another Tors TV show, Daktari. It’s like with the Bud Spencer and Terence Hill movies, I can’t imagine watching Asterix in any other language. It’s a fun time and reminded me fondly of my childhood.

So sphinxes and pyramids, while still prominent, weren't nearly as important as they were in the previous millennia in Egypt.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: A brilliantly effective Amicus anthology. While some of these films feel like a series of separate stories with a loose wraparound tying them all together - Asylum beautifully blends the two; meaning the tales of terror feel like smaller parts of a larger story. The setting is very well realised. It's a grand and imposing building, and director Roy Ward Baker even goes the extra mile in setting the scene by showcasing a series of macabre drawings which adorn the walls of the Asylum - each one depicting insanity in various forms. The four stories, written by Robert Bloch, are typically absurd. You can't blame these characters for going insane! We kick off with with some great comedy horror featuring…

reviews.text: Asylum might just lock up the award for best wraparound story in a horror anthology. As with most anthology films, the stories are hit and miss, but in Asylum’s case, the overqualified cast and sturdy craftsmanship kept me from tuning out before the next segment began.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: William Girdler lived fast, died young, and left behind a treasure trove of Kentucky-fried movies like ABBY and GRIZZLY. But he never made another one like this. A no-budget take on the “crazed woman in a nuthouse” trope that’s filtered through the stoned haze of a Rudy Ray Moore movie, ASYLUM OF SATAN is slow, but crammed with details. Papier-mâché monsters! Stick-on mustaches! Rubber spider attacks! Hooded cult killers! Actors in drag! Accepted for what it is, this movie remains a go-to for everything that was fun about pop culture’s fascination with Satanism in the early 1970s. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: It’ll just be a matter of time before William Girdler has his own reconsideration — or reckoning, if you will — in the history of cinema. If the blood feaster, Herschell Gordon Lewis, can get a section on the Criterion Channel, then look for Girdler’s one day. He was a prolific, guerrilla-filmmaking veteran of war who set out to start his own film production company with his brother-in-law, ended up in Hollywood making what is maybe the most successful Jaws ripoff to date, and over a six year period, directed nine features and wrote six, only to die a martyr at the hands of the cinema itself in a helicopter wreck in the Philippines as he was location scouting for…

reviews.author: COBB
reviews.text: If I told you about Asylum of Satan from beginning to end, you might think it's nothing more than the umpteenth variation on a more or less common plot involving the "what am I doing here" trope, an asylum, and Satanism, and you'd be right. What I think gives it a special touch is everything that peppers its development, imposing itself on the no-budget world where every choice is certainly a choice, sometimes laughable, other times bizarre, but always giving off a musty, sulfurous scent.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: A Cadillac ambulance pulls up to a sanitarium in the dark of night and delivers a "patient" on a gurney that orderlies of the sanitarium or "Asylum of Satan" carry up two flights of stairs where the patient is placed in a private room. It's cheap but effective, with a "nurse" with a weird bang that forms a circular loop on the forehead just adding another creepy element. Satanic priests in white hoods sitting around tables on the lawn while it doesn't scream terror, still manages to work its magic. Directed by William Girdler, this was his first film in 1972.

reviews.author: nosferatu47
reviews.text: Satan worshipers are so versatile in the venues in which they operate. This time it's an asylum that houses white, hooded figures that are served one egg in the shell on a plate for average meals. The facility is run by a suspicious Dr. Specter, who tends to offer up his patients to devilish deities in weekly dark ceremonies held in the basement. Asylum of Satan feels very Herschel Gordon Lewis, but with a little less blood, and more cheap f/x featuring obvious fire extinguishers blowing through wall vents, and such. But this is not HGL, it's William Girdler's first film. On the Girdler scale this doesn't even touch the cinematic highs of Grizzly or Day of the Animals, but…

reviews.text: A wild, trippy, satanic hellfest inside a creepy old asylum, with all sorts of gaslighting, mindfuckery, cultists in hooded cloaks, screaming, and the protagonist's boyfriend running around town in checkered pants shouting at people to help him find her while giving them no helpful information whatsoever. A lot of it is bland yet it's overall very delightful, and the ending is both WAY too short and SO worth waiting for

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: Even with a $5 budget, this has all of the Girdler charm in spades -- the irresistible exploitation hook, a handful of competent performances, and some inspired cheapo effects. Even at their cheapest, Girdler's movies have a quality that separates them from the rest of the trend-chasing gutter from which they sprung. There's something to be said about the central drag performance (and its ~shocking~ reveal), but I'm still not quite sure what.

reviews.author: D Edward
reviews.text: William Girdler’s earliest directorial effort, and it’s exactly what you’d expect with a title like Asylum of Satan. There’s an asylum. There’s a Satan. There’s worshipping of Satan. It can drag more than it maybe ought to, but there are some cool horror beats and grim atmosphere that I did enjoy with this one.

reviews.author: KriiLunAus
reviews.text: This movie is a colossal bore. It is like when the Greek government gave Corman permission to film on location he decided that meant he had to try to make an actual film instead of just an entertaining B-movie. It is a movie of contrasts. Beautiful locations and incredibly chintzy props and costumes. Long winded neo-Shakespearean dialogue spoken by beautiful but bad actors. Massive battle scenes shot so that you can only see half a combatant at a time. Having your Olympic wrestler protagonist grappling verbally with issues of moral philosophy and justice instead of just grappling dudes in togas to death is such a misguided choice, and ultimately not an entertaining one.

reviews.author: Karl Janssen
reviews.text: I'm predisposed toward liking this one because it features two of my favorite peplum stars: the carved-from-granite Gordon Mitchell (billed here as Mitchell Gordon) and the sexiest woman of the sixties, Chelo Alonso. It's a good thing they're both fun to watch, because the story is very slow, even by '60s B-movie standards. The descendants of Circe and Polyphemus are out to exterminate the descendants of Ulysses as retribution for his having tricked them in The Odyssey. Mitchell as Maciste (he's never called "Atlas," despite the title) volunteers to save the cute baby king. You have to wait until the final half hour for most of the fun action scenes, like Mitchell's battle with the cyclops and with former Mr. Universe Paul Wynter. There's really nothing special to set this one apart from so many other entries in the peplum genre, other than its two stars.

reviews.text: Let's start out with the fact that within a year the production team completely recast. Losing directors between entries, that happens all the time. Losing a single cast member, that can happen on occasion. Having to recast the ENTIRE cast is a bad omen. On top of that, we have even more ludicrous pandering to Randian philosophy instead of trying to tell a story, even having a point where actual conservative pundit Sean Hannity shows up AS HIMSELF to praise the fictional hero in this movie. Also, "Who is John Galt?" is a stupid catchphrase that sounds even dumber when these people try to give it meaning. The fact of the matter is this movie would have you believe being a selfish asshole is a virtue and that altruism and human compassion isn't, which says it all.

reviews.author: Adrian Zachow
reviews.text: Shot in Japanese, dubbed in poorly lip-synched English, and featuring a hero who is a corny extrapolation of Flash Gordon and Superman (both serials hugely influential), Atomic Rulers of the World ends up overcoming its B-grade nature with its earnest approach, lively plot, imaginative sets and action set pieces. Garishly attired Starman is sent to Earth to foil the plan of a fictional nation run by a slimy villain (a nation of decidedly American looking folk) with plans to destroy Japan with a nuclear device unless it surrenders. The spirit of old serials is alive and well in this. Another of many fascinating documents of Japan's attempts at dealing with their WWII defeat under the might of nuclear weapons - pacifism, xenophobia (here, warranted), and a dash of denial can all be identified as attitudes being forged here by a nation trying to move away from the past.

reviews.text: Interesting concept of adults being converted into living dolls by a crazed doll maker played by John Hoyt who operates a doll factory on the fifth floor of an office building. Even though he has miniaturized them they still have their adult personalities. However, some of them have accepted their new roles and have become content to escape from the responsibilities. Hoyt's become like a god to some of them but to John Agar and June Kenney, who want to get married, he's like science and technology that's run amok. A small girl in the Brownies comes in to the factory and you can kind of see the childhood contrast this makes which is kind of interesting. While it lasts, it's pretty sharply done, with one woman doll taking a bubble bath in a teacup while a teen girl doll sings a teener song.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Jess Franco's entry into the Bond knock-off arena is a sturdy pulp thriller that bears a surprising number of his (pre-zoom lens) trademark obsessions (a jazzy floorshow dance, of course, but also some sadism). Filmed in high contrast black and white and full of odd angles, it's also one of his better looking early films. Eddie Constantine is perhaps the least handsome Bond stand-in of them all, but he manages to be at least a bit charming even when tasked with delivering on-the-nose lines like, "How many James Bond movies have you seen?!" to his Q-equivalent. The (presumably white) English dubbers went to town on all of the Chinese and Mexican characters, so expect some winces (and laughs if, like…

I’m in the minority of liking this one quite a bit, a fun mix of sci-fi and spy movie tropes with tongue firmly in cheek and Eddie Constantine getting some great comic business as he has to juggle two corpses and a fainting love interest in his hotel room at the same time. Watching in the original French version is the only way to go, and I imagine may be why those who’ve only watched the American version are not fans of this. This is just so much fun!

reviews.author: Nathaniel Thompson
reviews.text: A visually sumptuous and often hilariously cracked sci-fi spy yarn from Jess Franco that manages to swirl together elements of James Bond, Jean-Luc Godard, Alain Resnais, and Fritz Lang among others. For some reason Stephen Thrower really trashes this one in his essential tomes on Franco, but at least in the far superior French version I thought this was ridiculously entertaining. The peculiar jokes about Chinese and Mexican characters have rubbed some viewers the wrong way, though given the larger picture of how Franco usually operates, he was probably ribbing the absurd, exaggerated racism found in spy thrillers around this time. (At least I hope he was.) Crazily underrated.

reviews.text: Livelier than Franco's later, dreamier films, Attack of the Robots starts with a bang. Then things get procedural and it begins to resemble the German krimi films of the time. Procedural maybe, but playful. The Spanish didn't take their criminal investigations too seriously. Eddie Constantine seems to be having a good time, and Sophie Hardy is adorable. As usual, Franco's black and white photography is outstanding and the smoky jazz soundtrack makes everything cinematic. We get cool costumes, stylish set designs, unconvincing robots, unconvincing fights, and I think there's some international intrigue (the plot isn't exactly cohesive). The robots seem to be controlled by their eye glasses. There is more outright comedy than I've seen since Franco's debut feature. Some…

reviews.text: Hard to see this as anything but Franco's take on Alphaville, stripping the arty wankiness from Godard’s sci-fi inflected Lemmy Caution story and doubling down on and intensifying its pulp roots by throwing more traditional eurospy elements and a whole lotta Asian caricatures into the mash. Franco's spy films have been some of my favorite discoveries of this year, and this is no different -- not quite as inspired and weird as Sadisterotica or Kiss Me Monster, but just as fun.

reviews.text: I saw a donkey walk on earth and, for a moment, it was not a donkey, but a reliquary of the suffering of this world. His eyes, big and dark, reflected nothing but mute acceptance, as if he had contemplated the essence of existence and decided to desire nothing. He was kicked, he was whipped, carried inhuman weights, but never rebelled to the point of hurting anyone. Not out of some foolish belief that no action would change anything, but from having observed the mundane for so long, that men were like this: ignorant, inattentive, brutal in their own insignificance. Audrey Rose has a decidedly mixed effect on reviewers, some love it, a lot don't. Luckily for yours truly I don't mind unsuccessful films, bad ones even, & I certainly wouldn't call Audrey Rose a bad film. I just think it's not an entirely successful one. And coming out four years after The Exorcist possibly didn't help, as the marketing of it made it seem like a new terror classic had arrived. It's not.

reviews.text: Fell asleep multiple times during the hypnotism sequence only to be awakened by the shrill screams of exasperating child star Susan Swift. I wish this had more in common with The Exorcist and The Omen, which is how it was marketed. Rather it's a lethargic bore with occasionally handsome photography and a decent performance by Anthony Hopkins. A late career dud from Robert Wise that both propagates and idealizes Hinduism and theories of reincarnation. The movie ends quoting scripture from the Bhavagad-Gita, and the author of both the screenplay and novel based this on his own "personal experience." A wet blanket movie that takes itself seriously while offering not a single memorable scare in nearly two hours.

reviews.text: While Audrey Rose isn’t Robert Wise final film, it was the last horror film he had made. His very first film was The Curse of the Cat People, and while that film goes a different direction from Cat People, it is a sequel to a famous horror film of the 40’s. In some ways, Autopsy is fairly typical genre fare; but it's taken to a new level thanks to hallucinations, solar flares and other general weirdness, which give the film a delightfully surreal atmosphere. The start of the film sets the tone - a montage of grisly suicides leads into a plot focusing on a pathologist writing a thesis on suicide, who teams up with a priest to investigate the death of his sister. The focus is always on the mystery and characters - there is not a slew of gory of murders here - and the film is rather slowly paced, but the intricate plot and well drawn characters keep things bubbling…

reviews.author: hiruko
reviews.text: Roger Corman decides to get a financial slice of Irwin Allen’s disaster success and succeeds with this perfect mimic of his own. Take the Jaws plot, replace the mayor with real estate developer Rock Hudson, make Robert Forster the chief Brody type, and finally trade a great white shark for some fluffy white powder. Millions of tons of it. And see what happens next. It’s the big weekend winter sporting event at the resort too. Some of the lousiest athletes competing in various events, including a snowmobile race straight out of a Monty Python bit, where no one can actually ride. Just falling off when going over bumps, crashing into trees, crashing through ice on a lake, crashing into each other. Continuously. It’s impressive. And of course the whole thing is wrapped nicely in a thick blanket of multiple multi connected couples drama, where if the snow doesn’t get you, the STDs will.

It's super goofy. Anthony Quinn's last movie. Apparently the film went direct to video at the time. It does seem very cheap for a Stallone film. The score was awful. The actors were very entertaining for awhile. I think Madeleine Stowe is pretty funny in parts. Stallone is well cast as the character. The script is very werid. The movie tries to hard to be a screwball comedy.

I tuned in religiously over the show's 5 seasons waiting for it to deliver the goods, but between the Prime Time Entertainment Network's dicking with the series finances and J.M.S.'s inability to tell the tale he wanted to tell, this ultimately wound up unsatisfying. Still, it provided the impetus for a slew of other sci-fi and fantasy series to delve into multi-season storytelling.

reviews.author: Ben Crew
reviews.text: Monte Hellman's films have all been 3/5 for me but I really enjoy watching them.Jack Nicholson talked about how when Spielberg and the rest of the film school generation entered Hollywood, his group resented them because he and Hellman and Corman did everything on their own.No one taught them, no school gave them equipment, they just did movies for as low of a budget as they could.I think that's why I really enjoy these Hellman movies. They're simple and made by talented people who put 100% into making them. The love for making movies radiates off the screen.A simple movie with a simple plot, but good themes and good early Jack.

reviews.text: When it comes to my horror, I like my monsters, I like my dark castles, I like my rubber bats. When there is that overt element in a film, that’s where the escapism and fantasy comes in. Watching Cat People last year was my first exposure to the more “nuanced” approach in a long while— and that opened my mind up to what I could take from a film beyond what I was accustomed to. Back from the Dead is almost within that vein of film philosophy, opting for implied horror and tension, while still giving enough of a payoff that probably suited drive-in audiences. But this one really grabbed me as an unexpected surprise, leaning into that 50s pulp-atmosphere, and…

First, she’s the proper 50s housewife Mandy, until she miscarries and then wakes up as Felicia, his devil-worshiping former wife who died six years ago. There are two hilarious things that the film glosses right over: first, he never told his current wife that he was a widower, nor that he was ever married previously; second, both he and his previous wife were apparently involved in a satanic cult, but I guess he just moved on with his life?

reviews.text: Perhaps the most interesting thing about Hugo Haas’ films is how improbably effective they are. Typically made on shoestring budgets and starring Haas himself, they’re almost always stories about a middle-aged man (Haas) and his inappropriate/doomed/misguided affection for a much younger woman. They’re also usually not very well acted — the women, always, are cast based on their looks first and their talent second (the fact that Cleo Moore starred in five of them is evidence of this), and the men often are as well — and yet, somehow, the movies end up working.

reviews.text: Surprisingly grounded for a Sundance dramedy about a struggling Los Angeles couple who turn their fights into songs (with the help of a kooky neighbor played by Fred Armisen, of course), “Band Aid” is a thin but knowing portrait of how marriages stretch, sag, and pull back together. It’s a premise that writer, director, producer, star, and lyricist Zoe Lister-Jones knows from first-hand experience, as she and husband Daryl Wein have collaborated on a number of different films together. From scrappy winners like “Breaking Upwards” to undercooked misfires like “Lola Versus,” they’ve never been shy about blurring the line between their personal and professional lives. How ironic that Lister-Jones only finds her voice now that she’s flying solo for the first time.

reviews.text: "Terror Circus," or, as the poster art blares, "Barn of the Naked Dead," is a a dull genre exercise that does not announce its genre intentions until it is far too late for its audience to care. The story of three women whose trip to Las Vegas takes a turn for the depraved when their car breaks down, the film unfolds like a crime drama as the women are abducted and bound in a remote barn. The production supports the story with no frills until horror elements appear in the tale, with the need for gore and prosthetics making itself known. Still, that switching of narrative gears does nothing to inject liveliness into the moribund piece of work.

reviews.text: Hardly anyone is dead; even fewer are naked; it delivers on the barn though in fairness. I’m a huge admirer of Alan Rudolph’s work, choosing him as one of my filmmakers whose entire filmography I’ll work through chronologically this year, but these early BA (Before Altman) pictures are tough going. Marginally more watchable than Premonition (but probably less interesting), with a good central performance from Prine and an enjoyably gonzo final ten minutes, but it’s considerably duller than any film with that title and poster should be, and there’s almost zero hint of the director Rudolph would become. Budgetary limitations can make many cinematic sins forgivable, but not how listless this is; his heart clearly isn’t in this exploitation game. Strictly for completists.

reviews.text: Baron Blood is rarely seen as one of Mario Bava's better efforts...mainly because it isn't...but I've always really enjoyed this silly gothic horror romp. The plot focuses on a young man that returns to Austria, and soon after getting there decides to recite an old incantation to bring back his ancestor; the titular Baron Blood. Chaos ensues! The film has all the usual Gothic sets and Bava really knows how to set a scene. The plot is pretty great. The central concept has shades of Lovecraft's Charles Dexter Ward, and Bava takes the story in unexpected directions; mainly the whole ghost subplot. It is a little wayward at times and is probably a little overlong but the film s never boring. Joseph Cotten hams it up nicely and I really love the look of the Baron. The cut up face, big coat and hat is great! It's not a seminal classic but it's good fun from start to finish.

Add to it some kind of 70's conspiracy storyline and you get a cinema experience that offends all of your senses and does not even provide any worthwhile accidental laughs. None-the-less, it makes for uncomfortable viewing, and what details there are are often shocking. I almost felt as though Denis had taken lessons from Breillat before making this one.

Atmospherically, its stunning.. the ghoulish Tindersticks score accompanying these dark shadowy images shot in the rain. And the elliptical editing works really well both in terms of implicating nearly everyone (except the children) and in warning us that what we are heading towards is a glimpse into the very heart of darkness. reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Dominique Strauss-Kahn infects Denis' sensual cinema, which has always had a tendency toward the dark and unnerving, but never to this extent. Even grace notes like a shot that hones in on a hand that pulls a sister close (a gesture of fierce, protective love that belies the anger in the brother's voice), or a woman looking at a flexing back pulling a dress shirt taut, are stripped of their joy, merely pauses for air before the unstoppable, brutish power of masculine capitalism destroys everyone. Tindersticks' score may well top their TROUBLE EVERY DAY work, a series of Carpenterian pulses that turn the economic engine Subor's Edouard represents into The Shape.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Every year at least one or two movies come out that traffic in the idea that revenge is a complicated ethical quagmire. This is the best and the most subtle of recent memory. Details are teased out so slowly and methodically that at several points "Which ones were the bastards?" becomes a legitimate question. It's like Night of the Hunter if every adult character was Robert Mitchum's character. Even Lilian Gish's disembodied, floating head was an accomplice. The host of this screening said that in Claire Denis' TIFF introduction of Bastards she stated that, "Redemption is an invention of the movies." It can't rain hard enough to wash away the filth and sins of the parents in this movie. Won't somebody please think of the children?

reviews.text: One of the funniest lines I remember, from an old critical review, described this camp classic something like this - ‘The most deliriously paranoid cold war film I’ve ever seen’. Back in 1967 I’m sure that was absolutely the case. But, as large scale tunneling technology advanced over the decades, the film’s premise, ironically, became more, and more plausible. And so, I really enjoyed this campy, retro sci-fi, and its now more plausible premise. At least in shallow seas and across land boarders. Also interesting is that it’s a British film, about a breakaway Chinese military, targeting the USA. So, in a way, the Anglo-alliance was in full paranoia and propaganda mode, regarding the “Yellow Peril.”

The threadbare story, which involves anthropologist Professor Sutwell's (Bob Cummings) investigation into the mating habits of American teens, serves only as a device to show off scantily clad young ones as they surf, dance, sing, throw pies, and make out. All of the regulars, including Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello, are along for the ride. For the most part, it lacks the consistent silliness of the later efforts in the series, but it's still pretty mindless. On the bright side, Cummings has some decent lines and, considering the overacting surrounding him, gives a surprisingly subdued performance.
