I doubt that's what anyone really hoped for at the time, but there we are.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: This dirt-cheap production for Roger and Gene Corman's independent Filmgroup company is the first directorial credit for Two-Lane Blacktop auteur Monte Hellman. If you wanted to do an auteurist reading, you could say that its many boring scenes of people cross-country skiing anticipate the existentialism of his later work. Credit where due: Hellman offers consistently more elegant compositions than Corman typically did on a film of this budget. Like so many drive-in potboilers of the era, this movie doesn't show its monster until the very end — presumably because it's embarrassingly cheap, but frankly, I'd much rather look at a cheap monster for 65 minutes than a bunch of people talking.

The last trip to the presented Blood Island, "Beast of Blood" falls into a the same categories of successes and failures as the films in the series before it. Way too long of screentime for the level of context it is delivering drags it down but when the film goes all out in schlocky horror it wins. reviews.author: Corey
reviews.text: Severin’s Fear in the Philippines closes out with a substantial bang, concocting a devilish brew of mad science from a nonsensical, but entirely gratifying return to Blood Island. Deep-red gashes, John Ashley’s dodged-perishing via ship explosion, Celeste Yarnall’s inexplicably sensual “journalism:” Beast of Blood erupts within seconds, blasting brass over a most wonderfully barely-70s credit sequence before embarking on another voyage to an island of diabolical experimentation—part Stockholm Syndrome, part third time’s a charm, Eddie Romero’s solo directorial outing proves there’s an abundance of guts somewhere in this series’ rotting corpse, imbuing the tired seams with just the right amount of camp, debonair, misery, and disgust. Quite the foray into headless serum siphoning for 1970–grotesque, but in a buttery popcorn fashion that functions as a proper film before highlight reel/last-five-minutes climax.

reviews.text: Famously written on the fly after production had already begun, Beat the Devil is a unique result of studio filmmaking—unique because, unlike other transparent b-roll, it's actually quite fun. At times the plot feels like a story being told by someone out on a bender, jumping heedlessly from one event to the next without thinking about how they'll land or where they're going—they wanna go to Africa, but the ship is broken, oh no! so they decide to take a plane instead, but they drive their luggage into the ocean, oh no! so they go back to the boat, but the boat capsizes, oh no! etc. etc.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Truly feels like a film being put together before our very eyes, even 60+ years after it was actually (somehow) made. It really makes you value the time most of the personnel involved, from Huston and Bogart on down to the rest of the cast and crew, spent in the studio trenches, since this is every Hollywood spy thriller to date filtered through a proto-New-Wave sense of improvisational playfulness. The best studio product of the 30s and 40s makes you feel like the creative process was so streamlined and efficient that the directors, writers, and actors could probably just make a movie up on the spot, and this proves that sensation to be accurate. Kind of.

reviews.text: A beautiful, sad and thoughtful exploration of masculinity, ego, regret, and of jealousy so deep-rooted that it can destroy lives. Its almost entirely plotless, has hardly any dialogue and is slowly paced; everything is so magnificently understated and subdued to great, poetic effect. The performances are naturalistic and by its hypnotic visuals and rhythm (those training drills really have an almost musical feel to it), and its great use of music, it becomes a real treat with an ending so sad but so sublime.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Claire Denis loosely and beautifully blends Melville's navy court-martial/mutiny novella and her own childhood as the daughter of a French civil servant in colonized West Africa into a strange and sensual non-linear post-colonial ballet of repressed desire, austere meditation, and tactical military ritual turned staged homoerotic opera. One where a jealous quasi-love triangle between Denis Lavant's French Foreign Legion sergeant stationed in Djibouti, his CO that he loves and respects, and the new recruit who he feels is stealing his superiors affection away from him; a crime the kid is then nearly killed for during an absurd, clearly personal-vendetta motivated banishment-punishment that ends in the sergeant's present day expulsion to normal civilian life he's having trouble adjusting to.

reviews.text: Every single film by renowned filmmaker Asghar Farhadi has wonderfully captured a certain section of Iranian society & Beautiful City is no different. The title referring to a juvenile detention center, this film tells the tale of A'la, whose friend Akbar has just turned eighteen which means he will be executed soon for the crime he committed two years ago. Knowing that Akbar has repented enough in the two years, has a good heart & doesn't deserve this punishment, A'la gets out of that place & later, accompanied by Akbar's sister Firoozeh, tries his best in persuading the victim's father to spare the boy from certain death.

reviews.author: Varghese
reviews.text: Every film director should take a long hard look at Iranian Cinema. Considering the restraints they have at their disposal they always manage to carve out slice of life dramas replete with every facet of life albeit brimming with rich characterizations and entertaining as well.Life is a dilemma and Farhadi knows how to use it. Making a decision is one of the hardest things a human being has to do.Does seeing someone get killed make you indirectly happy even though your own life will not gain anything from it? The director perfectly understands how the human psyche works.There will always be discrimination between men and women but in small touches one can see the rebellious spirit prevailing thru the individuals…

The film acknowledges this tension in having Belle and the Prince discuss such similarity and in her clear hesitancy towards this development, something she initially says she is disappointed in before saying she is not. reviews.text: I'm going to give this a mild recommendation to vintage horror fans.First, this is of some interest due to being Jack Pierce's final film. The Beast makeup is very similar to Chaney's Wolf Man, but with bigger hair. So that's cool.Second, the story deviates from the familiar fairy tale and instead turns this into a gothic werewolf story of sorts. The vibe here is very much in line with stuff like Corman's Poe films, or Twice Told Tales. So you've got your creepy castles and cobwebbed dungeons and angry torch-carrying villagers. It's also got the same sleepy pace as those other films, so a certain amount of patience is required.

reviews.author: Matt Lambert
reviews.text: An unexciting take on the beauty and the beast tale, it's basically a G-rated werewolf picture without the mood and horror. I found this fascinating since this is the last directorial effort by Edward L. Cahn just before he died the following year. After pumping out nothing but westerns, crime noirs, and sci-fi B-movies for two decades I can't wrap my mind around why he wanted to do this. This is also his first movie in color, and it looks pretty good all things considered, with lavish low budget production value. I really would have liked to have seen what Cahn could have produced in the 60s decade. Would he have continued on with off the cuff projects like this or double back to making 10 westerns a year in his house?

reviews.text: Decent troubled teen/JD ensemble piece, the partly cloudy West Coast hit to the meatgrinder of The Blackboard Jungle (mostly as this one’s largely about social standing, with no race involved other than whites). Dick Clark is a caring new teacher in an uncaring high school (student pop 1,000 and appearances kept up), and his baggage (parenting an orphaned nephew, football glory days ended by tragedy) bolsters his sympathies towards his students (greaser hood Michael Callan, young woman in trouble Tuesday Weld, naïve and passive Warren Berlinger). Things come to a head as you’d expect, but the story is told with some care, and Clark is young and hungry enough to give depth and hope to a tired role.

reviews.text: Adapted (I understand loosely) from John Farris's early novel Harrison High, this is a high school delinquent movie the Paul Wendkos way. His mastery of camera movement, chiaroscuro lighting and multiple story threads results in a minor film but one that bests Richard Brooks and Blackboard Jungle. A "problem movie" that doesn't sacrifice lustiness and welcome jolts of Noir adrenaline, in particular a wayward youth's involvement in one botched nocturnal heist and a climactic knife fight in a classroom lit only by slatted lunar streetlamp and a glowing aquarium dense with scrambling fish like all those cracks in a Deadwood whorehouse wall. Dick Clark should be commended for his likability and effort to give an impassioned performance, and the rest…

It gets bogged down in the subplots like a romance and the various travails of the kids, so it ends up being a bit of a slog to get through. It’s an interesting look at the era’s JD anxieties, though.

reviews.text: The transcendent dominance of the violent tone in contrasting light and shadow transforms the beautiful artificiality of the setting in a darkly poetic portrait with a high tendency to capture continuous allegorical characteristics of the abuse of power over the defenseless, counterproductively the almost religious connotations are compacted in a narrative that tries to make the whole film work as a parable, focusing more time on the less functional, narratively speaking. But, who am I kidding, this film has a terrifyingly machiavellian Boris Karloff, frenetic and always entertaining playing a tyrannical character, and certainly, the b-movie elegance produced by Val Lewton adds that touch of atmosphere enhanced by subtlety unified with a menacing, impenetrable darkness. The irreplaceable cinematography by the underrated, assiduously effective Nicholas Musuraca is an essential ingredient that engenders an eerie visual purity, intense expression and skillful dexterity in creating a disorienting state of mind with prodigious cinematic lighting.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The final onscreen text suggests mental health facilities have improved since the time this film was set, and while that is true, it's an exaggeration to suggest our mental health systems (especially in America) are adequate to the task. Nevertheless, the suggestion of change was enough to quicken the heart as Lewton, Robson, and the usual team took advantage of the horror movie genre to homage Edgar Allen Poe, draw from William Hogarth's imagery, and kinda also reference Freaks. I don't know if anything other than Hogarth was intentional, but certainly the ending invokes Poean horror directly.

reviews.text: I’m going to call this untethered gothic. It has a lot of the hallmarks of the genre: family secrets, inheritances, big houses, vibrant colours, decay, perverse attractions, rolling fog. But it’s also a film filed with secrets, where things aren’t clarified or explained or given reason to. And I’m not convinced a re-watch would reveal them. I think it was designed that way. Which kind of makes so much of it down to atmosphere. But when it’s as macabre and dreamlike and beautiful and uncomfortable as this, I don’t mind it at all.

reviews.text: I miss Eurohorror. "Bell from Hell" delivered on that sweet spot of Gothic perversion, family secrets, and gruesome imagery—that effectively used a slaughterhouse. It's so repellant. The screams will haunt you. Their energy permeates this entire film. It's hazy. Dusty. It guts the melodrama into a mad-character study that could pair well with other broken momma's boys like "Hatchet for the Honeymoon" (1970) and "‎Star of David: Beauty Hunting" (1979). The plot is fractured as it bends back with flashbacks and summons the surreal (three sisters and their mother waiting at the door). Jean Rollin's films - and even Jess Franco - are prettier. Bluer and greener. Brighter. Less concerned with inner and outer rot. There is no god here;…

(1962) proved anything, is that the horror genre suited Joan Crawford perfectly, even if it was low budget horror that opened its arms to Hollywood has been royalty, as David Kalat writes, “Crawford had it particularly tough. Cue cat fights, solitary confinement and an eventual prison escape. And yet underneath her apparent toughness Michaels displays a vulnerability that comes out whenever she observes fellow inmate Nora (Peggy Knudsen) interact together with her lawyer fiancé (Tom Drake) who is idealistic enough in a boy scout kinda way to want to change the system but also so dull and useless that he never even managed to protect his own sweetheart from the penitentiary after she took the wrap for her brother.

reviews.text: This might have made a pretty good 30 minute Twilight Zone episode, and (though it’s a remake) I suppose it should get some credit for having been made in 1944, but it’s quite creaky and at 112 minutes far too long. It takes almost an hour just to get to the point where the people on this ship realize they’re dead, suffering through overly wordy scenes and some pretty stiff acting. Some of the afterlife judgment is interesting (even if predictable), e.g. Sydney Greenstreet’s Examiner character dispassionately chastising a rich businessman who thinks he can continue to push people around with money which no longer has value, but others not so much, and there is a heavy dose of moralistic sermonizing. The premise is interesting, but there’s no depth to the examination of life here, or depth to these characters. Eleanor Parker is engaging in the melodramatic ending scene, if you can make it that far.

reviews.author: Silversaxophone
reviews.text: Tedious fantasy labours over its moral points, which are trivial at best, and show a disdain to those who sacrificed and lost their lives in WWII. Its unconvincing spiritual basis appears to be Catholicism, not that it really matters — it is just another reason to dislike the film. It is a remake of Outward Bound, which I have not seen, but the presentation is drab and dully theatrical. Surprisingly, the cast is top tier, so somebody at Warner Brothers was invested in the concept; but it is one of those oddities that appeared occasionally in a time of stressful uncertainty — films such as A Guy Named Joe, Here Comes Mr Jordan and Once Upon A Time, all of which are earnest, silly and mostly dreadful.

reviews.author: PUNQ
reviews.text: Sutton Vane's play Outward Bound was always a slow sentimental journey. But it's one that touches your heart, if you let it. With it's sappy and mysterious approach to the topic of death, you get a alternative philosophical route to understanding the fears and aftermath of dying. I really appreciate the first movie adaptation, Outward Bound (1930) with Leslie Howard, but with that one coming out so early in sound era, it suffers from the technical limitations of the time, so this more ambitious update 14 years later with John Garfield was a welcome remake to get a proper feel of the source material.

reviews.author: Zynab
reviews.text: Kind of incredible that Arch Oboler came out with this scary ’losing my life to insanity’ almost-noir in 1945. The depiction of struggle with serious mental illness is campy & expressionist yet disconcertingly realistic in some aspects. There are a couple scenes in which Joan (Phyllis Thaxter in what I now consider her best role) is experiencing frightening auditory hallucinations that really got to me. A distorted version of her own voice tells her horrible things about herself and to commit violent acts. She is hounded to exhaustion by the voice, driven to run away from her home & loved ones and sabotage her chances not just for happiness but for survival.

The director, Arch Oboler, also had a background in radio dramas and the extreme melodrama of the story in slightly over 60 minutes does show a good effort on his part. She settles across country, where she eventually meets Eric, a kind man she wants to love, but is afraid to. But that's far from the worst of it, as the voice, which she thought she'd been rid of, returns, and will try harder than ever to ruin her life.

reviews.author: La Cinémathèque française
reviews.text: Eddie Romero est né le 7 juillet 1924 à Dumaguete aux Philippines d'un père ambassadeur et d'une mère institutrice. Très jeune il s'associe avec Gerardo De Leon pour qui il écrit des scénarios. Il passe ensuite à la réalisation et à la production. Il fut un des metteurs en scène les plus productifs du cinéma de série philippin d'après-guerre, enfilant les bandes d'aventures ou d'horreur avec une persistance frôlant l'admiration.Deux ans après The Beast of the Yellow Night, Eddie Romero réalise l'étonnant Beyond Atlantis, variation originale sur les conventions du cinéma d'aventure exotique, co-écrite notamment par Stéphanie Rothman et toujours coproduit par John Ashley. Un titre tout aussi révélateur de son talent, de sa versatilité et de son imagination.…

reviews.text: Great Value hypnofuck possession flick that feels like a drug-laced beverage on a sweltering August afternoon. Beyond the Door is exactly what would happen if, one day, The Exorcist and Rosemary’s Baby dropped a bunch of acid and proceeded to have weird, kinky sex on the synthetic shag rug on the living room floor of the former’s dusty San Francisco apartment. That song in the opening credits is as groovy a demonic soul train line as you’ll find and things spiral into madness from there with poorly dubbed, foul-mouthed, Campbell’s Pea Soup-sipping kiddies; head-plugged, puking, evil possessed mommy; porno ‘stache papa and a bobbled up, bogged down and boozy Richard Johnson. reviews.text: This low-budget schlockfest tries to pass off a guy in a moth-eaten gorilla suit as a menacing Sasquatch, kidnapping buxom '70s babes to propagate the Bigfoot bloodline. A couple of curvy women get snatched by hairy beasts in the woods, while a ragtag crew of small-town heroes bumbles through a rescue mission. John Carradine’s traveling salesman is the film’s saving grace. He’s a sleazy, fast-talking huckster peddling who-knows-what, stealing every scene with his gaunt face and theatrical drawl. You can tell he’s slumming it, probably to pay off a bar tab, but his charisma almost makes you forget the plot’s absurdity. The Bigfoot “family” angle is pure exploitation gold: hairy monsters with a thing for busty captives, aiming to breed a new generation of shag-carpet cryptids. Still, if you’re a Bigfoot flick connoisseur, it’s cheesy enough to be watchable.

For fans of gooey shit only.

The cloaks of stiff power and romantic nihilism are equally deceptive and fallacious.

reviews.text: Dan Duryea as masked rider stagecoach bandit Black Bart, tussling his way through the California Gold Rush with Yvonne De Carlo and Jeffrey Lynn. I associate Duryea and De Carlo with film noir, which makes this Universal western play like a hardboiled crime flick transplanted to the nineteenth-century frontier. Western journeyman director George Sherman sketches exciting stagecoach robbery action paintings, but there's only so much one can do with a script this hackneyed. Utterly forgettable, then, though Luci Ward and Jack Natteford's clinker-filled screenplay does muster one great line: "Virtue is its own reward" in the mouth of champion slimeball Duryea. Incidentally, De Carlo plays Lola Montez; I wonder if Max Ophüls ever saw this.

reviews.text: Louis Malle could never be accused of making the same film over and over. Black Moon sees him experimenting again, this time in fantasy fairytale territory. It's apparently meant to be some sort of riff on Alice in Wonderland. We begin with a young girl trying to escape a gender war (literally a war between men and woman) and happening on a farmhouse in the middle of a forest, filled with talking animals and a breastfeeding old lady. Malle was evidently going for a surreal vibe and a feeling that anything could happen, and the film achieves that but in doing so abandons any notion of an actual point, while the constant spontaneity starts to get tiresome after a while.…

reviews.author: cuckoochanel
reviews.text: In Louis Malle’s sensual, surrealist fairytale, Black Moon, he eschews any formal narrative structure in the service of a reflexive behavioral experiment. “A film about touch,” Black Moon is a sensorial feast of rich texture, color and sound in which scrappy teenager Lily (Cathryn Harrison) escapes a ruthless war of the sexes, absconding the fray through breathtaking woods and idyllic countryside until she reaches an enchanted mansion untouched by the effects of the apocalyptic outside world. She meets a host of characters whose mysterious behavior, along with her own intuitive responses, form the amoebic surrogate for a conventional plot.

reviews.author: Cinematic Underdogs
reviews.text: Blissfully Yours is blissfully sensual. In fact, it is so sensual I watched it a second time without the subtitles off just to revel in the oscillatory intonations of high-pitched Thai, the serene rustling of leaves, the hypnotic buzzing of insects, the mesmeric gurgling of the stream, the dissonant whirring of machinery. Conflating the physical and metaphysical, the spiritual and everyday, the ordinary and extramundane, the inhabited landscapes of rural Thailand are depicted by the film as suspended in a space of contradictions: a space where bucolic and urban forces collide, where ancient animism coexists alongside contemporary rationalism, where naturalistic rituals of timelessness intermesh with the regimented customs of hyper-capitalist modernity.

reviews.text: Wacko shocker Blood and Lace is caught somewhere between the tacky, suggestive '60s and the full-blown sleaze of the '70s. Although that might ordinarily signal a dull compromise, one-and-done director Philip S. Gilbert got the mix of tease and tension exactly right. After an opening POV murder (way pre-Halloween), we meet protagonist Ellie (Melody Patterson), a twentysomething youngster who spends her first minutes onscreen with her voice conspicuously dubbed by June Foray. Ellie's mother, the beloved town tramp, was clawhammered in that first scene, so overly-concerned cop Vic Tayback deposits her at a shoddy orphanage for adult-looking teens run by onetime Oscar winner and It's a Wonderful Life star Gloria Grahame. The sour old biddy starves her wards, chains them…

reviews.author: STEVEN
reviews.text: Blood and Lace is one of those slasher films that hit before the golden age and totally twists in on itself with a nasty attitude. I admire earlier works like these, because there weren't really any established genre conventions other than the mystery monster and their victims, meaning that there was emphasis on the unsolved murder and detective plot. It's a good-looking feature, released as a pre-PG horror event for damn near anybody to dig into. Somewhat sleazy, but not entirely, and a fascinating look at the transition between two distinct decades. I liked it!

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: A prominent feature of the Bud Spencer / Terrence Hill slapstick are aggressive soundtracks. It's quite common for a musical piece to reappear every two minutes, so that even if the plots degenerate into seemingly random situational brawls, the reoccurring music simulates a forward motion in plot. For what amounts to rapid-fire Three Stooges prat falls, these musical motifs play up the absurdist tendencies of the humour, light hearted nature of the works, and can function as a comedic punch themselves (needle drop as running gag). Instrumentals make for the quickest paced pictures, while ones with simple lyrics repeated ad nauseam can take on surreal qualities - SuperTrooper being the most prominent offender. Enter Guido & Maurizio De Angelis' FANTASY. The…

reviews.author: PacificNil
reviews.text: "Der Bomber" erschien in Deutschland 3 Monate vor "Rocky III - Das Auge des Tigers" (Stallone 1982), in Italien 2 Monate nach dem dortigen Filmstart. Trotz dieses guten Timings markiert dieser Film endgültig den Niedergang der Spencer/Hill-Komödien, auch wenn Terence Hill hier nicht mitspielt. Denn der Tatsache zum Trotz, dass der Film immerhin an letzter Stelle der Top 10 der erfolgreichsten Filme des Jahres 1982 auftaucht, sind die Zuschauerzahlen der Plätze 3-10 geradezu erbärmlich im Vergleich zu früheren Jahren - in denen oft Filme des Duos auf Platz 1 oder 2 standen. Nicht unschuldig daran ist Michele Lupo, der die Komödien infantilisierte und in seinem Stil sehr betulich wirkt. In den Achtzigern wandte man sich nach zu vielen Lupo-Filmen von den "Prügelklamotten" ab und auch heute gelten fast alle Filme dieses Regisseurs als schwache Beiträge zum Werk Spencers und/oder Hills. Eine launige Tanzszene mit Bud bringt den Film gerade noch in den Durchschnittsbereich.

It's a big man vs. little man political fable that shifts between the seedy underbellies and the ivory towers of New York City but never finds the spark that promotes itself from a colourless mystery to a cerebral shocker.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: It is with an eye on the style of the narrative, rather than on the subjective attitude of the director to the genre, that I will finally choose my epithet. I say freely of the westerns I have yet to name—the best in my view—that they are “novelistic.” By this I mean that without departing from the traditional themes they enrich them from within by the originality of their characters, their psychological flavor, an engaging individuality, which is what we expect from the hero of a novel … The best example of this “novelization” of the western from within is provided by Edward Dmytryk in Broken Lance (1954) … a western that is subtler than the others with more individualized characters and more complex relationships but which stays no less rigidly within the limits of two or three classic themes.

Als Horst-Wendlandt-Produktion versteht sich der Film auch als Parodie auf Karl-May-Filme und besitzt einige sehenswerte Comedy-Setpieces, von denen eines, in dem sich Bud Spencer vergeblich bemüht, sich schlafenzulegen, in den deutschen Kinos nicht zu sehen war - allerdings jetzt auf Bluray enthalten ist. reviews.text: In reading about Spaghetti westerns, one recurring theme is that the Italians - with memories of their second world war loss still in mind, strongly identified with the beaten Confederacy in their recreations of the American west. The Good, The Bad and The Ugly - with its prison camp - is one of the only obvious examples I've come across, usually seeing veterans from both sides of the Civil War, with narrative indifference in assigned uniforms. California, however, wears its "southern pride" on its sleeve. Like his earlier Blood on a Silver Dollar, Giuliano Gemma is once again a Confederate soldier who finds himself in the north at the Civil War's conclusion. Initial scenes show the desperate situations the southern…

reviews.text: While California has some action in it, it's more about the period of rootlessness and its characters who are wandering through it in a muddy landscape in the aftermath of the Civil War. With Giuliano Gemma as California, who takes the name Michael Random which he applies to himself when asked his name. Random, the name and the character, nicely encapsulates the mood of drifting through this world. With Miguel Bose as Willy Preston a young ex-confederate soldier who befriends California, plus William Berger shows up later as Preston's father, this feels like Django from 1967 with that pervasive cold muddy semi-sadistic vibe but with more warmth and emotion. Second half of the 70s Italian westerns like this and Keoma showed the depth of the genre. Definitely worth checking out.

I might have to watch it again to be sure, but this could be a great film.

reviews.author: Rod Sedgwick
reviews.text: An extremely compassionate biopic observation on a agonized artist, as laid out with minimalist execution by Bruno Dumont. Juliette Binoche delivers an incredibly tortured performance as the titular Camille Claudel as we spend time with her in the asylum she is imprisoned in, against her will and with broken soul. She spends most of her time trying to escape the bellowing and wailing inmates, detaching herself from them, wishing to not be associated with their kind, yet it seems that they are all drawn to her caged spirit, and take pity on her grieving, even when she is pushing them away. She yearns for her brother to return and hear her case, even if he is the one who put…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Attempts to define Camille as victim of patriarchal religious society but cannot help but define her in general in relation to the men of her life. The opening text scrawl identifies her as the sister of a famous writer and the student/mistress of Rodin, and Dumont's camera speaks for Binoche even when she is isolated. The use of actual mental patients might have been an attempt at honesty, but instead it feels like a self-conscious realism fetish borne out through exploitative medium-close-ups that linger without any human insight on their faces. Broadly speaking, Dumont's rigidly centered frames speak to how unwilling he is to actually delve into the madness. Binoche is captivating (she's Binoche), but the self-satisfaction of this venture is suffocating.

reviews.author: Deaner50
reviews.text: I watched another film about sculptor Camille Claudel. This time portrayed by Juliette Binoche. Picture this winter 1915. Camille is confined by her family to an Asylum, in the south of France. She patiently waits for a visit from her brother. This movie is not for everyone. It has a great committed performance by Juliette Binoche. It takes place in a Insane Asylum the whole time. The extras and supporting actors are all super believable as fellow patients. It's a perspective of Camille's personal hell. The movie doesn't give the audience any kind back story about her past. It's a dark and kind of dour film. It is well made. I think I prefer the other Camille Claudel film to this one. This is one is a bit of a bummer.

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: This is a monstrous tale about the early stages of Camille Claudel’s incarceration in a mental institution. She’s clearly at her wit’s end, but is she insane? Immediately following the death of her father, her surviving family have committed her, and now she’s desperate to be released. She’s far more lucid than the other patients, and if she shows signs of paranoia, and is prone to outbursts, it’s hardly surprising. She would remain in the asylum for nearly 30 years until her death.

reviews.author: Julian (Seeking Film)
reviews.text: When a male artist exhibits some form of mental instability, the world is quick to label it a byproduct of genius, a necessary trade-off for the offerings they bring unto the world. When a woman exhibits such tendencies, the general wisdom, even in rationalizing the genius buried beneath the mania, is to institutionalize her; a tortured male genius is left alone, but a tortured female genius is locked away. This isn't the entire angle with which Bruno Dumont approaches Camille Claudel, 1915, but it's certainly a latent reality that becomes unmistakably clear the longer the film goes on.

His industrial background gives him a kind of flat, cheap realism and focus on the tangibility of locations/architecture that he weaponizes to completely disorienting ends with an experimental, psychological horror style that is gothic, eerie, and palpably harsh and hostile feeling. At others, however, it approaches awful, marred by hacky, poetry-101-deep dialogue, a completely impenetrable narrative, and wildly variable performances. reviews.text: I was hoping this forgotten early seventies' private detective movie would be a real gem, especially given neo-noir's place within New Hollywood cinema. Unfortunately, Chandler was quite bad. If the film is known for anything, it's being taken over by the studio who cut the material down to ribbons at the last minute. That's unfortunate and it's definitely a problem but I'm also not sure the original vision would have been much better. Director Paul Magwood lacks any cinematic flair. reviews.text: Still the best film ever made about 9/11 -- about the 21st century -- Cloverfield is an unparalleled expressionist masterpiece. People talked about how it ripped its "don't show the monster" technique from Jaws, but it's closer to Lovecraft than anything else. Furthermore, it's an idea wholly indebted to the film's own era. We're afraid of what we don't know, what we can't see. Films like War of the Worlds come close to touching on post-9/11 anxieties so potently, but the first-person perspective gives Cloverfield the edge. Putting us in a single subjective point-of-view accentuates the terror (emphasis on terror) of everything we can't see or understand. The uncontrolled images create these chaotic spaces and incomprehensible geographies. It's an event…

Frank Lovejoy and his world-weary toad voice gives a strange performance as the title character. The screenplay is by Daniel Mainwaring (Out of the Past; Invasion of the Body Snatchers), who skillfully and subtly plays up the HUAC blacklist resonances in the dramatic innocent-on-trial climax. The dispassionate direction in Cinemascope is by R.G. Springsteen.

The prison setting includes Millard Mitchell as Ford's cellmate. It's just one of those movies that's got the talent, plus hardly any of it's wasted. Columbia Pictures, thank you. reviews.author: brotherdeacon
reviews.text: It's not for everyone, but if anti-authoritarian mega-violence and full-throttle biker action scratch your itch, Crazy Thunder Road may just be for you. Although rather mindless and Manga-Male throughout, it's still an incredible debut film from student director Gakuryū Ishii. The technical level in action choreography, camera movement, lo-budge production design, editing and rock score, leaves nearly all biker films in its dust. Of course, if you appreciate characterization, thematic modulation, cogent plot, or a briefing in societal ethics--I'd look elsewhere. Then again, If you're down with Japanese punk, or the DYI cyber-punk of George Miller's Road Warrior, or even Mitsuo Yanagimachi's early Bōsōzoku documentary Godspeed You Black Emperor, then maybe this is the spit-in-your-eye scripture of alienation/retribution you've been searching for.

reviews.text: This anarchic punk mash-up of The Warriors, Mad Max, and proto-Deadbeat By Dawn was director Gakuryu Ishii’s graduation project. Paving the way for Akira and cyberpunk in one frenetic swoop, Crazy Thunder Road is a low-budget storm of anti-establishment revolt and social commentary, as a nationalistic militia tries to aim and groom the rage of clashing biker gang youths.

reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: Often hailed as Japan's Mad Max, Crazy Thunder Road becomes all the more impressive the more you learn about its production. Being a graduation project by director Gakuryû Ishii, it may be a narrative mess but the highly experimental style and limitless rockabilly energy produced a movie that radiates of pure aggression. There's a rough and ready charm to the effects and Kinji Fukasaku-influenced action, often drawing comparisons to Fukasaku's own anti-establishment protagonists with added grunge, grim and neon lights. The soundtrack is honestly my favourite part of the film, using songs by Japanese bands of the time in a near musical sense, it's combined with frantic editing and heightened emotions that immerse you completely within its context. Fast-paced, quick-witted and brilliantly stylised Crazy Thunder Road points toward a new style of genre filmmaking even if that direction is somewhat confused in execution.

reviews.author: Bob McCully
reviews.text: Another trip through Gakuryu Ishii's back-catalogue and I must say this one was a little underwhelming. Ishii takes an early stab at bombastic stylization with this biker-gang-flick, total warzone antics as these leather-clad tribes duke it out over a bouncy punk-rock score. It's pretty chaotic and initially I got a nice rugged jolt from it, but I eventually found myself wading through the plot looking for something to bite my teeth into. The constant brawls are shot so franticly that they feel more like zany mosh-pits than brutal violence, an element that drains the much-needed angst from what should be a gnarly ride.

In my opinion, the main problem is that it doesn’t move along quickly, so these longer three stories don’t go bang-bang-bang (yes, that’s a thing) like the five shorter stories from the previous film. Supposedly there WERE to be five tales but two were cut for budgetary purposes. Trim these three down, add in two more short ones and this may have had that magic.

reviews.text: It amazes me how Bergman recontextualizes the color red. This is not a film fraught with danger, with hellish landscapes, nor a film that is frantic or fiery. It is a film of deep, powerful emotion, but the hue Bergman uses is blood red, a deep crimson that would otherwise suggest horrors. Instead, we get drama. Though there is a hint of supernatural, and though there is a moment of what constitutes Bergman's version of body horror, this film takes the color red and turns it into something other filmmakers would use sepia for.

reviews.text: Look, I know it’s cliche to compare this thing to Gremlins, but like…come on…it’s pretty much just Gremlins. A lighthearted horror-comedy about a bunch of silly little delinquent alien furballs terrorizing simple middle America townsfolk? They get hungry and you aren’t supposed to let them eat or else things get worse? They have sharp teeth and an evil laugh and roll around in balls like Sonic the Hedgehog on bath salts? It’s Gremlins. Well, except for the silly ass shape-shifting Ravager-looking extraterrestrial bounty hunters. That’s certainly an added flavor. As is that ‘Power of the Night’ song which someone somewhere thought was so good they had to play it like eight times throughout the movie. Sure could’ve used a hell of a lot more action, though. Less antagonistic porcupine behavior, more devouring young Billy Zane in a barn. Notes to live by for any movie.

reviews.text: Second sequel to the 1986 original relocates the action from smalltown Grover's Bend to some generic apartment building, and suffers quite a loss in quality. I'm not suggesting they should have done exactly the same plot as Critters 1 & 2 again; but this really feels lightweight and pointless. The film is slow to get going, the first Critter attack isn't until 25 minutes in, which is a fair time to wait considering the whole thing is barely just 80 minutes long. The body count is rather low and there's no real stakes. The Critters themselves are once again the major highlight and there's a few decent attack scenes, though too many where they just sit around waiting to be shot. It never grinds down to all out boredom but this is watered down Critters and it lacks the charm and fun factor of the original films.

reviews.text: Sometimes it's the unheralded films that make a difference. In the summer of 1947 RKO released Crossfire, a tight murder thriller attacking Semitic prejudice, which also happens to be the first film in which the word "Jew" was uttered on the American screen. It was a hit both critically and financially. At the end of that year, 20th Century Fox released Gentleman's Agreement, a more sober, lengthy and worthy treatment of the same topic. Despite five Oscar nominations (including Best Picture, Best Director and Best Supporting Actress), Crossfire was totally shut out of awards the following spring, due to the catastrophic entanglement of its producer and director, Adrian Scott and Edward Dmytryk, with the House Un-American Activities Committee. Gentleman's Agreement…

As a film of investigation the same story is repeated many times and new details slowly emerge. The mystery plot isn't that deep but the execution is engaging. A big theme of the film of anti-Semitism, and there's a long dialogue scene that pushes anti-hate and anti-racism sentiments. It is very clunky, but the message is strong. reviews.author: Will Menaker
reviews.text: "I was once full, but what was inside me is outside now,” A former psychology student obsessed with mesmerism, turned amnesiac gets a series of totally normal and sane people to commit murder simply by confounding them by not answering their questions, talking in circles, smoking a cigarette and asking them "who are you? Tell me about yourself." If this was just a movie about serial murder via hypnotism it wouldn't be one of my all time favorites, but Kurosawa does something far creepier and harder to get a handle on: an epidemiological portrait of the howling void at the center of an entire society and the cauldron of violence simmering beneath the veneer of a compliant politeness. Has one of my favorite last shots in any movie ever.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: A work almost too disquieting: Procedural pushed to obsession pushed to psychosis. Starts as a seeming vision of 90's Tokyo as a city of corpses and interrogation rooms, but even as it does work on sociological levels, (similar to Pulse, Kurosawa uses genre trappings to have us reflect on present spaces and objects) it's a film of the psyche first and foremost. I can't think of a movie that feels more scarring. Even reflections on voyeurism & cinema: by desiring to understand evil we risk getting to close to it, and if we get too close to evil we will become evil. Even as we travese physical spaces we enter psychological ones, like Mamiya's cell or the abandoned house. And when these spaces intercut, even a cup of water is terrifying.

reviews.text: As I mentioned with Pulse, one of Kiyoshi Kurosawa's best traits as a filmmaker is that his presentation of material has a lack of an emphatic expression to it. The shibui nature of his filmic style, as Bordwell suggests, offers us all the narrative information in the frame necessary, but rarely highlights its relative importance. The rigorousness of this formula thus puts an indelible amount of faith in the spectator to become involved in the narrative, finding horror in commonplace frames that don't tell us to find horror.

reviews.text: In 1977, 20th Century Fox had two science fiction films slated for release. One of them, Damnation Alley, which starred George Peppard and Jan-Michael Vincent as ragtag nuclear war survivors who are driven by necessity to leave their military installation and travel across the country in a sturdy all-terrain vehicle, was the expensive big-budget hopeful. Despite a number of problems during the production, studio executives plowed forward, confident that this movie, which was directed by Jack Smight (Airport 1975, Midway) and based on the Roger Zelazny novel of the same name, would be a blockbuster of epic proportions, and that it would be a game changer in the world of popular cinema.

I mean you've got glowing green skies, giant mutant scorpions, killer cockroaches stripping the flesh off people, rapey weirdos with sores all over their face, and dudes traversing the wasteland in badass supertrucks. That all adds up to a good time, as far as I'm concerned. Just wish all that stuff was in a better movie. But hey, I still had fun rewatching this with Jozlyn.

reviews.text: If Dancing in the Dust will be remembered for anything—which is a pretty generous proposition, if we're being honest—it'll probably be remembered as yet another example of a lauded director's debut showing glaring signs of early stylistic and thematic indecision. In this case, the lauded director in question is none other than Iran's current greatest storyteller, Asghar Farhadi. Before weaving sharp tapestries of domestic strife in modern Iran, the genius behind A Separation and The Past began with a relatively trivial tale of marital issues culminating in a seemingly haphazard trip to the desert (much like the debut film of our Lord and Saviour, Denis Villeneuve).

The town of Clifford treats Giuliano Gemma's character like garbage, because his job is to collect the garbage. A clear race allegory surfaces when he attempts to have a drink in the local saloon and court a prominent judge's daughter. He's not allowed to drink at the saloon, and he's told by the judge he's not to even make eye contact with his daughter. Yes, class issues are all kinds of ugly in the town of…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: Produced during the Nazi occupation in Denmark, this film is one of those rare births of an austere and somber reflection on the mechanisms of institutionalized fear, religious guilt, and the destruction of the feminine by structures of power. Released in 1943, the same year the Nazis began their open persecution of Danish Jews, the narrative is set in the 17th century (during the witch trials) which brings a certain painful resonance. The analogy between the burning of witches and the horrors of the Holocaust is not only plausible in my view, but it also imposes itself with symbolic significance.

reviews.text: Dreyer remains one of the best at using a sparse, cold setting and turning it into powerful emotion. What struck me most about this film is that none of the characters were truly wicked people. While what the inquisitors (or the Danish equivalent thereof) do is hideous, but Absalon is a man of faith and compassion in his way. He is integral to atrocity, but ultimately, he isn't himself wholly villainous. His views are distorted, but at their core, there is a humanity. Anne, meanwhile, may or may not be a witch, and she certainly wishes for others to die, but her greatest sin is to fall in love with someone not her husband--a sin I have no judgment for.…

Один таксист разводит камин украденным со службы во Вьетнаме огнёметом, Гэри Бьюзи срывает с незаплатившей ему стриптизерши трусы, полные чаевых, кэб братьев Варваров (вот уж забытый временем рудимент) едет исключительно задом, и только у Мистера Ти всё супер, и он противостоит наркоторговцам ради детей.Не такое стыдное зрелище как The Incredible Shrinking Woman, но всё еще плохо. По-настоящему порадовали шутка, когда вместо похитителя с выкупом персонажу на прослушку позвонила любовница, то, что герои регулярно напевают тему из Mission Impossible и какой-то запредельный уровень криповости Бьюзи, одними своим монологами вызывающий желание помыться. В остальном останется в истории как вопрос под викторину: "В каком фильме сошлись в кадре Адам Болдуин, Билл Мар и Мистер Ти?"

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Who needs a Freddy Krueger when we have a DEATH BED: THE BED THAT EATS? Spawned by the tears of a Satanic demon, the Death Bed lures unsuspecting humans to a house in the woods for one purpose—NOURISHMENT! And the concept of cinema was never the same again. Shot in Detroit during the 1970s and never legitimately released until the 21st century, DEATH BED is an essential chapter in absurdist DIY art-horror. Imagine Roger Corman’s legendary Edgar Allan Poe adaptations, but laced with nitrous, barbiturates, and an inhuman experimental synthesizer score. Plus a scene where Death Bed eats someone’s hands and replaces them with skeletons. This is our nourishment. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Knowing this movie for years only as the subject of a Patton Oswalt stand-up bit, I assumed from the title that it was some sort of proto-Sharknado bad-on-purpose thing. I was wrong. It's a dreamy, atmospheric mood-piece that seems to be taking place in a haze. All the dialogue is post-synched, which adds to the movie's foggy feeling. It takes its premise seriously, but not too seriously (there is a scene where a guy sticks his hands into the titular bed and takes them out, finding that only two perfectly-clean skeleton hands remain).

I don’t know if any other film can truly claim to be as bizarre as 'Death Bed.' This thing is absolutely bonkers. It catches you immediately off guard with its ridiculous title. But it has a great sense of humor about itself, some genuinely unsettling moments (particularly that agonizing scene of the woman trying to crawl away to safety before being pulled back by…

reviews.text: The plot of this movie: a demonic presence takes the form of a human being in order to sleep with the young woman he/it desires, and when the woman dies in the process of their lovemaking, the demon sheds tears of blood onto the bed they lay upon, rendering the bed eternally homicidal. That's the actual plot. And it's narrated by a ghost-dude stuck in a painting. So you think to yourself, "wow, what a strange idea for a movie!" No, trust me, the execution is even stranger. Much stranger. Zero budget, ceaseless voice-over rather than dialogue (that doesn't really translate well from script to screen, but I couldn't have given a fuck less), surreally amateurish cinematography, peculiar special effects...…

reviews.author: Digital Press
reviews.text: Since the title Death Bed: The Bed That Eats gives away what seems like a preposterous threat, it’s going to have to be great at giving us a backstory or satisfy us with creative kills. It does both! I was also surprised that what I assumed would be a comedy/horror isn’t joke-y but rather satirical in nature. It’s never taking itself seriously, but it isn’t doing its thing for laughs, either. It’s more tapped into “life’s rich comedy” than it is to “comedy club”.

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: The closest cinema will ever get to summoning a Paperback From Hell directly to the screen: Multiple POVs (and narration!), random nightmares, a big-time jumping exposition dump, and a convoluted ending filled with hilarious unexplained lore. No real characters to care about, only incidents and ideas. It's disappointing that the director never made any other films because he seems very much in control here, and I'd love to know what other wild tales he had up his sleeve.

reviews.text: An underground movement of vegetarians attempting to liberate an unemployed circus clown is just one of the elements in this surrealist black comedy set in a world following a cataclysmic event. Directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet (Amélie) it principally involves the owner of an apartment building attracting victims to slaughter to sell as meat to his occupants. It quickly calls to mind Terry Gilliam’s Brazil, as it has a weird and darkly comedic tone from the beginning and is fascinatingly unusual in similar ways. Delicatessen creatively integrates genres and delivers an impressively oddball exhibition of sounds and images.

It has the charm of Amelie, the dark plot of Sweeney Todd and some scenes you might claim to have come straight from Shape of Water. (But of course, this came first.) reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A bell rings incessantly. A clock ticks in the distance. For whom this bell tolls and this clock ticks, time is irrelevant, if not non-existent. Dreams, memories, hallucinations, hopes, doubts... reality. It sets in and there is no where to go. No light at the end of the tunnel for these two unnamed Konzentrationslager escapees. Only certain death by way of an unyielding, evil regime. Jan Nemec’s staggering minimalist masterpiece Diamonds of the Night does not bother with exposition. There is very little dialogue in the film. Instead, we are shown glimpses of the past and present. Distortions of reality both before, during and after the events taking place onscreen. Our characters enter a state of delirium as they wander aimlessly through the…

reviews.author: Mario Melendez
reviews.text: Jan Nemec's debut feature film is sustained by its minimalist form of eternal and tireless flight, only interrupted by evocative and dreamlike snippets presented in flashback format. It is in this simplicity where the director finds the way to transmit the sensations of suffering and overwhelm to the spectator, who witnesses an impetuous search for survival on the part of the protagonists, without a doubt Nemec was one of the outstanding authors of the Czechoslovak New Wave of the 60s, the most prolific decade of cinema in the former Central European republic, in which he directed this peculiar and evocative work about the Jewish holocaust based on the story written by Arnost Lustig about his own experiences in the horror…

reviews.author: Thomas Ringdal
reviews.text: Diamonds of the Night is an intense, in your face, depiction of two boys on the run from a deportation train on it's way to a concentration camp.Filmed up close and personal, aided by breathtaking cinematography, it manages to utilize the short running time to full effect, and I was hooked right away.Jan Nemec' debut feature is really something else, a visual nightmare of both the horrors of war, civil or otherwise (the unfolding events are actually not limited in scope to just WWII, as it is never mentioned), and sections of dream like sequences telling an alternative route the life of one of the boys could have taken.

reviews.author: Kyle Faulkner
reviews.text: Jan Němec's debut feature is undoubtedly his masterpiece and one of my favourite films of the Czech New Wave. It is an extreme essentialization of its source novel, Darkness Casts No Shadow, which recounts the true story of the author's escape from a death camp at the age of 16. Every aspect of the filmmaking is superb, each could substantiate its own essay, and all coalesce to elevate the film well beyond the 20th century's fixation with filmed theatre, without actually spilling into the realms of avant-garde. The sheer precision of this paring away of all that is extraneous (dialogue, context, etc) to the core phenomenology of the story produces a pioneering work of cinematic art that is profoundly experiential,…

reviews.text: ✭JDGM's Top of favorites✭ There is something very sacred about what we proudly call culture: ancient texts, those tales of incredible, almost mythical legends. The Song of Mio Cid and the Song of Roland are key pieces in Spanish literature. The Mahabharata and the Ramayana in Hindu culture represent the pinnacle of religious texts, as do the Arthurian legends of Great Britain and the Poetic and Prose Eddas of the Norse. The Iliad, the Odyssey, and the Epic of Gilgamesh, along with the Song of the Nibelungs, are among those anonymous narratives that shape humanity's culture, values, and identity—something we so desperately need.

reviews.text: 100-word review: Way to make the post-apocalyptic theme f***ing punk again; one of the few films, if not the only one, released between Beyond Thunderdome and Fury Road to pull off this particular aesthetic, though Mad Max makes better use of it thanks to its superior action editing. Doomsday's hodgepodge of influences, which it wears on its sleeve, make for a confusing watch, while this ought to be more of a comfort watch. The memorable brutality keeps this from being a bore, but in terms of plot, characters, and excitement, there are better post-apocalyptic action films out there.

reviews.author: san
reviews.text: Welp, this is definitely one of the longest films I have ever seen. Split into two parts, the film is about a criminal mastermind, Dr. Mabuse, who uses psychic suggestion to control people and win in gambling events — doing so, while also attempting to evade the town’s prosecutor, von Wenk. Fritz Lang uniquely elevates the cat-and-mouse genre with his stunning visuals and cinematic inventions. The only downside to this is obviously the runtime as the plot doesn’t really earn it, but despite this unpleasant issue, it oddly kept me invested all the way through.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Dr. Mabuse, the Gambler is one of the creepiest films of the silent era. It is quietly unnerving, with very dark ideas. This is a film of complete psychological manipulation, as our titular lead hypnotises and controls so many people. The Germany here is a dystopia, an economically unstable nation caught in the chaos of the early 1920s, which the evil Mabuse exploits for his own ends. This representation certainly reflects some then-contemporary myths about Jewish people trying to destroy and exploit the German people, but Mabuse is closer to a representation of the disturbing orators and manipulators that gained popularity on the political fringes, notably from the Nazi party. Lang's film doesn't necessarily have a political component, but its…

reviews.text: Fritz Lang's silent epic, taking place in Germany following the end of World War One. The film depicts the antics of a supercriminal known as Dr Mabuse - a forger and hypnotist who uses his abilities to manipulate those around him. Seemingly all powerful and feared - as one character puts it; "he is damnation and salvation"! The film depicts a situation where a man such as this is allowed to rise due to a society afflicted with apathy. The character himself forsakes his humanity for his lust for power. There's two major female characters in the film - one loves him but he doesn't care, the other one he just wants to possess for his own self gratification. The…

En ambos casos el detective se tenía que enfrentar a poderes superhumanos y así encontrar la identidad del criminal que estaban buscando. Otra similitud es que los personajes son muy inteligentes y utilizan sus cerebros para, de alguna manera, tratar de estar un paso adelante del otro. Por supuesto, Dr. Mabuse: The Gambler es una película muda expresionista, nada que ver con el anime japonés contemporáneo, pero aún así es fascinante encontrar este tipo de paralelismos entre obras cinematográficas tan apartadas en el tiempo. reviews.text: A biopic can never tell its audience the whole story, yet at the same time what is the use of a biopic if it can't? Watkins, understanding this, prioritizes the context that surrounds the Norwegian painter more than the painter himself, the intent being that understanding context surrounding a person reveals more about them than they could themselves: Munch therefore almost always appears as an inscrutable cipher whose inner emotions only manifest as haunting paintings to be interpreted.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Possibly the most personal of Watkins' metafactual texts, given that it concerns an an artist's creative and therefore spiritual transcendence being suffocated by a succession of social constructs. Munch's self-loathing is opposed by Watkins' legendary (not necessarily unearned) persecution complex (watch some interviews with this guy, he's amazing), all of it mirrored in constant sex/death associations and the encyclopedia-style listing of important historic events that marks each jump forward in time. Bleak and furious, terrified that we are stuck in these pointless, vulnerable bodies, slaves to one structure or another, unable to articulate our souls.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: It's all the things I want in film: politically and artistically challenging, Art=Politics, self-aware (i.e., transparent), emotionally moving, brutally personal (it invites me to relate Munch's story with specific events and people and emotions in my own life), freeform, jazzy, out-of-sync, out-of-wack, out-of-time and yet time-less, complex, un-hectoring, un-obvious, made with human feeling, aware of its subject's limitations when it comes to the lower-class and to women, aware of its subject's exceeding romanticism when it comes to the lower class and to women, brutally critical yet not wholly dismissive (a distance that's not quite objective), roving, roaming, wandering, refusing to distinguish between past-present-future, non-thesis-driven, warm, tender, bitter, dejected, cathartic, and just plain beautiful. And that's the tip of the iceberg.

Watkins uses his key style of direction to unlock finer emotions in his characters. Most notably is the theme of existentialism which, whether they know it or not, is present in nearly every character in the film. It doesn't help that the narration drives home, more than anything, each character's point of death. More often than not it was of a tragic or gruesome variety. The extreme emotions to the end of their tales should eliminate the power of conflicting and irrelevant moments. What good is a moment of happiness if a character…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Edvard Munch is a biopic presented as a documentary, with narration and interviews. It's an innovative, experimental work, though Peter Watkins had worked in this style before. Films on history are recreations, but Watkins removes that façade by using an anachronistic style. His faux-documentary has no pretence that this is a story. It's a recreation with a narration, and there's no ambiguity around what it is. The story is presented as a document of history, and that makes for an informative watch.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: A science fiction epic about forced-allegiances, survival, and eventual brotherhood, Wolfgang Petersen's "Enemy Mine" is a story that would be effective in any genre. Revolving around two individuals, enemies from birth, who form an uneasy alliance in order to preserve their lives, the story would compel as, among other genres, a drama, comedy, or Western. As science fiction, Petersen is able to dress his story in flash and spectacle. That spectacle, however, does not prevent the richness of the narrative and its characters from shining through. With its combination of genre trappings and textured story, "Enemy Mine" makes for an outstanding experience.

reviews.author: Alli
reviews.text: A sci-fi drama about a human and an alien who end up stranded together on an unfamiliar planet, Enemy Mine is a futuristic film full of heart. I love this film. He may look like a lizard, but that is the point. The love, dignity, and integrity of his character and the friendship developed with Dennis Quaid's Davidge that becomes the foundation of the film will stand the test of time. You have my word. reviews.text: American fighter pilot Dennis Quaid crash lands on a scary, stormy alien planet and meets a new pal who he thinks at first is a sci-fi horror movie monster he needs to kill but turns out to be more of a lovable outsider who helps him in his survival movie antics, teaches him about the crimes of imperialism/not to be a racist anymore and gives birth to a little ET he needs to both care for and eventually violently defend from his own army. It's a supremely goofy premise that plays like the darker, social message version of something like The Last Starfighter but it's given a surprisingly dense, tactile visual treatment by Wolfgang Petersen with lots of impressive set design, make-up, and matte painting work (even some solid FX in the big siege shootout) that keep this engaging to look at even at its most eye-rollingly sentimental.

Fortunately, this disappointment was only fleeting, as it soon turned out that what really matters is Dennis Quaid and Louis Gossett Jr. grumpily learning to share a single habitable crater in a bizarre parable in which the Cold War is ended via a kind of interspecies cuddle therapy.

But man, those stock images. There's a point where Bethany McLean talks about "pulling a rabbit out of a hat" and Gibney spends like 20 seconds on a clip of a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat. Thanks! I enjoy getting a dementia test along with my documentary.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: The amount of bad press that investment bankers, huge corporations, and what most people would call "unscrupulous greedy bastards" have had in recent years following the global financial crash of 2007-2008 has filled headlines time and time again. Gordon Gekko famously said in Stone's Wall Street, that greed was good, but that's hard to tell someone who's just saw their 401 and their pension pot frittered away in the largest corporate fraud in history. This documentary will make you scratch your head at the insanity of what Enron and it's bunch of crooked and deluded executives got up to, but if you're anything like me you'll be quickly looking to see what happened to these guys following the investigation.

reviews.text: I liked the Super Giant series enough to check out his Americanized Star Man iteration. Boy is this ever a mess. They took the three weakest and most disconnected ones and slammed them together very haphazardly. Worst of all they cut out the “Saracen” sword dance from Kingdom of the Poison Moth which is the best part of these entries. Not sure if making the Cult a bunch of aliens instead of vague middle easterners is more absurd than how they were originally presented or not. They also use aliens and mutants sort of interchangeably to describe the villains, to keep things extra confusing if you’ve not seen the originals. Despite being credited as one of the directors, less than a minute of this is footage from one of the Teruo Ishii entries.

reviews.text: The story could have been far more intriguing had it started at the point when the son discovers that his mother had become a vampire. This is the dramatic push of the final thirty minutes of “Family Blood,” a horror film so bloated with heavy-handed metaphor between drug addiction and vampirism, the work never gets the chance to take off. It appears that co-writers Nick Savvides and Sonny Mallhi (who also directs) are unable to decide whether the picture is a drama that just so happens to have horror elements or a full-on body horror movie. Due to this indecision, the screenplay suffers from a sort of malaise: curious one second, dead dull the next.

reviews.text: Haunted by the nightmarish events of her past and unable to accept her position in a society so dismissive of women, Amy (Amy Everson) copes with the everyday horrors of her life through art. Finding even the most trivial social encounters unbearable, she is utterly uncomfortable in her own skin. Capturing her struggles through a series of hazy, color-corrected vignettes, Jason Baker’s melancholy Felt depicts a harrowing reality faced by countless millions of women without offering any solutions to what is shown to be a startlingly-invisible problem.

reviews.text: A dizzying mash-up of hundreds of iconic films, rapidly-edited and reconstructed into a classic Hollywood love story. Palfi uses cinematic archetypes for satirical grist as vastly divergent styles collide and legendary stars strobe through a single story arc. Bracingly disorienting (the fascination does give way to fatigue), but it's a wild trip through film history.

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: I'm very much obsessed by the editing in the first mortar attack. They cut on the moment of impact to another image of warfare with each blast, and it creates this disorienting effect where you cannot plant your feet with these images. They're too unsettled by battle. In addition to that each cut matters. They aren't just doing it for the sake of excitement, but to tell a story of lives lost and the fragility of the rearguard in their current trapped position in the mouth of a mountain. It's akin to placing a lid on a candle and watching the fire be choked out as a montage of life lost. Here and gone. A poetry of dead soldiers that…

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: "Fixed Bayonets!" has the misfortune of following-up writer/director Samuel Fuller's own "The Steel Helmet," which is not just a great movie about the Korean War but one of the greatest war movies ever made, full stop. That said, "Fixed Bayonets!" is...actually a pretty damn good war picture on its own merits! It helps that "The Steel Helmet" lead Gene Evans is on hand here, playing a major character named Sgt. Rock (had to have been an influence on Joe Kubert's comic creation, right?). And this is another excellent example of Fuller's penchant for action, with some vertically-moving tracking shots that really convey a sense of scale to each battle. Might be the most violent American movie of its decade, at least that I've seen...?

reviews.text: Fixed Bayonets! is an early Sam Fuller film that shows he was just as forceful and direct as he was later in his career. Fixed Bayonets!, though studio bound, is a snow-set battle in the contemporaneous Korean War. It is chockful of action sequences and generates amazing tension despite the limitations of the set; though to be fair to Fuller you actually soon forget the visual detail, as he has such a great ear for tough dialogue and merciless view of misfortune. Fixed Bayonets! has one of the best sequences of Fuller's whole career, the landmine walk, but scene after scene is engrossing as he pits the valour and courage of average soldiers against the situation not of their making.…

reviews.text: Time to finish off The Flying Guillotine series with the actual sequel that preceded The Vengeful Beauty, is not directed by Ho Meng-Hua, and took two years to make due to production issues (including three of the original cast leaving the industry or Shaw Brothers). Flying Guillotine 2 definitely feels uneven, like it is spliced together from several different scripts or versions or reshoots, but the highs are pretty high. The evil emperor (now Ku Feng) is still using his Flying Guillotine Squad to silence dissenters. But since Ma Teng (now played by Ti Lung in what amounts to a cameo for most of the film) devised the Iron Umbrella to defeat the weapon in the original, the emperor has to…

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: Messy Wuxia, with a hundred characters (A genre staple) that has some hyperactive direction and a great last act, once the main characters get to bubble to the surface. Lots of heads get lopped off, so I can't say I was disappointed in that regard.

reviews.author: Tom Spearing
reviews.text: I’ve always been a bit unsure of precisely what distinguishes a wuxia movie from a kung fu movie, but my inkling is that this and the first Flying Guillotine lean more into the former with their heavier emphasis on armed combat and more fantastical story elements. Neither seem like pure wuxia outings though, especially this sequel, given that it contains much more kung fu than its predecessor. But saying that, the combatants here do display some superhuman abilities—an agility and lightness of movement that seems to defy gravity at times. There isn’t an awful lot of information about the film online, so I’d be genuinely interested if anyone can shed more light on my loose attempts at categorisation here.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Flying Guillotine II is tighter and more action heavy that the original. But also feels way more disjointed and has too much plot and characters for a 90 minute runtime. But one thing is for sure, it is never boring. As a sequel it’s kinda of an odd duck. Ma, the main character from the first one, now played by Ti Lung instead of Chen Kuan-tai, is not really the focus of the story anymore. He’s merely part of an ensemble here. If anything the focus is much more on Shih Szu's character, who’s trying avenge her mother’s death. The role of the emperor has also been recast now played by Ku Feng who had a different role in part…

reviews.text: While this stands as only the third installment I've seen out of the Guillotine films I think I feel comfortable announcing them as my personal favorite wuxia films. Master was one of the first of the genre I saw with all its pure psychotronic insanity and almost no story to be had I still love it just as much as in High School. I saw the first one last year and though not at all what I was expecting the film proved great in an entirely different way. It's kind of Masters's polar opposite with less fighting and violence instead focusing on a well-crafted plot boasting stellar production.

reviews.author: Scrambled Face
reviews.text: For three years after the original Flying Guillotine, the concept of the decapitating weapon had been mercilessly mined by low budget producers. I mean, Jimmy Wang Yu was in two different FG ripoffs by the time this sanctioned sequel hit theaters, and all the Shaws had to show for themselves was the sorta-similar Dragon Missile from two years prior. The troubled production of Flying Guillotine 2 saw the previous movie's leads both walking away (like Wang Yu before him, box office draw Chen Kuan-tai ceremoniously broke his contract, while Liu Wu-Chi simply disappeared from the set one day, as did the actress first hired to replace her) and director Cheng Kang replaced by Super Inframan's Hua Shan. That may sound…

reviews.author: Carlo Vanstiphout
reviews.text: Hua Shan's movies aren't known for their cohesiveness, and this is no exception, even if the main cause here is production issues. Nonetheless, if the man has the choice between ending a scene 5 seconds too soon and 1 second too late, he's always going for option 1. Respect. All the art for this (including the new one from 88 Films) seems to ignore the fact that rather than Ti Lung it's Shih Szu who is the main protagonist here. She leads an all-female squad of flying guillotine users, and is a badass. This movie also features a super flying guillotine, a flying guillotine 64, AND somehow Akira Ifukube's score for Daimajin. Solid.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: It is fascinating how Ray RKO period can be divided almost exclusively between masterpieces and potboiler assignments (Knock on Any Door is probably the exception, an ambitious project compromised from the beginning). This one was made to make Howard Hughes happy and it shows, save for a few moments between Wayne and Ryan, it mostly is pedestrian war stuff from the era, it doesn’t even have the madness of something like One Minute to Zero. The aerial footage that is supposed to be the film calling card is worse than I remember as well. This is one of the few Ray movies to be a big hit at the time, but it is now near the bottom of his page here despite the bigger stars, I assume it is just a little to indistinct even for Wayne fans.

reviews.text: top gun, 1951. the anti catch-22. like any naive leftist with a sense of country, i wish i could say the film made me nostalgic for a time when the us government at least pretended to be against fascism instead of aspiring to it, but this isn’t that. it’s hardly even a nicholas ray picture. he was hired to point, shoot, and keep his sympathizer mouth shut and let the anticommunist motion picture alliance for the preservation of american ideals president john wayne do all the talking in what amounts to nothing more than an exercise in hollywood ww2 military cosplay ordered up by rko radio pictures chief (and known aviation fetishist) howard hughes while he was busy designing brassieres for jane russell. on the plus side, it’s in technicolor.

reviews.author: Blair Russell
reviews.text: This seemed apt for Memorial Day Weekend, the holiday in the United States where every person in the military who gave their life while serving is celebrated. This was selected as it is part of a DVD collection I’ve had for ages and for some, the title will be baffling. However, its origin is simple: it is military slang for United States Marine Corps soldiers, the term allegedly due to the past practice of wearing a leather stock around their necks. Indeed, this covers a regiment that does battle in the air and the setting is the campaign of Guadalcanal. Only the basics of that need to be known: it takes place soon after the Battle of Midway and the…

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: Given how great of a director Nicholas Ray was at telling complex, intelligent films, it's a little surprising that he'd be responsible for a picture like Flying Leathernecks that isn't bad per se, but is a fairly basic war movie. It's got little indication that it's from the director behind classics like In a Lonely Place, Johnny Guitar, or Rebel Without a Cause since it follows a very familiar path set out by other John Wayne war flicks like Sands of Iwo Jima, just that this time it's about pilots rather than Marines. The combat sequences are alright and the colour photography looks nice, but it's narratively pretty rote as it basically feels like 100 minutes of scenes alternating between aerial battles and bland melodrama. Not much of the stuff there, be it the characterization or the conflicts, is particularly interesting, which really drags Flying Leathernecks back from being anything noteworthy.

reviews.author: Jake
reviews.text: nicholas ray’s venture into the war genre is at its best in the moments that lack any fighting, the moments where the film is allowed to bask in its tenderness, the humanist moments like when john wayne’s dan kirby listens to his son’s sweet message on his record player, or the revering camaraderie shared amongst the unit of soldiers. the aerial combat sequences possess a slightly thrilling dynamism, and make for an immersive combat experience (especially considering this is over 70 years old), but this isn’t the first time nicholas ray has took to the skies, and here it lacks the same storytelling craft as in his debut work, they live by night, where a cut to an overhead shot…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Florinda Bolkan can't remember the last three days and chain smokes Dunhills while being bizarrely retraumatized by her hazy recollections of a movie-within-the-movie in which Klaus Kinski strands astronauts on the Moon. Actually even more intriguing than it sounds, a slow, inexorable descent into memory and annihilation prompted by repressed psychosexual splinters. Beautifully shot by Storaro, all golden daylight tableaux and deep blue nights, laced with rococo and stained glass, jaggedly interrupted by the dull black and white of the airless, dusty, deliberately artificial-looking lunar landscape. Weird as fuck and certainly unique among gialli.

reviews.author: pirateneckbeard
reviews.text: What a haunting film that has so many lingering visuals that just stick as we unlock Alice's life as she slowly goes down the looking glass. Honestly beautifully shot with a solid score that also sharply cuts out and let's us ruminate in our characters mind to what is unfolding but I love how they folded this souffle because I was always engaged and I feel like it really gave us an outcome that can reinterpret the whole narrative but do to how well this was done I find this material a remarkable watch and worth engaging if you can get your hands on it. For sure it's not for everyone but if you like a challenging storyline that gives you something you rarely see then I would recommend planting your shoe down and let this film leave it's imprints on your mind.
