reviews.author: Matt Winfield 🇨🇦
reviews.text: Between this and 1965's The Possessed, Luigi Bazzoni has created two of the most haunting, experimental, and esoteric mystery flicks I've ever seen come out of Italy. No black-gloved killers running rampant, no swinging sex romps, no detective work to be done – definitely NOT the giallo I was expecting when I popped this in. Just a story of a lone woman (Florinda Bolkan) with the last three days of her life wiped away like a distant memory, and following the trail of breadcrumbs to piece together the missing moments.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Less of a Giallo and more of a slow burning mystery, Footprints on the Moon draws its intrigue from the idea of amnesia and tells the story of a translator (a very good Florinda Bolkan) who has nightmares about Klaus Kinski conducting experiments on the moon. Eventually she is lead to an island named Garma, where apparently she has been before. The central concept of the film sees our lead character trying to work out who she is, what she was doing just a few days previously, and how this links to her vivid nightmares. Luigi Bazzoni's film is visually interesting - the island where most of the film takes place is bright and sun-kissed; thoroughly at odds with the…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Even apart from the story that surrounds her, Alice Cespi (Florinda Bolkan) is an extraordinary character. Reserved, independent, and seemingly intentionally quite isolated, she stands apart from most women on screen in the absence of either a romantic relationship or a desire for one, as well as in her solitary way of life, one we have every indication she's chosen for herself. Particularly when played by a woman like Bolkan, whose presence on Italian screens was almost always closely linked to her sex appeal, it's quietly thrilling to encounter a character like Alice who seems to have managed to keep herself so unentangled by social expectations and pressures.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Comes close to being great, but never quite gets there for me. Storaro’s cinematography is, as always, phenomenal—I cannot think of a DP who uses symmetry in framing better than him. Maybe it’s because I have seen some of these ideas executed better, more intensely and with greater precision (Last Year at Marienbad and Mulholland Dr. both came to mind while I was watching this one), but I wasn’t able to fully latch onto the story the way I’d hoped to.

reviews.author: Gentry Austin
reviews.text: To try and fully explain this movie would be an injustice. You must bath in its sepia blue moon light. Alice Cespi (Florinda Bolkan) is an Italian translator who is haunted by past trauma. Specifically, a film she watched as a child called Footprints on the Moon, about an astronaut who is abandoned on the lunar surface by an evil mission controller (Klaus Kinski). A word or phrase during a work lecture triggers her remembrance of the film and the next thing she realizes, several days have passed without memory. She finds a torn-up postcard of the Turkish city of Garma, so she books a flight and investigates.

reviews.text: A strange film from the less-than-prolific director of The Fifth Cord, Luigi Bazzoni and an uncredited Mario Fanelli, better known for his TV work. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Directed by French filmmaker René Clément, and adapted from François Boyer's 1947 novel The Secret Game, Forbidden Games is a compelling and beautifully delicate film about a five-year-old child in WWII France who suffers the loss of her parents and puppy in a German air raid and encounters a ten-year-old boy, and together they endeavour to endure the devastation which encircles them. The performances of the two children are excellent, and despite evoking a great deal of sadness, the movie also manages to be full of optimism and hope. This was the deserved recipient of the Honorary Oscar (aka Best International Film) at the 24th Academy Awards and is a heartrending story with unambiguous anti-war themes.

reviews.text: What transpires in the first five minutes of René Clément’s Forbidden Games is probably the most depressing thing to ever happen in a movie—even a French one. It’s June, 1940, and the people of Paris are scrambling away from the city amid a flurry of Nazi bombs. Among them is young Paulette (Brigitte Fossey), who exposes herself to machine-gun fire as she innocently sprints across a bridge to retrieve an adorable puppy that has scampered off. The girl’s horrified parents naturally chase after their daughter. A German plane strafes overhead, and only Paulette survives—not even her dog is spared, its small legs twitching to a slow stop.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: In 1952, Rene Clement must have gotten major praise for pushing on with this courageous project, but has its power since then become deflated? Forbidden Games (French with English subtitles) opens with a Nazi bombing campaign of the French countryside, and it is a vigorous and frightening scene not just for its time but still impresses, and rattles, today – it is realistic except for the lack of blood. Little girl Paulette (Brigitte Fossey) chases after her dog while hundreds of Frenchmen are being fired on, and she makes moves that causes her parents to get struck during the raid.

reviews.text: Not among the best Giuliano Gemma spaghetti westerns, FORT YUMA GOLD passes the time adequately, if not very swiftly. Stylistically, this is more in line with an American oater, and even an Ennio Morricone score doesn't do much to distinguish it. The action sequences do take good advantage of Gemma's athletic abilities, particularly a genuinely terrific saloon brawl around the mid-point. If you watch this via the Mill Creek Blu-ray, don't worry, your speakers aren't blown: their master has just about the worst sound you will hear on this format.

reviews.author: Guilherme Simões Reis
reviews.text: Here we have a spaghetti with a simple but tasty sauce. Giuliano Gemma is a Confederate raider freed from a Yankee prison in order to avoid an unnecessary slaughter in Fort Yuma, and he will have the help of a beautiful dancer and a good old man in his dangerous mission. It is not an innovative movie, for sure, as many of the usual clichés are there in this highly conventional spaghetti Western (in reality, it is a co-production Italy-France-Spain) without deepening the characters: saloon brawl, piano-playing, shoot-out inside the mine, torture under the sun, honored Southern soldier... Though, it is an unpretentious nice Western, with good filmmaking, good soundtrack, good action, and even good (although not special) acting. Far from achieving the high quality of Leone's movies, this spaghetti Western with a similar name is still above average, anyway.

It's one thing, though, for Fuller to visually reveal who Stanwyck is; it's quite another for Stanwyck to take all of what Fuller is giving her and make Jessica Drummond as worthy of regard as Stanwyck herself is. And she does so with awe-inspiring ease.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Fuller and Stanwyck. What a match made in heaven. The West suits Fuller, allowing him to set up his nonpretentious, often moving but always steady and brutally direct shot patterns while capturing a great and raw beauty. The same, obviously, holds true for Stanwyck, who has been mixing raw sex with tough-as-nails defensiveness since the Pre-Codes. As with all Fullers, FORTY GUNS is blunt but complex in its contradictions: Stanwyck's dominatrix tyrant is puzzlingly disarmed by the man who disrupts her racket, but Fuller will not totally clean up her image for the sake of a moral. Immaculate cinematography and unfussy but inventive camera placements (especially under the carriage at the cold open) add yet more textures to an utterly wild, kinky Western.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: AKA: General Idi Amin Dada: A Self PortraitA fascinating, surreal, chilling documentary filmed in 1974 when General Idi Amin Dada was leader of Uganda. A sort of 'Idi Amin in his own words' as director Barbet Schroeder takes his life in his hands interviewing and travelling with the megalomaniac, brutal dictator who wanted the film to portray him as funny, friendly, smart and teller of truths.Schroeder mostly refrains from making comment, allowing Amin himself to reveal his delusional, hapless, despotic character.

reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: Advanced studies for Dreyer—rigorous in ways one doesn't even know how to particularly articulate. Dreyer's choices of when to edit and when to pan or move the camera at first seem defiantly baffling, until it all starts to form a logic with the narrative. The film has both a simplicity (woman's idealized version of love will always fail her), and yet an intense complexity that it's hard to know where to begin. Paintings are key here—reflections of narrative, all mainly Renaissance "representational" art, save for that final one of the grotesque woman (her Dorian Gray?). Compositions have a intense stillness to them that registers almost beyond comprehension—Dan Sallitt pondered after the screening that only Dreyer would pull back the camera…

A maior utilidade da boa literatura reside em impedir que um homem seja puramente moderno. Ser puramente moderno é condenar-se à limitação; assim como gastar o último centavo que há na terra no mais novo lançamento de chapéus é condenar-se a ficar fora de moda. reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: Here, love is the only miracle that exists, and it never comes. Dry and passionate, still and volcanic, Carl Theodor Dreyer poses a stream of arguments and counterarguments on what it means to live a fulfilling life, what it means to create art, what it means to love. This is truly cinema as dialogue. The characters are philosophical chestnuts, and yet Gertrud, a fictional construct, becomes a fully-breathing, complex person. None of it is resolved, which makes me think that Carl Th. Dreyer's goal for his final film was nothing less than capturing life itself for the cinema. It's terribly and wonderfully afflicting at the same time. Here, process is the ultimate: "When I'm near the grave and look back…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: In spite of the connotations of the term, “modernism” in almost all of its artistic media explicitly innovated by foregrounding the past. Whether the dense panoply of literary references in Joyce, Eliot et al. or Picasso drawing from art history stretching all the way back to the prehistoric to paint Les demoiselles d’Avignon, the great ruptures of the new relied on an encyclopedic knowledge of the old.

reviews.text: After Gone Baby Gone, Argo, and The Town, it's pretty clear that Ben Affleck should stick to acting. These films aren't terrible, but they're hardly worthy of the near-unanimous praise they receive, and Gone Baby Gone might be the most unimpressive of the three. A lot of fuss has been made about the "moral conundrum" in this film, and I suppose that on a purely hypothetical level, the moral quandary posed by the movie invites some debate. However, when it's confined to the parameters and context present in the film, it becomes less of a conundrum and more a matter of simple logic. There is no decision to be made here, and anyone who denies that needs to think it…

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: Albert Finney stars as Eddie Ginley, a Liverpool bingo-caller and would-be comedian with a weekly psychiatrist's appointment, who actually wants to be Sam Spade. He puts a Private Investigator ad in the local paper as a sort of 31st birthday present to himself and finds himself caught up in an actual case.The theatrical feature directorial debut of Stephen Frears and written by the underrated Liverpool writer Neville Smith, this also features an original score by Andrew Lloyd Webber. A black comedy that flits between real detective story and spoof. It's a great part for Finney who has great fun with it, despite being saddled with some casually racist (and anti-Scottish) dialogue which certainly dates the film. The supporting cast are excellent especially Fulton Mackay whose character's relationship with Eddie could have been the basis for a sequel or spin-off TV series, in my opinion.

reviews.text: Seems obvious that nobody would finance a movie solely about Toback's own life-changing encounter with LSD and so what results is a diluted end product. Toback is trying to tell his own personal story as cinema, but must couch it in marketable nonsense in order to get it made.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: The trouble with mainstream TV is that all TV is mainstream - there's no avant-garde TV, or independent TV, or low-budget genre exploitation TV. Even in those rare instances of truly transgressive material making it onto the airwaves (like Twin Peaks, or that time Takeru Kobayashi faced a grizzly bear in a hot dog eating contest), everything that shows up on your television screen is all coming from the same corporate pipe. It can be stultifying enough to watch, but imagine how the people producing it must feel? Luckily we don't have to imagine it, we just have to watch Head, and see The Monkees break out of their little black box - on the company's dime no less. I guess sometimes they do lend money to guys with a sense of humor.

reviews.text: There are a ton of funny people in this movie. It's written and directed by the same people behind "The State" and "Reno 911". So, it's really no wonder that I learned a very important lesson from this movie about a comedy rule I've never seen tested before.You know that routine (some call it the "long joke", but I've heard other colloquialisms for it) where the bit is funny, but then it goes on long enough to be tedious or cringey...but then it keeps going long enough to be funny, again? There are different variations on this theme, and it has been reproduced to varying degrees of success. "Hell Baby" has taught me that if you do that same thing, over and over, as your main source of humor, none of it works.

reviews.author: Karl Janssen
reviews.text: I watch a lot of movies set in the ancient world—Greece, Rome, the Middle East. I often wonder why more movies aren't made about the Aztecs, Inca, and Maya. Well, Sons of the Sun dares to venture into ancient America, even if it has a goofy way of getting there. This film is one of Mark Forest's series of several Hercules films. Hercules is shipwrecked on the shores of the New World. There he meets Prince Maytha, played by Giuliano Gemma. Maytha's father Huascar has been deposed from the Inca throne by his tyrannical brother Atahualpa. Gemma and a group of rebel Inca warriors stage an uprising, with the help of Hercules.

reviews.author: Sam Prime
reviews.text: A white man (Mark Forest as Hercules) washes ashore in an unknown land, the natives save him from almost certain death yet somehow also immediately conclude that he is the strongest man in the world. Later, Whitey insists on literally fighting a battle on behalf of the young native prince (Giuliano Gemma) while his secret motive is to save and seduce the native princess. He is roundly successful in this way. Later still, he teaches the natives how to build war machines so as to defeat their bitter enemy. War is waged. Staggering losses (including some of the absolute clumsiest sword-and-sandal death scenes), a rescue mission failed, something about a curse. A Pyrrhic victory if I've ever seen one.

reviews.text: When will people realize you can make over-the-top, aggressively ridiculous, badly written movies without being sexist, racist, homophobic, etc.? I am not saying you need to be wholesome. I am not saying you need to even be progressive. I am just saying don't put your villain in brownface or use the word "homo" as an insult. Topless, chain saw-wielding killers is not a premise anyone expects perfection from, nor even anything good, but if I could walk away not feeling like I just watched something made by a frat boy applying to the Klan, that'd make my morning more enjoyable. Anyway, I thought the line about not being zoned for ritual sacrifice was pretty funny, and I love a hard-boiled detective voiceover schtick. If you just want women with chain saws and cheezy comedy in a movie that is like an R-rated ripoff of Bloodfeast that is also inexplicably a noir parody, well, here you go.

reviews.text: Notable for being one of the first films to tackle racial elements head on (some publication say the first). At the time, there were three other productions dealing with similar social issues in the works, and producer Stanley Kramer was adamant that his had to be the first to market. Turns out, he was right. Home of the Brave was a hit and helped cement Kramer’s first company, Screen Plays, Inc., as an independent player to watch, especially after the massive success of Champion, with Kirk Douglas.

reviews.author: PUNQ
reviews.text: To that point, white Hollywood's bravest attempt at tackling racism. It even puts in perspective the effect of the N-word so that a white guy could understand. Thrown into the jungle with a otherwise all-white cast, James Edwards is the black man that becomes the face of these problems. He was fresh in Hollywood, so no prior roles as a servant or train conductor or anything associated with black roles in Tinseltown. He gives an honest and emotional performance, as this is not just a story or racism, even if that's the key issue intertwined, but also of mental health, especially relating to war. Talking abut racism in movies will always be clumsy, especially in the age Home of the Brave (1949), but I would say this one is done real good.

The film makes a couple of severe blunders towards the end, but overall is a very impressive effort from the cast, screenwriter Carl Foreman, director Mark Robson, and producer Stanley Kramer, who would go on the make a career out of "message films" like 'Guess Who's Coming to Dinner' and tales of the psychological affects of war like 'The Caine Mutiny.'

reviews.author: Sofa Sinema
reviews.text: Screenwriter, producer and second unit director of ski sequences Mike Marvin reveals in the commentary that he did try for thirty years to get a sequel off the ground, but couldn't get anyone to believe in it. Producer Ed Pressman's next picture would be the Oscar nominated and critical darling Witness, so his career was already on an uphill swing. Commentary moderator Mike Felsher (Red Shirt Pictures) presses Marvin on some of the salacious behind-the-scenes aspects of shooting in the winter wonderland of Tahoe in the early eighties. But the real gems of this candid track are hearing Marvin discuss shooting the complex aerial skiing and jaw-dropping stunts. He's a compelling and generous guy, not even taking credit for some of the movie's funniest dialogue. Man, ski ballet needs to make a comeback. That footage was exhilarating to watch and it was a bummer to learn that it's not really a thing anymore.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: When people refer to the traditions of French farce, what they have in mind are the plays of Georges Feydeau. For such a paradigmatic playwright, there aren’t many film adaptations of his work in English. This version of L'Hôtel du libre échange, which Feydeau co-wrote with Maurice Desvallières, and a 1968 version of A Flea in Her Ear with Rex Harrison are about it. Neither was a hit critically or commercially, which is a shame. You’d think Feydeau’s comic sensibilities would have resonated with English-speaking audiences in the late ‘60s. I suspect these films got lost among all the mediocre sex comedies the British film industry was churning out at the time.

reviews.author: Jim Beaver
reviews.text: I can attest from experience that Georges Feydeau's French farce Hotel Paradiso plays passably well before a theatrical stage audience, with a succession of laughs at its absurd characters behaving in comic desperation. But on viewing the film version, I am unconvinced that the wildly over-the-top characterizations and situations play nearly as well on the cinema screen. Alec Guinness, who reprises his stage performance in the film, comes as close to success as anyone in the film with a fine comic performance, and Gina Lollobrigida, of all people, does a quite acceptable job as his intended lover. But for all the splendid production design and the capable direction of Peter Glenville, this film adaptation seems forced and generally unfunny. Some things, it seems, are not made to be movies.

The live action cartoon How High is clumsy and imperfect, but it's just silly enough to forgive its many flaws. Meth is a master botanist who grows weed with the ashes of his late friend (Chuck Deezy), weed which when smoked invokes the intelligent fellow's ghost. Meth smokes a joint with Red in the parking lot before their big college entrance exam, and they do so well they end up at Harvard, in accordance with chancellor Fred Willard's mandate to bring in more "color." reviews.author: Scott Tobias
reviews.text: If you're a young Paul Newman, with all the world-beating beauty and charisma that goes along with it, you have to fight hard against an audience's natural sympathies to be an antihero. And as Hud, Newman fights hard indeed. You keep searching for redeemable aspects to this character-- and every so often, you get one-- but mostly he's selfish, unscrupulous and violent, and manages to alienate everyone who cares about him. Love the look of this film, too. James Wong Howe deserved his Oscar.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Insanely bleak, world-weary neo-western about the passing of an infected torch from the principled ranchers who in their old age have grown as hard as the land they work and the cold-blooded youth they've helped shape that believe in nothing but individual impulse and profit. Some of the most beautiful B&W cinemascope of the 60s in service of some truly stomach-churning, feel-bad character drama. A movie that makes you feel like one of those executed cows in that muddy pit. Was not surprised to learn that this was originally a novel by the the Last Picture Show guy. "It don't take long to kill things. Not like it takes to grow."

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: No Country for Old Men '63? This was way darker and carried a far more conservative streak than I was expecting. At one point in HUD I'm fairly certain that generational malaise is made analogous to contagious disease in livestock. The inflicted cattle are rounded up in a ditch and summarily executed by gunmen wearing rain gear to protect from the splatter. I don't think Martin Ritt and collaborators would have chosen this imagery if they knew Kent State was less than a decade away, but as they are safely on the wrong side of the "don't trust anyone over 30" slogan, I wouldn't accuse them of insincerity in this powerfully sad depiction of change. The lesson of the incident…

reviews.text: Hud Bannon is a cynical and unscrupulous thirty-five year old who lives in a large Texas estate with his family. His uneasy relationship with his elderly father Homer, a farmer with very healthy principles, cracks when his cattle contract a disease, bringing to light the deep differences between the two regarding the actions to be taken. However, their dispute is not limited to the administration of the ranch or recriminations about the protagonist's dissolute conduct, but also concerns Homer's fear that Hud represents a bad role model for his young nephew Lonnie.

reviews.text: Martin Ritt is a director who understands actors and their motives, and there is no better showcase for that than with Hud. Paul Newman’s role as the titular character is a slick and confident appearance, yet often lacks the awareness to discover his sincere identity. Patricia Neal - despite the fact that she won Best Actress instead of Best Supporting Actress - is exquisite and show-stopping within her brief scenes, capturing the intelligence yet possessing the desperation and difficulty of the situation.

reviews.text: Second pass because I want to get behind something this ferocious and technically adept but it's so repetitive, so criminally long and so fatally shallow that I have to stick to my guns and call it a failure. While my lizard brain thrills to the astounding violence and virtuoso camerabatics this is still a pretty tired consumed-by-revenge jam, so narratively convoluted and hypocritical in its rote moralizing that I'm wondering if it isn't just a big joke, that Kim is just making a comedy of errors that happens to be about a couple of raging psychopaths. I don't mind that this is a flimsy clothesline for expertly choreographed sadism, I mind that it's 2 1/2 hours long and almost gleefully stupid.

reviews.text: I Survived A Zombie Holocaust is a small budget indie flick zombie comedy and my gosh did I find that movie charming. I mean, it mashes up the hakka with a call back to Night of The Living Dead. Harley Neville and Jocelyn Christian put a lot of heart into a well written set of roles (written and directed by Guy Pigden) in a fun rompy zombie comedy. If you've ever enjoyed a zombie movie or three, give this one a watch. Of all the movies I watched this year, I've carried the most water for it because I earnestly love it. And I want more people to see it.

reviews.text: Wesley (Harley Neville) is an aspiring screenwriter who takes a job as a runner on a zombie film. However something in the water supply soon means that life is imitating art as the production suffers a real zombie outbreak. Written and directed by Guy Pigden, this Kiwi comedy-horror harks back to the early films of Peter Jackson with its cheap and cheerful production values and a lead character who is a loveable loser. What's surprising is just how funny it is, the gags at the expense of the film production hitting the target every time, plus the zombie action is fun once that part of the story kicks in.

reviews.author: Dustin Baker
reviews.text: I love surrealist horror, but it works better when the creators have a firm grasp of what they're trying to portray. It's easy to distinguish when someone's putting shit up on the screen just for the sake of looks. And this certainly looks great, with echoes of Silent Hill imagery. But the story isn't enough to sustain interest, especially when the most compelling elements don't arrive until at least 45 minutes into it.

reviews.author: LM_
reviews.text: I must pinch myself, just to make sure I’m awake. *Pinch*. Talk about arrestingly hypnotic and abstract. And that’s the contrasting imagery inside (dreams) and out (landscapes) of the subconscious. Watching “III” is like being caught in a trance. It’s visually sublime captured by its elegant cinematography and otherworldly score, but frail storytelling does keep this grim, surrealistic Russian horror-fantasy from reaching great heights.

And while the finale might overstretch its own reach, the narrative doesn't become convoluted and its a film that needs to settle in your mind and ingest the soul of its exploration of fear.

reviews.text: An old man sat on a swing, the snow formed a blanket on his hunched back, his heart was warmer than ever. For the past 50 years he had rushed through life, and we all know bad things happen to those who hurry. They would look back and realize all the effort was for nothing. The man got disconnected with his only son, lost all his friends, and most importantly, forgot to admire the grossly incandescent sun. "Not enough time" was the excuse he used to give himself. reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: It is called "To Live" and when the protagonist decides to do so, people in the background starts to sing "happy birthday", let's just say that even by Kurosawa's "captain obvious" standards, Ikiru is not subtle. Yet, movies are to be lived not read, and Ikiru is so expansive, so detailed in its imagination of that man's final days and Shimura's performance of it so affecting that nothing like that matters. Every underlined image hit like they are fresh and unexpected. Mr Watanabe wounds so real, Kurosawa's in your face approach just making it more so.

reviews.text: Solid, well-scripted diamond caper with touches of noir and comedy to keep it moving. Writer/director David Singer’s only feature film credit which seems like a real shame since he was definitely onto something here. Influences range from 40s noir to 60s crime comedies to 90s ensemble pieces, which are all strong wells to pull from. It also has a woman as the lead, which is rare enough in this sort of story. Virginia Kull heads a cast largely known for their TV work who all handle this wordy but snappy script with aplomb. She plays Cassidy, a struggling actor who takes a job as a diamond runner for a small jewelry shop and gets caught up in an equally small…

reviews.author: christofotiz
reviews.text: Imperfections is a movie that plays within the conventions of the heist film in just the right ways, while avoiding the clichés and pitfalls of the genre with the precision of a professional minesweeper. Indeed, director David Singer’s maiden voyage shows a bright future for the stories he’ll choose to tell, because Imperfections sparkles. Set in Chicago, the plot follows Cassidy, a down-on-her-luck actress who finds herself jobless. Luckily, the man her mother is seeing offers her a position at his business – a courier for the precious gems he imports. From there, ethics take a backseat to the thoughts of riches made at the hand of insurance fraud, theft and other such immoralities. Though this premise has the potential…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: In the Bedroom is staggeringly good. It's a powerful indie that exists as a real drama around ordinary people. A young man has his life destroyed and a crisis of family breaks out. One tragedy can tear apart everything, for domesticity is very fragile. Our normal lives take very little to be broken. The power of In the Bedroom comes from its very ordinary mood. It is deeply sad because it doesn't try to be melodramatic or emotional. It just exists. Of course, some of the dramatic turns are not everyday occurrences, but they never feel unreal. The filmmaking is slow and deliberate, with everything carefully and delicately placed. It has a quiet approach that keeps action offscreen, like something…

IN THE BEDROOM's is a fairly standard story, but it's one of incredibly quiet and consuming detail. The way that Ruth's eyes latch onto Matt pouring yet another glass of wine, the way that the sound of the lawyer jangling coins in his pocket rises to drown out everything else, Ruth waking to find Matt disassembling the swingset in the middle of…

reviews.author: John Charles
reviews.text: This Columbia western features a familiar plot (the Apaches' uneasy relationship with the white man, who constantly goes against his word, and the one American soldier who is able to befriend Geronimo and broker peace), but it is action packed and well-paced. While George Montgomery doesn't display much nuance as the white hero, veteran Mexican heavy Miguel Inclán dominates all of his scenes as the Spanish-speaking Geronimo. If when watching this you think to yourself, "Didn't I see this before but with Audie Murphy?" then you likely already viewed 1964's APACHE RIFLES from the same writers. Not only is that film a remake, it even uses footage from INDIAN UPRISING.

reviews.text: Watching Ink reminded me of Christmas Eve at my house. There is always it least one toy that has to be assembled. In the process of putting the toy together usually there are cool looking pieces everywhere. It can be frustrating...but with the toy's manual and knowing the end result (the box always has a picture) I eventually get the toy assembled. Well Ink has lots of cool little pieces....but it does not come with a manual and I was not sure what the end result was supposed to be. So watching this movie was somewhat frustrating.

reviews.text: My sister bought me the bluray for Christmas, so I figured it was the perfect time for a rewatch and a chance for her to see one of my ALL TIME favorite films. I will never get over this story. From it's captivatingly beautiful, unique look, to it's beyond genius and moving storytelling, and epic soundtrack, this film accomplishes more - in depth and story - than a lot of big budget movies. The last ten minutes are some of the best moments ever captured on film. Ink is a true work of art that I will always treasure.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: I'm not the biggest fan of American comedies usually, but this is a great blend of science fiction mixed with comedy and adventure, and captures that fun, playful spirit of '80s filmmaking. It's a delightful and absurd premise following a test pilot who is shrunk and accidentally ends up in the body of a hypochondriac, played wonderfully by Martin Short. From then on, it turns into a wild, imaginative ride and becomes anything but serious, and that's exactly where it thrives. It's the right sort of fun, and its mix of action, romance, and satire go effortlessly together, and the more cartoonish side goes well, but it never goes too far in its believable aspect.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Hadn't seen this one since I was maybe eight or nine because I always categorized it in my head as a more impersonal Joe Dante movie. And maybe it is. But the thing about great artists is, there's no off switch to the genius button! This is just a fantastic time. Great high-concept premise, all the stars are at their best, lots of great set pieces and nifty practical effects, and it moves like lightning. Feels weird that this didn't make $120 million in 1987 dollars. It should be one of those movies.

reviews.text: This is the good stuff. The American edit of the two best Super Giant entries. This stuff is as wild as the Japanese verions, but with the fat cut out. All the goods are here: the goofy kappa-alien/salamander men costumes, the acrobatics, the dancing, the random witch, the UFOs, and the amazing swamp castle. reviews.author: DerichHeath
reviews.text: I own this tedious slog for one reason: the story is set on Hart Island, a tiny patch of land off the coast of NYC that serves as a potters field for the cities unidentified dead; over 75,000 people have been buried there since 1890. I say "story" because this wasn't filmed on location. The place has tight security and practically nobody can visit it, unless they're either a maintenance worker or a Rikers inmate digging graves. To my knowledge, Island of the Dead is the only movie to use Hart Island, a real-life source of endless fascination for me, as a jumping point. Sadly, it was shot in Canada, and the disappointments don't stop there.

I just didn’t like it at all. It’s a bleak, messy, and often uncomfortable film that follows the main character through a series of exploitative and disturbing situations. While Chastain gives a committed performance, the movie itself feels aimless and unpleasant. I felt bad for her character, but I never got fully invested in her journey. The writing and pacing didn’t help either—it felt like one unfortunate event after another without much depth or meaningful development. Overall, it was an unpleasant experience, and I wouldn't recommend it.

reviews.author: Sergey Lysenko
reviews.text: In our culture and society, the figure of the Father is sacred, respected, and honored. The role is celebrated and extolled. But much less attention is paid to the role of the Son. What does it mean to be a son? What responsibilities does that impose on you? I can’t think of a work of art that explores these questions off the top of my head. But for me, one of the great personifications of the true Son in our culture is the figure of Christopher Tolkien. A man who spent his entire life exploring, cultivating, and expanding on his father’s legacy is awe-inspiring. And this film, which spends most of its time being a boring parade of talking heads, says more about John Tolkien’s Son than it does about Tolkien himself.

reviews.author: slothtroyer
reviews.text: I could listen to Christopher Tolkien talk about any damn thing for hours, and I would still come knocking on his round Hobbit door the very next day asking for more. It is interesting how one of literature's greatest storytellers produced a son who seems almost supernaturally gifted in the oral tradition (where it all began around a fire on a mountain eons ago anyway). Despite the other jolly old english folks in this doc, this thing could easily be retitled as "Tea Time With Christopher Tolkien." In many ways the doc takes it for granted, and sort of glazes over the fact that Christopher is more than just a talking head here, he has made the celebration, study, and…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Documentaries seldom receive sequels. When they do, the second film is naturally, if often mistakenly, perceived as an admission of inadequacy on the part of the first. Michael Apted’s seminal Up series demands another installment every seven years, but other doc franchises tend not to retroactively enrich their previous chapters by virtue of tacking on a new one. Josh Fox’s Gasland: Part II, to pick on a recent example, arrived less than three years after the first episode helped expose the horrors of slickwater fracking. Both films are skillfully assembled screeds, and the sequel’s more explicitly political tack helps it stand apart from its predecessor, but it’s hard to deny that the seemingly urgent need to make Gasland: Part II…

reviews.text: It's been a while since I last watched Restrepo, but my first impression of Korengal is that it feels like a less visceral, slightly more psychological addendum to the original. It's well done and all, but I'm not sure how necessary it is considering how complete Restrepo was. The film deals with the soldiers' reflections on their experience and overall place in war rather than showing too much of the heavy combat they face on a daily basis. It's a bit of a rough amalgam of topics ranging from relationships with villagers to the meaning of the word "brave," to racial dynamics within the company to the fear, disdain and respect for the enemy. The imagery is powerful and you…

reviews.author: Bob Hovey
reviews.text: Restrepo was a great documentary, and the fact that this is more of the same (with not a whole lot to distinguish it) means that the overall impact is lessened somewhat. Still, it leaves us with the same message... that wars are fought by our children, and they don't always know what they are fighting for, let alone whether or not it's morally right... all they know is, they have an unyielding sense of loyalty and brotherhood with the soldiers standing next to them, and they'll give their lives rather than let those other guys down. Too bad the politicians who send them off to fight don't seem to understand what's at stake for these kids who should be home tinkering with cars and getting laid, not risking life and limb for some cause they can't even articulate.

reviews.author: Nick Vass
reviews.text: Hardly illuminating follow-up to Junger's Oscar-nominated Restrepo uses the talking-head format by explaining Afghanistan's survivalist processes. Sure, this isn't revelatory information, and Battle Company are sharing viewpoints which feel like outtakes from the predecessor. But that's not to say Korengal doesn't have value, for that value, can be found in the juxtaposition of each person's feelings with some cinéma vérité footage. Bullets whooshing by the infantry men's faces, or as they call it, "bullet snaps" managed to catch my attention. The strenuousness is also undeniable as they climb up never-ending mountains. Sometimes, they even look for the enemy in seriously heated areas. Gripping stuff in that regard. It's not always reflective, and rarely meditative, but mainly a shared memory. If anything, you certainly feel for the soldiers and realize once again that war is hell and always be.

reviews.text: As a technical exercise, I can't praise Koyaanisqatsi highly enough. The question of what to even call it is enough to give reviewers pause—is it a documentary? a motion-picture essay? a visual poem? At its most basic level, it's essentially a 90-minute montage, and the way it plays with the Kuleshov effect (how an image changes in relation to what precedes & follows it) is equally brilliant and fascinating. It opens with a 2001-level cut across time from cave paintings to space travel where the exhaust from a shuttle launch seems to burn through the primitive artwork. You might think that an hour and a half without dialogue would be a hard journey, but the film is actually quite enthralling, thanks…

reviews.text: We often fail to realize how absurdly far humanity has gotten, and yet how incredibly small and vulnerable we still are. Enormous mountains, vast and endless deserts, massive jungles of concrete and glass juxtaposed with minuscule microchips that may have initiated the most significant global revolution in human history. Massive and indistinguishable crowds of people going on their day, caught inside their own worlds. And we’ve all taken those things for granted. How far will we go? How much time do we have left until this incomprehensibly gigantic system inevitably collapses on its own feet? What comes after that?

reviews.text: Was revisiting The Grifters via the recent Criterion Blu-Ray release (still good) and thought I’d check out another Stephen Frears film potentially in the same vein (it’s hard to find a real through line in Frears’ diverse filmography). The terrible rep of this “comedy” box office bomb is well earned - it’s, despite a solid cast, muddled and flat - no tension or laughs. I typically love Rebecca Hall and I can see why she would do this - after all with The Grifters Annette Bening under Frears direction secured an Oscar nom playing a savvy and (seemingly) flighty and morally dubious bimbo con artist. Hall’s stripper turned Vegas cocktail waitress turned book maker’s analyst could be a sort of younger more naive up and coming version of Bening’s Myra Langtry; but this isn’t 1990 Frears and they don’t have Donald E. Westlake adapting Jim Thompson.

reviews.text: This is the most playful horror film I've ever seen. This movie is like if the Eraserhead baby had loving parents. It's a cute story about a man-eating baby tree. I've been a huge fan of Jan Švankmajer for years, but surprisingly this is only the second feature film by him I've seen after Alice. This film differs heavily due to it being mostly live action with a very small amount of stop motion animation. It amazes me that Švankmajer's iconic style still comes through in live action. It's hard to tell what's stop motion or live action though because he manages to film both types of scenes identically. It's impressive and exemplifies how he isn't just a stop motion artist, but a filmmaker with a completely idiosyncratic style.

reviews.text: This flick is both fascinating and unsettling. It exerts a peculiar pull, arising from its blend of fairy tale, grotesque, and psychological chamber drama. The stop-motion elements and the haptic aesthetics – wood, earth, body – in particular create a sensual, almost disturbingly tangible world. Švankmajer succeeds in revealing the uncanny within the everyday: the desire for a child imperceptibly tips into the monstrous, and therein lies the film's greatest strength.At the same time, Little Otik feels cumbersome and narratively sluggish for much of its two-plus hours. While the deliberately austere direction and repetitive sequences create a claustrophobic atmosphere, they can also be tiring. Characters often remain more functional than emotionally accessible, making identification difficult. The satirical subplots—such as the neighborhood or the bureaucracy—are not always precise enough to fully unleash their social critique.Still, this adaptation of a Czech fairy tale becomes a dark allegory about consumerism, parenthood, and repression... with a very abrupt ending.

reviews.text: Those who cite the inspirations for American Odyssey movies don’t, as far as I know, typically include Magnet of Doom among other criminals-on-the-lam standbys like Gun Crazy, Breathless, They Live By Night (etc.). If I haven’t just missed the memo, I think this movie’s less-heralded position among Jean-Pierre Melville’s filmography might be because it doesn’t feel like a Melville film. Or, rather, it feels the most French New Wavey of his films, a loose-feeling tour of lesser-known America, absent the gravity of Army of Shadows or the slick tension of Le Samourai and his other gangster flic(k)s.

Ultimately, Karel learns that there is an infiltrator or spy passing information from the circus to the authorities. reviews.text: Somewhat neglected Elia Kazan movie based on the astonishing true story of the Circus Brumbach, which staged a daring attempt to flee totalitarian East Germany in 1950. Relocating the action to Czechoslovakia, Fredric March stars as big top impresario Karel Černík, who hatches an outlandish plot to cross the border into West Germany after communist officials nationalise his circus and order him incorporate propaganda into his show. Although it sounds on paper like an Italian neorealist flick or something from the Czech new wave, Man on a Tightrope is a wordy affair which gets a bit bogged down in Kazan’s rather earnest approach to character. Like Černík’s plan itself, it lumbers slowly to its destination before leaping into action at…

The location in and around Hollywood kind of supplies him with "donors" and has a unique feel for the period of the mid 70s. Watching Richard Basehart as the eye surgeon check out possible victims is pretty good and the scars around his daughter's eyes grow more gross with each new operation assisted by a pretty sleazy looking Gloria Grahame. reviews.text: I once read in a book about World War One how Italian troops were led by some of the most imbecilic, corrupt and privileged officer corps in Europe and, let's face it, there was certainly some stiff competition on offer. But it is true to say that for Italy, WWI was indeed a disaster. Peasant conscripts - industrial workers of major cities like Turin and Milan were needed to continue the output of their prodigious factories, making vast profits for industrialists such as Pirelli, who sold materials to Germany via neutral Switzerland - were ordered into innumerable full frontal attacks on the Austro-German lines along the desolate, frozen Alps. Some 600,000 men were lost in battle, reckless action or as…

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: Francesco Rosi's anti-war film is set a calamitous WWI battle in the Italian Alps and is meant to show the savagery and folly of war. Rosi, a Communist, based it on a memoir by writer Emilio Lusso who was an antifascist. So the film emphasizes the class differences between the patrician generals who revel in the glory and honor of victory versus the enlisted men who are sacrificed to this ideal. It's similar in may ways to Kubrick's Paths of Glory but more focused on the horrors of battle and the tragic consequences of the social stratification.

reviews.author: Josh Brunsting
reviews.text: One of the greatest war films ever made, I literally don't have the power of prose high enough to regard this film properly on this outlet. Coming hot off the heels of his turn in Investigation Of A Citizen Above Suspicion, star Gian Maria Volonte gives a decidedly lower key performance, yet carries all the energy one could imagine coming from the man that gave as bombastic a turn as you'll ever see in that aforementioned Petri picture. Ostensibly mining the same ground that Kubrick turned to for his equally entrancing masterpiece, Paths Of Glory, director Francesco Rosi takes a markedly more naturalistic, and occasionally surrealistic, look at the horrors of war, and all of the absurdities that battle comes…

reviews.text: The only movie I wanted to watch when I heard about Richard Donner’s passing (RIP) was Maverick, which is surely not his best film but is definitely the one I’ve seen the most. It aired approximately 1,000,000 times on HBO in the ‘90s, and I watched it every single time. I loved the con artists all conning each other vibe and the chemistry between the three leads. Decades later, I find all of that still intact, along with Donner’s assured, precise direction. (The visual storytelling in the poker scene is so sharp.) A problematic fav now? Sure. But still a favorite.

With its William Goldman-scripted foundation, it is a start-to-finish blast with energy to spare.

reviews.text: Hard to think of a better car chase scene in a Euro Crime film. Lee Van Cleef and Tony Lo Bianco steal a truck and try and cross into the French border, destroying a hundred dinky little Euro cars along the way, with French cops yelling "Mon dieu!" There's just a really shambolic, out of control aspect to the scene that makes it memorable, including a cop car that gets split in half and continues to drive with only two front wheels. Van Cleef offers his customary hawkish performance (which includes a power drill) and we get Edwige Fenech as a bonus. Lo Bianco is way too over the top with his comedy routine but it's still a fairly nasty, well paced crime film worth tracking down. Be warned that this movie is cut up in some versions (and missing the power drill scene).

reviews.author: Matthew Rice
reviews.text: A completely engrossing look at the lives of pilots on an aircraft carrier during the Korean War. A bit like Top Gun but without the boring bits. It's a fairly procedural look at this insanely dangerous job (and possibly pointless which they touch on) but I love it for that - it takes it's time showing the planes take off, one after the other, the scrambling crew, the briefings and so on...there's no over arching story here but you still become fully invested in the few pilots you meet. Two very memorable sequences...the film messages from home and the nail biting set piece where a pilot is blinded and his wingman tries to fly him back to the aircraft carrier simply by giving him calm instructions. There's some stock footage used but everything you see is real - no models or special effects. This was a real treat considering I had no expectations going in.

reviews.text: Mercy's primary conceit is its unique inversion of the home invasion thriller. As two pairs of half-brothers gather at their ailing mother's home, a group of masked assailants break in and pick them off one by one. Mom's religious background and troubled romantic history suggest that her unconscious body lies at the center of it all. Suddenly, at the halfway point, we (ostensibly!) shift our perspective, watching the same night unfold from the other perspective. The problem is that its staggered narrative flips to the intruders without revealing much of anything. What was the loud noise from earlier? Where did generic brother #3 end up? The movie's got you covered. Why is anybody actually doing anything? No idea. In both…

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: A pulpy, movie-of-the-week level story about assisted suicide collides with home invasion beats in "Mercy," a mediocre thriller that spends most of its running time on the precipice of being less than that. Revolving around a family whose matriarch is in her death bed, the film finds tensions about inheritance and ending the woman's pain give way to an assault on the family's home. The story is constructed in a way that maximizes mystery and tension, and the production is suitable for what the film needs to do. The film is not apt to make any favorites lists, but it ends up a better-than-expected diversion.

reviews.text: A healthy diversion for Micheal Gondry who was supposedly getting too inside his head lately. Microbe and Gasoline is a sweet road movie cum coming-of-age tale of two misfits. They connect to each other through unseen threads of geeky-ness and that's where the charm lies. Gondry's vision of innocence is seen through a lens of subtle sentimentality where he doesn't go too hard on his two lead characters who are out on an adventure. There's a naivety in every frame, a danger in every other, but isn't that just a way to let go of the nuts and bolts in your head? Microbe & Gasoline is about taking the high road and learning while you go through the various ups and downs.

reviews.text: Не видел «Молоха» в приличном качестве, но мутная картинка с самого начала подчёркивает портрет проклятого замка, а размытость движений гимнастирующей обнажённой Евы Браун обнаруживают в ней призрака, хотя она и оказывается самым живым персонажем фильма, всё сильнее отдающего мертвечиной. Гитлер испытывает омерзение при виде новорождённых щенят, рассказывает о ловле раков на мёртвую бабушку и предлагает гостям «трупного чаю» — Сокуров явно вдохновлялся «Клиническим случаем некрофилии». Чтобы показать Гитлера как зло, он показывает его как человека — скучного, жалкого и слабого. А обыденно-зловещее тут и так примерно всё.

reviews.author: Arturo Garavaglia
reviews.text: Con Moloch Sokurov porta in scena prigionieri. Prigionieri di un luogo, il castello, prigionieri di un personaggio.Hitler è descritto per quello che è, uno squilibrato totalmente in balia del suo ruolo incapace di discorsi di un senso logico. Un Hitler tanto grottesco quanto tragico, all'oscuro di Auschwitz (siamo nel 1942) e totalmente in mano ai suoi gerarchi fra i quali spicca Martin Bormann. Eva Braun, protagonista del film, è una donna padrona della prigione in cui vive. Può contraddire Hitler, ma non può mutarne i comportamenti. Ha la libertà di danzare nuda sulle mura del castello nelle affascinanti sequenze iniziali, ma del castello, e del suo ruolo, altro non è che una prigioniera.

reviews.text: Lots of early Baumbach-isms surface here. I think one of the tentpole strengths of a film like The Squid and the Whale is his ability to write unlikeable characters for whom you understand how they got this way, which makes empathy a lot easier. He hadn’t quite nailed it at this point, so a lot of his characters come off as sociopathic more than anything. Ignoring that, and ignoring the limitations that made this feel so much like a movie (I can’t articulate what I mean by that), this was a pretty well-constructed web that comes together about how you’d expect it to, for better or for worse.

Eric Stoltz’s Lester is more likable than the protagonists of the asshole trilogy (Squid, Margot, and Greenberg) that Baumbach follows this up with. Annabelle Sciorra keeps up with the neuroticism of this world effortlessly, Jungle Fever and The Sopranos were enough to sell me on how much of a talent she is. Chris Eigeman is immortalized in TV history as Malcolm in the Middle’s Mr. Herkabe, but his previous efforts with Baumbach show his more endearing side.…

reviews.text: In general, I find jealousy to be a boring plotline. It's a stupid emotion. It's petty, pointless, and ethically wrong. It's damaging and often sexist. It's ugly and once it enters the picture, the outcome is inevitable. (I am, of course, guilty of jealousy myself, but I don't think I've ever let it control me. That said, while I don't like it as a plot line or even a personal quality, I don't judge you if it's something you struggle with.) So the most impressive part of this film is that I didn't just outright hate it.

reviews.text: "Some of the oldest stuff looks the most modern." Two people in stasis as the dead things around them are brought back to life through editing both symbolic and simply evocative. As they drift around listlessly waiting for death (of others, and maybe of selves), the art finds new relevance, clarifying the present and, in some cases, looking toward the future. Like FILM SOCIALISME's postmodern tour of history, COLOR WHEEL's throwback 16mm, CERTIFIED COPY's spin on Rossellini, and UNCLE BOONMEE's national history-as-film history slideshow, somehow the most exciting and progressive films of the new decade are the ones most tied to the past.

reviews.text: Interrupted my Scream watch-through the Wes Craven way, with a little Music of the Heart between parts 2 & 3. Based on the true story of Roberta Guaspari, a teacher who started a violin program for Harlem elementary school students, this is very much a Wes Craven film even if it's not the kind we're used to seeing: broken families struggling to repair themselves, relevant social issues, kids just being kids at school. There's too much schmaltz and not enough story, and the filmmaking is bland even though most of Wes' usual team is on board, but it's an easy watch with excellent performances (Angela Bassett > Meryl Streep). Not my kind of movie at all, but glad I finally watched it.

reviews.text: The growing pains of youth. There’s that one moment we all have where our innocence is lost. The moment where we realize that life isn’t as easy as we thought. It could be your first heartbreak, the death of a pet, a traumatic accident, or in the case for this movie; the loss of the parent. Bittersweet hopefulness. Just a truly lovely coming of age film. A slice of life journey into one boy’s unstable life. But through these awful moments, he slowly becomes someone equipped with what it takes to tackle life. You remember the pain so that you can cherish those moments of seemingly inconsequential stillness and peace.

A sweet sentimentality is often in play, together with a willingness to be candid about youthful sexuality, and Hallström elevates it beyond being just a piece of lightweight fluff into a rather charming picture. reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Basically a DVD extra for ONLY GOD FORGIVES, but a pretty worthwhile one. I can't recall the last time I saw a director this honest about his insecurities (he worries his movie isn’t very good, and complains that he’s wasted years of his life on it) or his cynical calculations about audience tastes (“They want more of the same,” he moans when talking about the pressure to follow DRIVE with something equally commercial). Refn doesn’t come off that well -- he’s moody and self-obsessed and indecisive -- which is kind of interesting given the fact that his wife is the director. If my wife made a documentary that was this revealing and unflattering, I’d be furious. But I guess he got the last laugh; he dedicated THE NEON DEMON to her.

reviews.author: SilentDawn
reviews.text: While only slightly above the quality of an average behind-the-scenes documentary, My Life Directed by Nicolas Winding Refn has quite a few moments of brutal honesty and painful revelations. Set during the filming of Refn's Only God Forgives, Liv Corfixen captures her husband as he slowly moves through the process of tackling such an ambitious project. If you're a huge fan of Refn's vibrant creation (like I am), then consider this documentary essential. Some of the footage is as in-depth and honest as anything that you'll see in a film-making documentary, with emotional breakdowns and failed shoots of filming sometimes veering towards a personal level that I don't care to see. Seeing such familial struggles breaks my heart.

Gemma and his stunt double do some acrobatic parkour-type stunts, while French Caribbean muscleman Serge Nubret is on hand to perform the obligatory feats of strength. reviews.text: in an absolutely bonkers minor key, embellished with one of the strangest senses of space and interconnectivity i've seen in a slasher, and traipsing through an absurd wealth of thinly sketched but ultimately quite compelling ideas about trauma and masculinity and mythology, a solid late effort indeed. fractured identities flee into in the next generation, and, failing to escape their pain and guilt, one by one fold back into the lone survivor, as only the living remain to bear witness, to play the part of the heroic victim, and "fake it good", learning to perform a love of pain just to be human again, human still. smashed dollhouses, strewn bits of a childhood, visitations in the mirror, all of it amounts to the burden of simply living. if the high school segments weren't so affectionately, ridiculously lived-in, none of this might land. but pathos and pleasure go hand in hand, don't they?

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: I've had a lot of cause to think about memory lately. When people leave us, memories are all we have of them, and these memories aren't neatly filed away and preserved in one convenient box. Memories are always changing and evolving based on how we choose to mythologize our lives. They're also triggered by objects and places, and when you get rid of a place or object, you feel the weight of potentially losing whatever you have left of whoever you've lost. They're also not segregated into Good and Bad sections. When you're thinking about the goodness of what you've lost, your mind may also take you to the badness, because these things are not extricable.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: I also gave COWARDS BEND THE KNEE 5 stars, but this deserves a few more. It's, in my opinion, far and away Guy Maddin's best feature: an essay film that's part autobiography, part real history lesson, part bullshit history lesson, full of jokes and surreal flourishes. In his previous/other features Guy plows through his own memories as if they were a melodramatic three dimensional playscape, but here the three dimensional playscape has its own memories to add into the mix. The "hysterical truth" (to borrow Dennis Lim's phrase) achieved via this sincere but make-believe interrogation makes for the most moving of any of Maddin's features. I can't recall any other time I've gotten teary-eyed watching a hockey arena get demolished…

reviews.author: Disgustipated
reviews.text: This is how I would like to remember my city, a surreal documentary just like My Winnipeg. A mythical intersection between truth and fantasy. Besides as I get older the truth becomes fuzzier and the fantasy becomes bolder. What is more important, the story of my city or it's microfiche and records? Does it really matter, either way? We know in our hearts that the dirt was drenched with blood, tears of pain then flooded it all away and from the corpses of indigenous peoples and criminals did a city grow and take hold. We know because it feels heavy and dark and lurks in the shadows of our souls. Why do you think we all drink so much? That is my Sydney. And It's funny how your parents have a habit of being exactly who you think they are until you no longer know who they ever really were... but that is another story.

reviews.text: Maddin's narration is filled with numerous jokes that speak to his whimsical, abstruse sense of humor, and yet the glimpses of actual honesty and his almost philosophical commentary on some of the surreal, goofy imagery reveals the genuine consideration that goes into his fanciful method of moviemaking. Its mixture of psychosexual confessional, city symphony, documentary and farce, all naturally filtered through Maddin's love for silent-era techniques and variations, testifies to the manner in which the most primitive methods and storytelling devices in cinema history still seem like the most radical. Somehow, the shots of Winnipeg as it actually is today, with present-day buildings and cars inching along snow-covered roads, is the strangest thing here.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: For its first 29 minutes, this movie is nothing — just another macho cop drama resting upon routine uncertainty and tall, vaguely angry men. But then Gloria Grahame appears, and everything snaps into focus. She’s wearing a black dress with spaghetti straps and she’s singing; her face is blank and she’s aggressively emotionless, making it clear to everyone in the room that she feels nothing for her job and nothing for any of them. She’s utterly mesmerizing and, for the next 60 minutes, the movie is hers entirely. She’s desperate and sexy, then frightened but resolute, then brittle and withdrawn, pulling strings on and off of the screen.

reviews.text: Fairly cliché but solidly made old-school cop drama that appears to have been lost to time in comparison to the fiery theatrics of something like Training Day. Not a whole to Carnahan's violent adrenaline junkie vs. family man moral dilemma but it is elevated a lot by Jason Patric as the former undercover cop suffering the psychological consequences of going too deep and (especially) Ray Liotta as the temperamentally unhinged lieutenant he is brought in to assist in finding out who murdered his partner. The eventual revelations involving dirty cops, junkies and police brutality/suicide couldn't have possibly surprised anyone even two decades ago, but I really took to the grungy, grainy, slow-burn structure and style of it. It's a better macho melodrama than action-thriller which was really unexpected considering the direction Carnahan's career went in after this.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Nintendo Quest" is a 2015 road documentary directed by Robert McCallum. The narrative follows the main director's friend, Jay Bartlett, as he attempts to pick up all 678 North American officially licensed games for the original Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The one conditional element is that he has 30 days to accomplish this quest and none of the games can be purchased online. The goal of it all is to seek how many can be found in person, which becomes insanely hard as some games ("Stadium Events" and "Little Sampson" specifically) can go for thousands of dollars.

reviews.author: Mary-O James
reviews.text: The people are likable cause they're Nintendo-obsessed Canadians but this feels like a documentary made for them, by them. There's not enough interesting Nintendo background info or enough documentary-style pathos to keep someone invested. It ends up looking like a Saturday morning special. For a film that bookends itself by telling the viewer to go out there on a spontaneous journey with your friends and make new ones, it shows none of those moments, just some bland, non-dramatic haggling. Shame about Jay's dog, though. He could've put that Nintendo money to better use in nursing his pet, rather than on some indulgent obsession.

reviews.text: Salò o le 120 giornate di sodoma (1975) was not the first time that the self-proclaimed cinematic poet Pier Paolo Pasolini borrowed classic literature in order to criticize the Nazi-Fascism of Italy. Remember that Salò is a toponymical metonymy for the Italian Social Republic (RSI), since such city was its seat of government during the last days of Benito Mussolini’s regime, making it a puppet state of Nazi Germany. He mixed the politics of Nazi-Fascism with Marquis de Sade’s book and created a furiously brutal criticism against the politics that pervaded Italy during its war times and during the aftermath of World War II.

reviews.text: Alan Smithee gives early warning. Bill Moseley and Kane Hodder as junkers posing as paramedics hunt "teenagers" responsible for the hit-and-run of their mother. Loads of CW drama follow a girl, before abruptly switching focus to another, between a handful of sequences with the veteran pair. Moseley gets opportunities to emote while his screen brother remains mute. Flashbacks to their childhood don't add much beside explaining why Hodder wears a face mask. In odd aesthetic choices, the picture has a gaussian blur and slant toward the bottom left giving everyone long faces. Director Christian Winters is nowhere in the extras but a producer's commentary laughs over the Smithee credit. Shame, even if Winters's intentions were bad that's preferable to what's still mediocre. Watched via Epic Pictures's DVD.

reviews.text: In many ways a hopeful rework of all the paranoid alienation of In a Lonely Place in pulpier genre terms. Ray’s romanticism and empathy put to great use. The film main subject matter, the thin line between caring too much and not caring at all doubles as an appreciation of Ray’s own work method. Indeed, the film most astonishing feature, those 20 minutes between the moment Ryan shows up in front of Lupino’s door and she leaving to go look after her brother the next morning, are some of the best modulated drama in all movies. And what else can I say? The manner in which Ray builds from Lupino’s blindness to how Ryan learns to actually experience another person, some things just defeat our words.

reviews.author: carrieandtracy
reviews.text: Hard as nails, then the tone shifts dramatically. It’s too easy to dismiss the love story as mawkish and simplistic, “Tough Guy feels sorry for Blind Girl.” There’s something deeper — more soulful, even spiritual — at work in the connection between Ryan and Lupino. It’s maybe not as narratively satisfying as traditional noir, but it aspires to something greater. It damn near kicks the protagonist OUT of his noir, then travels him into a religious parable. And he is as perplexed and lost and agonized as any lead in a Ray film.

reviews.author: covkate
reviews.text: I knew I was going to love this right from the start. Sometimes I just get that feeling; everything seems right. This is a film of two parts, the first being an excellent study of the dark heart of the city. It's a beautiful start, like a textbook of noir, with some great dialogue too. It shows Robert Ryan's character struggling with loneliness, rage, and rank cynicism, drowning in the darker side of human nature that he comes into contact with every day - and with nothing and no-one in his life to act as counterweight, he's sinking fast. Getting handy with his fists one too many times, he's packed off to deal with a murder case in the country…

reviews.text: Robert Ryan is, fundamentally, a physical actor. Even as he sometimes struggles to sell the words he's asked to recite, or to fully engage with characters he's asked to sell, his face and his body are enormously reliable storytelling tools. And, in Nicholas Ray's On Dangerous Ground, it's those things that make the movie's central relationship -- between Ryan's brutal, desperate cop (Jim Brent) and Ida Lupino's brittle, saintly blind girl (Mary Maiden) -- work.

reviews.author: Steve Moyle
reviews.text: Turkish director Nuri Bilge Ceylan's Once Upon a Time in Anatolia is a masterful exploration of the human condition and is a film that I'm finding difficult to describe although I do feel like I understood a lot of what it's essentially saying about the sin and guilt of it's characters. The amount of depth to be found here makes for a hard review after just one viewing at least for me, the film is just so engrossing and meditative though. It's surely long but managed to just hold me in it's grip as I admired the masterful cinematography and complexities of the very natural performances. The dialogue is beautifully poetic and I'm not sure what else to say at this point other then that this is truly cinema in it's purest form, endlessly fascinating and hypnotically effective.

reviews.author: 𝑅𝑜𝑛シ︎
reviews.text: This film is about the transitory, often unseen moments of intense beauty that occur in a world overrun by violence and desolation. It's a dark film that haunts the recesses of the mind, but allows just enough room for the light to creep in. Words can fail the men, whose stories of lost wives and other ghosts drench the movie in an acute sense of loss, one that is offset by the effulgence of the natural world, a gift that none seem to see. The dead haunt “Once Upon a Time in Anatolia,” but so does beauty. More than anything, a film about death -- or perhaps more specifically, mortality…In Ceylan’s hands, this landscape becomes a metaphysical one. The endless…

reviews.text: I once had an English professor in college stress the importance of the first and last sentences in a novel. Words that often carry a more significant level of intention in the writing. You’ve got the kickoff, the tone setter, the establishing language, the first chance to draw in and hook the reader. And then you have the wrap up, the au revoir, the sequence of words the author presumably hopes will rattle around in your head as you close the book, leaving the world you were just immersed in to re-enter your own. Often, while visiting a bookstore, I like to grab a book off the shelf and read the first and last sentences. It’s a good way to…

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Writer-producer-director Tsui Hark’s sprawling vision of a changing nineteenth-century China begins with this riotously entertaining epic, a blockbuster hit that cemented Jet Li’s status as the greatest martial-arts superstar of his generation. Li displays his stunning, fast-yet-fluid fighting style as the legendary martial-arts teacher and doctor Wong Fei-hung, who, with a band of loyal disciples, battles a host of nefarious forces—foreign and local alike—threatening Chinese sovereignty as British and American imperialists encroach upon the Mainland. Once Upon a Time in China’s breathtaking blend of kung fu, comedy, romance, and melodrama climaxes in a whirlwind guns vs. fists finale that is also a thrilling affirmation of Chinese cultural identity.

reviews.author: eddie
reviews.text: Tsui Hark's action scenes make me want to stand up off the couch like a great live sporting event, and I think it has to do with a false sense of spontaneity he creates. martial artists can change direction mid-air, the camera will follow, and the cutting makes it seem deceivingly immediate/spur of the moment when of course many of these maneuvers must have taken full days to complete. he's an action painter the same way people describe Tony Scott, whooshes of motion and color fill the screen while every cut obscures the real sense of time — and somehow the chopped up choreography plays back perfectly smooth in my head. Tsui Hark is the god of cinema.

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: Breathtaking. Anyone passionately looking for the true classics of the wu-xia genre should encounter this stylish Hong Kong masterpiece that even gently reminds us of the existentialist beauty of the famous Samurai trilogy by Inagaki combined with the cultural elements of a folk way of living. Action lovers should also appreciate this branch of filmmaking. An extraordinary art-direction embellishes an epic-scoped journey proud of its cultural origins and constructed of dualities: peace vs. violence, guns vs. kung-fu, peace vs. self-defense tradition, nationalism vs. foreign oppression, Eastern conservatism vs. Westernization... Even for the standards of Tsui Hark, this achievement is gigantic.

reviews.author: jryn7
reviews.text: It’s well-accepted what a strong and influential movie Once Upon a Time in China is to all the Hong Kong martial arts films that came after. It was so popular that it yielded five sequels and a TV series, and it exploded Jet Li in popularity. All that being said, I prefer my martial arts films to have weapons, like swordfighting wuxia or gun fu like John Woo or John Wick movies. Watching people just beat on each other in long hand to hand combat fights wears me and my attention span out, and Once Upon A Time In China is not a short film…with a million subplots of varying intensity. Still, that’s a personal preference issue of my own,…

It’s nowhere near as good, but it does share characters weaponizing conventional morality to harm their enemies, which is interesting given the emphasis on maintaining the status quo I associate with the 1950s. (It feels significant that both of these are period pieces.) I suppose this is not significantly different than what Sirk did in All That Heaven Allows or There’s Always Tomorrow, so I may just be imposing patterns. But I did appreciate how this movie was invested in found family, a rare thing in contemporary melodramas.

reviews.text: Esse filme é literalmente uma aula sobre alguns princípios básicos do cinema. A premissa é evidentemente feminista: uma mulher vira delegada de polícia e tem que superar o machismo de todos os seus colegas além de perder o medo das operações de campo. A questão é que de premissas não vivem os filmes. A premissa é transformada em uma história roteirizada com cenas, diálogos, situações. Depois, há a transformação do escrito em mise-en-scène, na concretização visual daquelas cenas antes apenas imaginadas. Aí que está: diversas escolhas, tanto a nível de roteiro quanto de mise-en-scène contradizem a premissa, pois reforçam o machismo. O que dizer do jeito como os policiais machões são filmados de maneira glorificadas portando suas armas e chegando…

reviews.author: fey
reviews.text: Simply simple. Strictly straightforward. Operation Leopard is a distanced approach to depicting a conflict which otherwise would've been used to inspire shock. And sure, some of the coldblooded murder shown here *IS* shocking, but Coutard never emphasizes the event beyond showing what it is and then moving on. The best way to describe this film would be to call it "observational". It is precisely like war, a series of senseless killings and traumatising visions that don't truly affect the people involved until they return home and have to contend with ghosts of the past. Clever lines here and there, weariness and witty skepticism prevalent throughout, but the movie never tries to spread a specific message. It doesn't moralize the situation, simply shows you what is and makes you to conclude why it is so.

Porém, quando essas ideias saem do discurso e vão para a prática, fica claro como é difícil colocá-las em ação de verdade. Quando se trata de religião, isso se torna ainda mais complicado, já que muitas crenças se baseiam na ideia de que possuem a verdade absoluta. reviews.text: For his follow-up to the neorealist masterpiece Rome, Open City, Rossellini trades in intimacy for scope with Paisan; a film that examines the importance of communication, connection and commitment during wartime. Told through six vignettes, with each penned by a different screenwriter (including a young Fellini), what we have here are essentially moral tales set against the backdrop of the allied invasion of Italy. Each vignette takes place in a different city, from when the Americans first land, to the Winter prior to the conclusion of WWII, and tell varying tales of struggles with lingual or culture barriers, moments of realization and courage, and the atrocities of war. reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: When a film is divided into episodes, each with its own story, the challenge is finding a thread strong enough to hold them together. Too often anthologies feel scattered, like they’re pulling in many different directions at once. But when it works, when each episode feels like a variation on a single theme, the result can be staggering. Paisan is one of the finest examples of that balance.
