reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Filmed in the ruins of post-war Italy, Paisan is a vital neorealist portrait of a country in chaos. Across six stories, it starts with the Allied invasion of Sicily and then moves up the Italian Peninsula, following liberation through the eyes of ordinary people. Paisan is a collage of a country, centered on a series of friendships between Italians and Allied soldiers. It is a film of human understanding, about crossing the language barrier to find hope and kindness. In the very first story a woman and a foreign soldier are able to find a peace with nothing but a few words. At times Paisan is harsh, filled with impoverished people and the suffering of civilians in wartime. Bloodied bodies…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Once again incorporating documentary footage with a neorealist narrative to substantially meaningful effect, Paisan is another extraordinary war drama from Roberto Rossellini. It's the second entry in his neorealist trilogy, and while perhaps it is the least well known of them, it's undoubtedly comparable in respects to greatness. Constructed from six separate instalments, with none of them succumbing to overwhelming melodramatics, it accentuates a collision between two very diverse societies.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Bazin said this film's individual unit was not the "shot" but the "fact," and if PAISAN's sketches indulge in types and ordered mini-narratives, it is Rossellini's open but nevertheless controlled aestheticization and his minute, compartmentalized vignettes depict realism as it should be. Rossellini excels at setting up a social backdrop but working resolutely through an intimate focus that digs into characters in means that stretch beyond social conditions. If De Sica's films, for example, are directly a product of the surrounding rubble and poverty, Rossellini's themes in PAISAN—miscommunication, perspective, loneliness—stretch so far outside the military and socioeconomic context that at times it is the characters who seem to birth the stark ruin around them, a collapsed Tower of Babel.

Lulu isn’t a femme fatale in the classic sense; she doesn’t manipulate or plot anything. She simply exists, free from what the world seems to impose, unbound by bourgeois morality and patriarchy, and it’s precisely this freedom that made me scared of her fate. reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: Samuel Fuller's favourite of his films is a crackerjack story about the rise of a newspaper that wants to do NEWS the RIGHT WAY. I'm a little befuddled why their first two issues are about a guy who's a hero because he jumped off the Brooklyn bridge, but it's impossible not get caught up in Fuller's pulpy propulsion and energetic direction that's at at once insanely precise (Amazing long takes on a giant set) and sloppily saved in editing (Blatant jump cuts into blow-ups of a wide shot). It's the kind of nervy panache that makes Fuller Fuller. It's more interested in the feel and the passion for printing news than the moral question of why it must be done, but by the end, every audience member will want to run out and start a gosh darn paper themselves!

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: "Playing for Keeps" is a glossy, handsomely shot film the can't quite make up its mind. Is it a romantic comedy featuring affection-hungry soccer moms? Is it a redemption story of a washed-up, former soccer star? Is it a father-son bonding film? Is it a reconciled marriage fantasy? The film's biggest issue is not that it tries to be all of the above. It is that it tries to be all of the above and does it in the dullest, uninvolving manners available. With its full plate of story threads and cast members, "Playing for Keeps" ends up being unfocused and tedious. There are some bright spots, but, for the most part, the film is too much of a slog to enjoy.

reviews.text: This might very well be getting that Canadian genre cinephile bump (I grew up about 25 minutes away from Pontypool) but I do genuinely think "what if Night of the Living Dead was a locked-in War of the Worlds radio play starring Kawartha Lakes' Howard Stern?" is an amazing premise for a movie, and Stephen McHattie is so good at doing the Talk Radio thing that it effectively carries it through the more derivative zombie movie elements. Also helps that it has a legitimate cinematic interest in its Romero-esque ideas about the literal breakdown of the communication process, and has a pretty fantastic low-budget chilly, doomed atmosphere that it holds true to right til the cut to black.

reviews.author: DirkH
reviews.text: This film suffers from the 'third-act syndrome'.It tries to do something new with the 'zombie genre' and for the better part of the film it succeeds. The build up is gripping, the tension palpable and the acting is great. Without resorting to any cheap effects the director managed to instil in me a real feeling of dread and suspense. Even the rather far-fetched reason as to why the 'zombies' are what they are and do what they do seemed plausible, probably because the film builds up a lot of credit in the first two-thirds of the running time.The conclusion, however, just derails somehow. The solution to all their problems is creative, but acted out in such a ludicrous way I found myself going from tension to short outbursts of sarcastic laughter to a mere sigh during the final credits.A shame, but still, worth the watch if only for the first parts of the film.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: "Power of Grayskull: The Definitive History of He-Man and the Masters of the Universe" may not actually be THE definitive history of all things He-Man and the Masters of the Universe, but it is a solid documentary detailing the rise and fall of Mattel's '80s toy line and the TV and film output that followed. Interviews with the toy creators make up the bulk of the documentary, and the information presented is compelling for an audience interested in Gen-X staples. The film excels when it allows Dolph Lundgren to wax nostalgic about his role in the film or picks at the sexism involved in the creation of the She-Ra line. Though there may not be enough of those informational thunderbolts, the documentary still rates as a capable piece of non-fiction film.

reviews.text: Rock star fascism with a heavy dose of O Lucky Man aesthetics and religious iconography, a sort of rock'n'roll fantasy that really would only have worked during this era when superstardom was still relatively new, when the idea of conquering the world through pop music felt real. Thus, it feels dated, a paranoid boomer story that thrived in a world where the Beatles and the Stones still looked like gods. (Now, everyone is in Beyonce's shadow, as they should be.) In La Commune, Watkins would take the trappings of political imagery to their extremes in service of a leftist history piece, but here, he lays on thick the propagandist visuals in a rock'n'roll martydom piece, excoriating Britain, the church, the music industry, capitalism, and celebrity (and the worship thereof) all at once. But but but these critiques don't feel new or interesting anymore--we've seen it all come true.

reviews.author: Ruth Scouller
reviews.text: An Australian documentary about the market of Bordeaux wine in China, narrated by Russell Crowe. If that intrigues you, this is worth a watch. If not, give it a miss. Whilst I found a lot of the discussion very basic, it's nevertheless an entertaining documentary which appealed to me (despite some cringey culture clash positioning, although to a degree such attitudes are believable given recent French history). Mildly interesting viewing for wine enthusiasts, but best filed along with modern China documentaries. Wine just happens to be the hip luxury collector item under the spotlight here, an inviting way into a more interesting discussion on global economics, particular in the wake of China's rise. Whilst the filmmaker's approach to the subject, and tossed up conclusions, are somewhat disagreeable, its nevertheless well presented. Empty calories, but an easy watch for those with even a passing interest in the modern, globalised world.

reviews.author: Adam Nayman
reviews.text: A self-portrait of the artist as a noble, principled warrior, with a climax set outside the big pay per view showdown - all the better to seal a victory that resonates beyond a corrupt, sensationalistic showbiz milieu. If you were to tell me this was Mamet’s best produced and executed film as a director, I’m not sure I’d argue. It lacks the element of surprise (which carried House of Games) and it’s a strictly B-level cast, but the raggedness of the actors is quite endearing on the whole, with Tim Allen in particular killing it as a parody of ex-action-star sleaze. It’s funny to watch something that was made contemporaneously with Mamet’s rightward heel turn, and feels inflected though not infected by it; compared to truly abject stuff like the Phil Spector movie, it’s not only smarter and better but just so much less *strained.*

(And star Jimmy Wang Yu would do something similar later in his career, when he followed up "One-Armed Boxer" with the psychedelic kung fu classic "Master of the Flying Guillotine"). The original "One-Armed Swordsman" smoldered with a sense of anti-establishment rage, to the point that viewers have long cited it as the wuxia genre's answer to "Rebel Without a Cause." reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Live in the Chang Cheh universe and want a quick death? Be a bad guy - chances are, unless you're one of the supreme villains, you'll just get hit with a sword or some other bladed weapon and go down after a quick blood gush and maybe a grimace on the way down. If you're a hero, you're more than likely going to pay for your moral peace of mind with extreme suffering, a lingering death while you fight, fight, fight until your last drop of blood hits the ground. You might even be forced to do yourself in, a sword through your stomach to take out the bad guy behind you, or slicing your own arm off in order to make some kind of persuasive point. Anybody can do the right thing when it's easy - what do you want, a medal?

The film is a comedy above all else. Return to the 36th Chamber is obviously very self aware and the humour is varied, with some aspects working better than others. reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Liked this a lot more than when I first saw it years ago. Lau never really did comedy as well as his younger peers, so this can be a bit embarrassing (poor Hsiao Ho and his teeth, for example), but the movie is a whole is a lot smarter than I remembered. A parody of the first film, but one that nonetheless follows all the rules it establishes about training and praxis. But this revolution is a small scale one, involving only a group of workers at a a single factory, and is wholly shorn of any degree of mysticism or spiritual belief (it is, after all, ultimately a comedy).

What I expected was evil!John Ireland and some other dudes terrorizing innocents in a small western town; what I got instead was a domestic-on-horseback, a sort of found family love story, with a little bit of grudge-holding murderer thrown in. And, if you can ignore the fallen woman nonsense that accompanies every prostitute love story in a western, it’s really quite sweet. Gloria Grahame always feels very modern to me so it’s hard to buy in her roles like this one, but she is pretty winning as the resilient hooker with a heart of gold (TM), while Robert Sterling is blandly handsome, and manages to deliver some moments of real sensitivity as the cowboy with a target on his…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Gloria Grahame is great and this RKO western has some interesting material about the limited options for women in the old west. The studio made relative few genre entries, but like most of those it has a rough starker surface. There's some terrific use of locatio. Mark Robson directs and while this is a bit talkier than his action oriented instincts often gets, it is among his strongest efforts. Robert Sterling is a major limiting factor if this starred one of the studios better leading men like Ryan or Mitchum, it would probably had a reputation as a minor classic.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: Mixes together a lot of tropes to excellent effect. Robert Sterling as a rancher with a young brother played by Claude Jarman tries to shield the youngster from dancehall girls of which Gloria Grahame is one, and so low the esteem she and her fellow dancehall girls can hardly step foot in any decent ranch house without being scowled at. Grahame puts up with a lot of judgement from Sterling but the young Jarman knows she's a good woman and starts to hate his asshole brother. Anyway, Jarman is pretty good, big enough to act kind of like a young Jody Foster, and directed by Mark Robson, it gets pretty dark intermittently with John Ireland and two other murderous prison escapees with nothing to lose in some action that's well above average. The chance encounters on the trail with the judgmentalism gradually softening in the fight with the real bad guys.

The story-telling from director Mark Robson teeters at times a little too much on the overly wholesome side because of the presence of the boy, but overall it’s well-balanced and doesn’t overstay its welcome at 88 minutes. I also liked how he left the fate of one of the dancehall/working girls (Myrna Dell) to our imagination in a chilling moment, maybe the film’s best. I’m not sure I can imagine liking the film without Grahame though, she’s just stunning.

reviews.text: Certain actors got stereotyped during the Golden Age of Hollywood, whether it was in Noirs or Westerns, Musicals or Gangster films, and breaking out of those stereotypes proved difficult for some. The Studio system saw them control who did what, and their big stars made big money for them, so why risk having them do something that might not work? The Musical genre had Fred and Ginger, Judy Garland, Esther Williams, and a host of others. Noirs had Alan Ladd, Humphrey Bogart, Glenn Ford, Victor Mature, and more, and the Westerns had Wayne, Cooper, McCrea, and many many more. And then there was the Gangster genre, led by Edward G. He listens to Derek and he tries new ideas, introduces new elements to his figure and environment. It doesn't work, Cagney loses his cool and is shown the fates. He holds near his failure for its loss and beauty.

Two underage middle-class girls prostitute themselves, believing it is a grown-up way to pay their own way to European holiday. reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: A film that connects child prostitution and religion is understandably open to criticism and debate. The concept has the potential to be tremendously sleazy, dangerous, and just downright irresponsible. And yet, to enter this provocative world of holy whores and Old Testament wrath is much more abstract, more prone to metaphor, than its tawdry premise actually reveals. Rather than show the egregious sex acts themselves (which occur offscreen), SAMARITAN GIRL becomes this strange, symbolic meditation on redeeming morally reprehensible men by turning sex into a tool of sainthood. It sounds backwards, and it is, but where this religiously-infused nightmare starts making a lot of sense is during its second critical half when a father begins to reign apocalyptic fury on…

reviews.author: Maki
reviews.text: If there's one thing this movie did right, it's crystalize why I don't enjoy modern "bad" movies. It's too easy to make a competent, good looking movie now. You can get dozens of takes without worrying about running out of film. You can get cheap CG to cover up mistakes or take the place of practical effects. This has left modern bad movies either super-boring or super-ironic. Samurai Cop 2 decided to go the super-ironic route. On paper, that makes sense, considering the majority of fans of the original Samurai Cop love it in an ironic way.

reviews.text: The inherent problem with Samurai Cop 2: Deadly Vengeance is that it lacks the sincerity that the original film had. Here, director Gregory Hatanaka goes out of his way to cram EVERY possible reference to the first film that he could into its bloated run time. This sequel is almost too self-aware of itself and ultimately tries too hard to be a bad movie rather than achieving the same result with competent earnestness. Tommy Wiseau's cameo sums it all up. It's nice to see most of the original cast back once again but that's about as far as any form of praise this film…

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: Cinema undiluted, yet clouded; quintessential, yet corrupted; lucid, yet vague; high-minded, yet smothered in dirty shapes, postured to perfection. Designed to transport, to form a familiar, albeit foreign environment for its viewers through patient, sincere and expressive manipulation of audiovisual details, resulting in a pure-form, sensory-cinema experience. Indeed, Satantango is meticulously crafted to shift its viewers from their (position in a chair, or) place in reality, into the gut of a nonentity-like vehicle, slowly drifting, but at the same time quickly catapulting through the process of a bleak, syncopated, rhythmic flit with the dark heart of a total eclipse. In essence, caliginosity and crepuscule as an unfathomable, esoteric and profoundly inexplicable display of medium-mastery. And, in the end, one of the human race's single greatest accomplishments, both inside and outside the field of artistic creation.

reviews.text: Not one of the better Adkins/Johnson collaborations. The milieu - post-Dien Bien Phu/pre-American intervention Vietnam - is an interesting one, as is the Casablanca-like collection of desperate fugitives and ex-Nazis. But the storytelling is a bit sloppy (the love interest could not be more boring) and the fighting is mostly uninspired, aside from two slobberknockers between Adkins/Cung Le and Adkins/Marko Zaror. You have to wade through a lot of crap to get to the good stuff.

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: Far from Scott Adkins and Jesse V. Johnson's best collaboration together, but Savage Dog still has the necessary great action to make up for the subpar story and basic plotting. Aesthetically, this one isn't too bad-looking for a low-budget DTV actioner and Johnson certainly makes the most of what he's given, but it's also clear that little attention is being paid to the story and this really hinders the first half as a lot of that is rather slow and uninteresting. Once the action begins in earnest though, it's a lot of fun seeing Adkins do his thing and the fight scenes are all pretty varied and executed to a typically high standard with brutal fights and clean editing. Having Keith David in the cast is also a huge plus since it's always nice to see him, with his presence and the action being enough to make Savage Dog a solid film for Adkins fans.

It doesn't all work (What's up with the weak sound design during the fight scenes?), but the gorgeous visuals and the lengthy violent climax (Practical blood hits! Woo-Hoo!) won me over. I was worried for a second that Marko Zaror wouldn't fight, but then the film goes "Ah, we were just kidding. Here's a re-creation of the SPL Wu-jing fight!"

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Close-ups have never been less personal than they are in SECONDS: nearly every face seen in isolation belongs to someone else, a given mask that consumes the host. This was a banner year for jaundiced visions of the American Dream, from an EDM-inspired, fauvist teen flick to an outright flesh parade from America's best living filmmaker, but SECONDS arguably goes further than any of them in vivisecting the hollow, indeterminate goal of the American Dream, and how people will take any chance to chase desires they cannot even identify, and how exposure to the inevitable failure of the pursuit of an undefined goal destroys them. The finale, which exposes the shadow company at the heart of the film as perhaps the only true fulfillment of that dream, recycling its clients to furnish new ones in a perpetual profit device, is so horrifying that James Wong Howe's impeccably hallucinatory cinematography is almost secondary in generating a mood of unease.

It’s an adaptation of Camillo Boito's 1882 novella with a dramatic commandeering of cinematography by G.R. The centurion who has been in charge has been abusing the slaves, and Marcus puts an end to that practice. In retaliation, the centurion instigates a slave revolt and pins the blame on Marcus. Six slaves escape into the desert, and one of them (Gordon Mitchell), rescues Marcus and takes him along. They reach a Roman provincial town and disguise themselves as the Wolf Head Gladiators, seeking to earn enough money to hire a boat and sail far away. The very low budget "Spartacus" knock-off is pretty haphazardly scripted, but is a pretty decently entertaining cheap actioner.

reviews.text: Blood sprays the camera lens and suddenly the wisps of red are ribbons flapping on a pole. Christ is superimposed on stain glass. The camera rests statically on the roof around an open courtyard in wet autumn or frosted winter, watching rituals and daily routines. The camera swims through the air, following intense motion through bald forests. A doe sits behind a veil of trees next to a thin, wooden cross marking the grave of a lover. Parajanov's fevered mythic tragedy is a parade of images that, as some have pointed out, exceed the narrative they illuminate; a simple fantasy turned into a period portrait, a Carpathian church mural come to life.

reviews.text: Not to be dramatic but it’s one of the most beautiful films ever. An avant-folk dirge that contains all of Earthly life within it, a solar deity incantation metastasized into a rustic-pastoral drone. Its mysticism towards seasonal/cyclical change is only spiritual insofar as spirit is contained already within matter, dirt, soil, history. Similarly, as a magical realist parable or gnostic/syncretic fable, we see that paganism is inextricable from Christian culture, superstition, decorum, clothing, habit. Every Orthodox ritual is a callback (conscious or not) to a heathen past. A radical shift in perspective; the landscape is defamiliarized through anarchic camera technique so as to approximate the way the land would have been perceived by the characters in their respective time and…

reviews.author: David Sims
reviews.text: I had forgotten just how wonderful and clever this film is. Especially in its plotting, how it leans into every Shakespearean trope and twist and reveals them for the wonderful devices they are and as the building blocks for almost any romantic comedy. It's so devoutly reverential (Shakespeare's poetry is literally transformative for almost every character) and at the same time so up-front about how mercenary and formulaic his plot process could be. Then this happens, then that happens, etc., etc., but when you watch the audience watch Romeo and Juliet for the first time, it hits you what a thing that must have been. To be surprised when Juliet gets up and sees Romeo dead!

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This film often doesn't get a lot of respect, even among Italian horror fans, and I'm sure the reason for that is at least partly because it was released as an unrelated sequel to a crappy horror film. However, the fact is that Mario Bava's last full feature sees him go out with a bang rather than a whimper. Shock is beautifully realised schlocky haunted house feature that is engaging throughout with a number of interesting elements thrown in for good measure. Dario Nicolodi gives a powerhouse performance in the lead role and gets good support from some Italian regulars. It had to be said that the film lacks a bit of edge at times but all the slow build horror really pays off in the end and the final fifteen minutes are just great.

reviews.text: So it would seem that director Sergio Corbucci decided to really let his hair down for his final Spaghetti Western. The White, the Yellow, and the Black is a parody of the genre; taking the basic set up from Sergio Leone's famous western with a similar title and the main plot from Red Sun. It's an East meets West type thing as an outlaw and a sheriff become involved with an inept wannabe samurai when some Indians steal a ceremonial horse intended as a present for the US government. The film benefits from an absolutely great cast of genre stalwarts, with Eli Wallach, Giuliano Gemma and Tomas Milian in the central roles. It's a good job too as I cant…

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Sergio Corbucci's final spaghetti western suggests that the director was keenly aware of changing public tastes, but is still woefully out of touch. A parody of Red Noon sees a horse meant as a gift from the Japanese to the US government stolen by Native Americans, and it falling on a sheriff (Eli Wallach), thief (Guiliano Gemma), and inept japanese servant (Thomas Milian) to mount a rescue operation. All three are great comic actors, while the Corbucci machine promises a serious technical polish and visual daring that doesn't disappoint. Even resembling his Spencer/Hill comedies over his distinctly violent westerns, this still had all the elements needed to be a memorable swansong to Corbucci's west. reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: They Died with Their Boots On, or better known as Silver Saddle, is the third, final and definitely my least favorite of director Lucio Fulci's westerns. But I still found it to be a pretty entertaining film. There's certainly some downtime here, and all things considered, this feels like a pretty light effort from everyone involved. However, it should be noted that this movie was made at the very end of the spaghetti western cycle. And at that point in time there was not much new left to do with the genre in terms of style, narrative and themes. So it's all been done before and often better, but the good cast and Fulci's solid direction make it worthwhile for genre fans in my opinion.

Blood gets hired to shoot a Barrett, which sounds great to him until he realizes his target is a mawkish little boy (Sven Valsecchi) in a Little Lord Fauntleroy getup. reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: Sleep Tight is a slow, insidious sort of stalker/home invasion movie, whose primary character, Cesar, is both frightening and pathetic, as the best monsters frequently are. This is a feel-bad movie, by design, as it is about the material basis of happiness, how the people around us influence our well-being even if we are unaware of their actions, beneficent or to the contrary. The idea that someone would be undermining your sense of self, your sense of alrightness-in-the-world, without your knowledge, and that they could do so without meaningful discovery, is certainly upsetting. I found Sleep Tight to be extremely effective in episodic bursts, which is an intentional part of its structure, to ramp up tension, then allow the audience to collect themselves and get accustomed to the new state-of-affairs, until the next step is taken. Jaume Balaguero is really good at apartment-based horror, and this building is certainly a beautiful one, despite housing such intentional misery.

reviews.author: John (Magic Rat Movies)
reviews.text: Sleep Tight, the latest fright film from Jaume Balaguero is an altogether different type of horror movie to his classic REC, far more subtle and cerebral yet every bit as sinister and suspenseful. This is a beautifully crafted and understated study of psychosis, obsession and infatuation helmed by a genuine genre talent. Early on there's a scene of masterful misdirection, seemingly perfectly innocuous and benign, but as the true revelation of what's unfolding plays out, it becomes a truly dark and disturbing jaw-on-the-floor moment. Sleep Tight is a film full of such subtly unnerving moments, aided enormously by a magnificent lead performance from Luis Tosar. To say any more about this fabulous film and risk giving away its expertly crafted twists and tension would be unfair (even if there was a recent inferior Hollywood thriller with an almost identical plot), but be content in the knowledge that this is in every way a superior suspenseful psychological shocker.

reviews.text: If you ever get down on having missed the 'scene' in 70s NYC, watch this movie. Wren is a hugely unlikeable protagonist, only pursuing relationships she thinks will allow her an 'in' into the countercultural hierarchy and validate her delusions of self-importance. Because of that, I think this movie is very useful in showing the emptiness and cruelty inherent to a lot of self-contained art and music scenes: they are sustained by the oversized egos of a few (mostly male) talents and the bottom-feeding desperation of many others, not unlike mainstream industries such as Hollywood.

reviews.text: What a perfect, unsettling, and well-thought-out indie horror film! Starry Eyes follows Sarah (played by Alex Essoe), a young actress who’s chasing stardom and finds out the hard way just how dark that path can get. The film is both captivating and disturbing, with Sarah’s descent into madness for fame driving the whole thing. Essoe is absolutely incredible here, she owns this role. The gore and blood effects are used just right, never over the top but really effective when they do show up. The score is great, and the direction is sharp, building up the anxiety as Sarah spirals. The third act? Absolutely brutal, no holding back. It’s a dark look at what people will do to make it in Hollywood, and the feeling of hopelessness sticks with you long after the movie ends.

I cringed and winced plenty of times during this film — and not just because of the graphic imagery, which is horrifying enough (though thankfully, it never crosses into torture porn). With good ol' Arnie's aid, director Roger Spottiswoode cast Sylvester Stallone in the role of the project's lead. Stallone was to be a tough cop whose life takes a turn for wacky as his overbearing mother (Estelle Getty) comes to stay with him. While in no way exceptional, Stop! Or My Mom Will Shoot is aware of itself without leaning too far into the schtick, which ultimately leaves it worth watching. 67% ⭐️⭐️⭐️

reviews.text: It's often a shame (no pun intended) when a great director reaches their last film (or at least my favorites), perhaps because often these end up being final works are not by design but by happenstance (7 Women, The Messiah, Around A Small Mountain). And oddly enough, (though perhaps because of this?) these last works rarely feel like than culmination's of years than they seem like formal advancements. Street of Shame - it's odd that the movie continues to be regarded by it's NA distrubution title, the direct translation 'Red Light District,' makes far more sense - is quicker, tougher, faster than previous Mizoguchi's, resembling more the direct representation of his mid-30's films than the Brechtian theatre of his 40's…

reviews.text: "A Rua da Vergonha" aborda a prostituição no Japão pós-guerra, especialmente no contexto da possível criminalização da profissão, seguindo a vida de mulheres que trabalham em um bordel chamado Dreamland. Mizoguchi constrói uma narrativa realista e profundamente humana, sem recorrer a melodramas excessivos, destacando as dificuldades e contradições enfrentadas por essas mulheres. Ele evita retratar a prostituição de maneira romantizada ou moralista, colocando a sociedade japonesa no centro da discussão.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The camera jerks back as Michiko resists her father, rising, widening our frame of reference, as if anticipating a flinch and opening our eyes at the same time. This small movement seems to suggest that Mizoguchi expected viewers to sympathize with the father in the scene up to a point, that this was almost a pivotal moment, perhaps a shocking one--it escalates to shocking, certainly--and that jerk is an indication that he understood that audience well enough to move with them and guide them.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: no progress, only a growing tolerance for pain and despair, a disturbing schoenberg-esque atonal score, a series of individuated portraits that accumulate into not just a community and business in crisis but a total failure to treat human beings humanely -- the rhetoric falls flat, the streets are empty, lives are left broken and swept up into a dustpan. this business is a gambling den and the house always wins -- a political film where voting changes nothing but the makeup that the exploiters wear and the lilt of their rhetoric. a better world not possible, but left tortuously dangling on the end of a stick to keep you walking blind into the future until your legs give out and your arms will no longer drag you and there will be no one left to hear your cries.

reviews.text: Mizoguchi's final film is a return to his classic setup, of poor women in difficult circumstances. After his 1950s output saw a few thematic diversions and a much larger scale, it's quite apt for Mizoguchi's last work to be a more traditional setup. It's also one of his best films.

reviews.author: AnonymousWalker
reviews.text: Of all Jan Švankmajer’s feature-length films made after 2000, this one strikes me as the most interesting. I really like the formal choice to turn the film into a paper stop-motion animation based on photographs; I like the plot, which directly draws on the psychoanalytic and myth-critical theories of Freud and Jung; I like the cinematographic choices with extreme close-ups of the characters, I like the atmosphere of absurdity and, at times, a certain surrealistic flair (this applies, first and foremost, to the director’s beloved tongues, which live a life separate from the body). Furthermore, the plot here doesn’t meander but comes together into a cohesive whole, which, in this case, works to the film’s advantage. Of course, as with…

reviews.text: Wild, absurd, and just down right bonkers at times. Jan Svankmajer uses a sort of live action/animation style that was used frequently by Monty Python and it works really well to capture the same type of whimsical tone to match the subject matter. The story follows a middle aged man that is in some sort of midlife crisis that causes him to have a near split personality in his dreams, which he is married to a younger woman. For a more current Svankmajer film this felt like something out of the ‘90s and I mean that as a good thing, the film transcends time in certain ways and is one of the most unique films I’ve ever seen, even for Svankmajer standards.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A CGI driven remake of Chor Yuen’s Death Duel directed by Derek Yee (who co-starred in the original 40 years ago) and produced by Tsui Hark. There is a weird match between the period extravaganzas Tsui made in the last decade and Yee’s tradition of quality work which tends toward a wooden plasticity. Sword Master lacks the kineticism to make all those CG vistas into something more than an unease mix between a Yimou wuxia and a videogame cut scene. Choreography is disappointing subpar as well. It does pick up some in the third act, but rather late.

reviews.text: The best Hal Needham movie the stuntman never made. James Garner (who truly feels like the gruff, charismatic Tommy Lee Jones prototype here) goes Full Rambo on a podunk town, using a refurbished Sherman tank to demolish everything in his path after its shitkicker sheriff locks up his last living son (C. Thomas Howell!). It’s a strange slice of PG-rated matinee exploitation, hovering between slimy (with multiple scenes of denigrating violence against women and black people) and wholesome (Garner’s “might is right” militaristic take on “father knows best”). The back hour is just wanton destruction and dangerous looking stunt work, as we’re made to morally choose between drooling sadistic rednecks and a total lunatic soldier in this right wing power fantasy. Kind of amazingly demented in more than one way, really.

reviews.text: Dang, I need to watch more anime features. TEKKONKINKREET is based on a manga called BLACK AND WHITE named after the two main characters. Black is about 13 or 14 and is a tough and White is 11 and goofy. Both Black and White will do whatever to protect their city Treasure Town from yakuza, unfriendly businessmen (who want to rip off kids and families by turning the city into a Kiddie Kastle), and aliens. This film is a trip narratively with lots of psychological angst especially towards the end. Visually, the animation is a mix between traditional and CG. Where CG tends to bother viewers (including myself) in live action features, it works well in the animated realm. Anime and adult animation fans will eat this up. As far as the casual audience goes, I would personally be wary of recommending it to anyone but the more adventurous and curious.

reviews.text: The animation in this is so good. But holy fuck, plot wise, it's a mess. I understand the approach they went for and having to fit in a graphic novel into a feature length film forces you to creatively snip/rearrange. I don't agree at all with how they handled the character development or progressed the story by jumping everywhere at once. Having come off of the astoundingly good Ping Pong: The Animation, it's clear that you have to give material such as Taiyo Mastumodo's work air to breathe. It's a jumbled and frustrating film, made even more frustrating for how kinetic a lot of the animation is. It brilliantly melds 3-D and 2-D, plus they nailed the energy of Treasure Town well. It's just not a good way to experience the story, and I highly, highly recommend the actual manga version.

reviews.text: After continuing the supernatural themes of 1977’s Suspiria with his next film, 1980's jaw droppingly beautiful Inferno (please acquire that for a new reissue Synapse!) Argento returned to the fabled Giallo genre which he helped popularize with what I believe to be his best crafted film as a director. In his prime, flowing with creativity and imaginative gusto, we received 1982's Tenebre. With its black-gloved killer, pulsating score from frequent Argento collaborators Goblin, spectacular camera-work and shockingly gory murders, Tenebre delivers everything you could ask for in a surprisingly cautionary giallo—style AND substance.... Pushing every trope to the excessive edge, and fucking the blueprint which he helped write, tearing it down in the process.

Replacing the B&W of the original with deep blues and searing oranges lends new visual possibilities to Tsukamoto's already unhinged style- the final 20 minutes are a scorcher for the history books. Unfortunately, the middle drags a bit, but that's my only real complaint- well, that and the music doesn't quite go as hard as the tunes in the first. More of a remake than a sequel, but stands comfortably alone rather than being overshadowed by its (admittedly a tad superior) precursor. More than just a worthy follow-up, Tetsuo II: Body Hammer is a terrific movie in its own right.

reviews.author: Seth Brundle Fly
reviews.text: An overly ambitious Tetsuo crippled somewhat by its "more is more" mantra. Body Hammer (one-half the twin spawn of Tsukamoto's The Adventure of Denchu-Kozo) is a bombastic blast of cyber-industrial aesthetic, body horror violence, and that trademark stop-motion phantasmagoria we've come to love in Iron Man, but now in Technicolor. Tsukamoto paints with a new pallette, on a bigger canvas, much more succinctly — leaving less room for interpretation. And outside some phenomenal mid-point battles, hairier balls, and exquisite imagery (centerpieced with a mind melding sequence spliced with explicit frames of porn and mushrooms), the final piece mostly falls short of its less muzzled, more nebulously defined older brother; a film I saw as being nearly perfect.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Zulawski seems to take even the most straight forward stories--two men and a woman in a love triangle--and infuse it with a certain amount of oddity. Imagery that should be out of place--like an orgy, or sex with a bloodstained body, or Klaus Kinski--in a typical romance seems perfectly at home when Zulawski is behind the camera. His world is one of a decaying Europe, where the magnificent architecture and art of its past is filled with grime and wear. Like the setting, the love triangle at the center of this film is both filled with people falling apart and broadly symbolic.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: In L'important c'est d'aimer, Żuławski poses the question: can principals and dignity prevail in a world full of filth and amorality? The microcosm we’re presented with here is the wild world of fringe-show business in France, put forth in a heightened, at times even surrealistic way to communicate just how absurd and frequently repugnant it can be. Of course, the core values and themes Żuławski is touching on are not at all limited to this niche sphere. No, what we are seeing is a clear-cut example of the age old adage that art reflects life, with a meta-spin given the specific context of the film itself. Another ingenious masterstroke from the Polish virtuoso, on the surface this film can be seen…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Early Hammer Horror and the first appearance of Peter Cushing for the studio. Released the same year as Curse of Frankenstein, The Abominable Snowman features a group of explorers on the hunt for the fabled Yeti in the Himalayas. It's a very well produced film, featuring high quality sets and some stunning snowbound cinematography. The film really sets its scene well. The drama falls somewhere between an adventure yarn and psychological horror - it's really not the creature feature one would expect going into it. Presumably due to budget limitations, we don't get to see much in the way of the Yeti itself - it doesn't fully appear on screen until the last few minutes, which is a bit disappointing.…

reviews.author: Mike
reviews.text: It's official. I'm on the Hammer Horror Train. I don't know why I've avoided Hammer all this time, because they are SO my type of movies. Much more psychological and morally twisted than their American counterparts were at the time. This film, while simple and sometimes even a bit too slow, follows a similar theme that I saw in "Curse of Frankenstein" - who is the real monster? The Yeti that hide on the mountain, or the humans that go hunting it? Acting is solid, thanks to a very well written script that manages to steer clear of most cliche's. Respect is shown towards the Tibetan Buddhists. And, who doesn't love seeing the "villains" of the film be two rowdy, trigger happy Americans who don't have any respect for the land or its inhabitants? Can't wait to dig deeper into Hammer!

reviews.text: I love Nigel Kneale screenplays. The protagonist is usually a scientist, or a group of scientists, who uncover small, inconsistent facts, that build into larger and larger hypothesis that eventually encompass both ancient folklore and science fiction, but never once condescends to clearly spell out to the audience what the truth actually is: we can only grasp as close to the truth as our human brains can theorize and test, using the scientific method. Quatermass and the Pit is the pinnacle, but see also the rest of his Quatermass screenplays, and The Stone Tape, and this. Peter Cushing is the scientist, burning with curiosity about the legendary Abominable Snowman - are they the last remnants of a dying race, or…

reviews.text: 🕵️‍♂️ I was already very much in love with all of Mel Brooks' parody movies and the unique style they employed. Although this is not a film of his, it is heavily influenced by his work, and I absolutely adored it! The fact that it featured the same main team as Young Frankenstein, which might be my favorite from his entire catalogue, made it even more enjoyable for me. The story provided a fun adaptation of Arthur Conan Doyle’s work, cleverly incorporating all the classic elements from his books. At the same time, it included awesome humor and musical components while paying great respect to the original works, showcasing Gene Wilder's genuine admiration for them!

Black and white nuclear adventure in samll town America with James Griffith haughtily ruling over a disparate group to make an army of transparent men. Each has their role in Griffith's crazy but not bad plan except the danger from nuclear radiation. But it's so crazy none of them has really bought into it in the least and Griffith strains just well enough as the plan merge with atomic disaster and the mushroom cloud. Crime and nuclear fission don't mix.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: There’s potential for an interesting story here — contrasting visions of what the future looks like, both sides with compelling arguments for their own point of view — but boy does it get botched. Watching this, it’s not a surprise that William Castle’s westerns are his least popular films, because he has no idea what he’s making here. Is it an examination of contrasting ranching philosophies? A comedy starring wacky Cesar Romero and a cockatiel that ogles women? A love story? Or, hey — how about an action movie with piranhas and pitchforks as weapons! No surprises for guessing that he chooses all four, and that none of them work. The last 20 minutes in particular are just a catastrophe…

reviews.author: Holerbot6000
reviews.text: Watching the documentary about William Castle, I learned that he basically honed his craft making B pictures for the Hollywood studios, and I am assuming this is one of them. It's an unabashedly pulpy western set in the wilds of Brazil, with Glenn Ford as a cowpoke who just wants to sell his Brahma Bulls so he can fulfill his dream of having his own outfit. Along the way, he must contend with Frank Lovejoy as a wonderfully low key villain and Cesar Romero as an apparently amoral gaucho bandito. Somehow, they sandwich in a sultry musical number featuring a very hot Abbe Lane and even though Xavier Cugat is nowhere in sight, his presence is keenly felt. I wonder sometimes if Castle was a disciple of Sam Fuller. His films often have that same bare bones abruptness to them but still manage to be engrossing and entertaining.

reviews.text: Man, I just love this movie. I love the cast full of people who look like normal human beings rather than movie stars. I love the people they play, and the way they act like humans rather than movie characters. I love how some of them grow (or don't), and how their relationships fray and strengthen in the pressure cooker of a crisis. I love the shiny sets and the bright colors, and the determinedly, defiantly procedural narrative. And I love the constant, M*A*S*H-esque loudspeaker announcements, and the gloriously incongruous, high camp dazzle helmets, and the way audio from the future Congressional hearing sometimes leaks into the present.

reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: One of the most consistent praises The Andromeda Strain has earned is how scientifically grounded it feels. It doesn’t even nearly reach for superhero theatrics or implausible quick fixes, but it places its faith in sensible, intelligent people who rely on collective knowledge and methodical work to solve a crisis. It treats the “what if” of an alien virus not really as pulp fantasy but as a plausible scientific case study, it's showing us step by step how such a deadly agent might appear, spread, and be contained. A lot of the drama comes from those details, observing the procedures, the sterile environments, the tense debates, and the gradual process of identifying and clarifying what exactly they’re dealing with.

reviews.author: Richard
reviews.text: I am a big fan of the decade or so between 2001: A Space Odyssey and Star Wars, which was a real golden age for smart sci-fi movies, and The Andromeda Strain is another great example. I particularly like how it trusts that watching clever people think very hard can be genuinely thrilling. It might be just a group of scientists in an underground lab trying to figure out why an extraterrestrial microorganism has turned a small New Mexico town into a charnel house, but it is gripping precisely because it treats procedures, protocols and expertise as drama, not despite it.

reviews.author: funwithfilms98
reviews.text: In the 1950's, Ray Harryhausen had become well known in the world of stop-motion animation with successful sci-fi films like The Beast From 20'000 Fathoms in 1953, and Earth vs. The Flying Saucers in 1956. However, that same year also featured one of Harryhausen's most overlooked films, that being the feature-length documentary known as "The Animal World". Directed by Irwin Allen, who had previously won the Oscar for best feature length documentary with 1953's Sea Around Us, The Animal World was Allen's attempt to show the progression of life on Earth over time, with Allen shooting real live-action documentary footage of animals in the wild, as well as a short ten-minute long prologue showing the prehistoric world of the dinosaurs…

reviews.author: Hatercles
reviews.text: The cheerful chipmunk, the fearful fish, the troublesome turkey, the randy rhino, th mischievous monkey and even the dreaded dinosaur are featured into this look into the many creatures on our planet, most remembered for a sequence set in prehistoric times via stop motion by Ray Harryhausen. It’s interesting to see a nature doc made for mass audiences from this time. The narrator, big and boisterous, describes the animals with interest and yet a sense of bemused superiority, constantly mocking them, with the result a lot of this feels like America’s Home Videos. However, there’s something sad in seeing all animals and nature from 60 years ago, knowing how much destruction we’ve done to the planet since then, and yet most of these species still exist.

I also have a few complaints about this one. The dialogue and audio were as bad as it gets, sometimes entire lines would be difficult to interpret. With no captions it made parts of this one a bit difficult to understand. The make-up was also fairly fake-looking, and many of the characters were so plain they really beg to be forgotten. It might an extremely old flick all in all, but if you're a big Lugosi fan this one is still worth a watch regardless.

reviews.author: sallitt
reviews.text: The Ape Woman. It’s really good. Tognazzi is convincingly venal, yet develops a soft, sentimental side without changing his original nature; Girardot’s innocence is pro forma, as marriage justifies a multitude of sins for her. The wonderful scene in which she coaxes Tognazzi into bed manages to show at the same time his physical aversion to her and the growing urgency of his desire, and the film builds on this when he protests (in the French ending) against her acquisition of a normal appearance. It’s fascinating to compare the three endings: the censored one is worthless; Ferrari’s original ending is acidic and a bit arbitrary, but features a few appealing small gestures of melancholy, like Tognazzi advising the master of ceremonies to go easy on a heckler; and the French ending is the most organic, the truest, and the most unforced, and rather sweet despite the defeat of Tognazzi becoming a regular laborer.

reviews.author: mosquitodragon
reviews.text: In The Ape Woman, an environment of exploitation and prejudice is normalised. A woman born with a simple cosmetic condition is relegated to the status of a creature, because this is just what we do. Superficiality is our fixation, and we can create division without even the aid of obvious physical differences. If skin colour can make you a second class citizen, then a rare form of hair growth turns you directly into an animal.

"La Donna Scimmia" è un film grottesco, cinico, corrosivo nei confronti di una società moderna solamente a chiacchiere, che si contraddistingue per una totale assenza di morale (basti pensare al protagonista di Ugo Tognazzi) e che si dimostra crudele nei confronti del diverso, nei confronti di chiunque non sia conforme ai limiti imposti (anche fisici ed estetici, in questo caso) da una deriva a senso unico, pregiudizievole, che non riconosce chi non si adatta e che proprio per questo tenta di prevaricarlo, poggiando soprattutto sulla presunta posizione di "normalità" e dunque di superiorità.Qui Ferreri resta abbastanza asciutto, lineare nella regia e alquanto consequenziale,…

reviews.author: Four Winds Movie Reviews
reviews.text: Inspired by the story of Julia Pastrana, a 19th century woman who had hypertrichosis and was exploited as a circus freak. While there are two vastly different versions of this film towards the film's ending it illustrates its admonishment of exploitation and colonialism. Presenting a different attitude towards those living with medical anomalies than had commonly been shared on film. And in this case an intimate and sympathetic depiction of their personal experiences, while exposing our own inhuman mistreatment of those who are so callously considered inhuman. Tracing possible origins of our own prejudices and racist beliefs stemming from imperialism and religiocentrism. A revealing criticism on the need for control and our social failures personified through one of the most contemptible characters in film I have seen in some time.

reviews.text: "La Donna scimmia" (mal traduit, pour son exploitation française, par "Le Mari de la femme à barbe") s'inscrit dans la lignée de films autour de la monstration lucrative de corps non-normatifs qualifiés de "monstres" à l'instar de "Freaks". Cette comédie noire de Marco Ferreri montre les différentes formes d'exploitation du corps hirsute de Maria (Annie Girardot) et en particulier, celle que lui fait subir son mari, Antonio (Ugo Tognazzi). Jouant sur l'inversion, le film pose la question de "qui est le monstre ?". Néanmoins, dans un dernier plan, le film désindividualise le problème. Refusant de montrer les corps embaumés de Maria et de son fils (lui aussi hirsute) récupérés par le mari décidé à en tirer profit, la caméra contrarie notre…

A personagem-título só obtém uma posição e papel social, inclusive conjugal e familiar, ao ser explorada e instrumentalizada no trabalho, essa instrumentalização ocorre a partir do outro personagem central, nunca por parte de Ferreri enquanto realizador, e a personagem feminina nos cativa como também o faz com o marido aproveitador, a cena do espetáculo erótico um bom exemplo disso,…

reviews.text: The smutty sword-and-sandals picture starring Pam Grier that no one talks about, and for good reason. Conceptually, I'm all about watching Pam Grier shred some motherfuckers in a coliseum, but the cinematography and editing are shoddy and the story is neutered. It takes thirty minutes for the ladies to go from sex toys for the gladiators to gladiators themselves, and nothing of note happens until the third act. By now, Grier was well established as a ferocious feminine icon bursting with sex and power, but The Arena totally misuses her. And she's clearly trying her best not to be naked, but can't escape the lecherous gaze of the camera and it's numerous upskirt shots. The ratio of abuse to violent retribution is uneven.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: For most people, sitting through a horror movie from the 1950s is as appealing as getting a mosquito bite on your eyelid. But it doesn’t have to be that way. There are a select group of grayscale nightmares that transcend their cringe-worthy, boomer-era mores and stand tall next to ERASERHEAD and TETSUO: THE IRON MAN as fascinating DIY headtrips. SHE DEMONS. DAUGHTER OF HORROR. NIGHT OF THE GHOULS. And of course, THE ASTOUNDING SHE-MONSTER. In this case, the gateway is the She-Monster herself. With her two-story high eyebrows and glittering leotard, she looks like a long lost member of Big Shim’s gang in SHE MOB. Or like she should be hanging out in the backseat of Divine’s car in MONDO…

It takes a cheap kidnapping thriller and mixes it with a silent space vixen in a very Ed Woodian fashion and while it's obviously not a good movie in any shape or form, I found it quite likeable for the most part.The She Monster may not be all that astounding and is hardly even a monster, but she looks pretty cool in her catsuit and make up and I liked that she came with a little twist (that's only revealed at the end).

reviews.author: Luscious Johnny V
reviews.text: The second of Reeves' two Aeneas flicks, this one depicting the Trojan exodus and Rome's genesis. Unfortunately, it cuts out the first half of the Aeneid entirely which means it cuts out all of Virgil's best beats, too — the death of Laocoön, Dido's big freakout, Aeneas's visit to the sibyl and their descent into Hades. Instead, it focuses on the Trojan colonization of Latium which is all hack-and-slash tribal warfare with a bunch of indistinguishable local jefes, and a little boring. If nothing else, it's a peplum that feels visually and thematically like a western — immigrant settlers move in, manifest destiny is claimed, native tribes (or nativists) resist — which reminded me that the siege weapons during the climactic battle in Heavens Gate are of Roman design. But this whole origin myth hits a little differently in the age of Europe's and Italy's ongoing refugee crisis.

With that I arrived at "The Awful Dr. Orlof", or "Orloff" as varied sources have an included "f" at the end. Why its creators felt the need to draw a movie that might have been engaging at 60 minutes out to a glacial 80 minutes I will never know, but what I do know is that Crox Alvarado is its one and only highlight. In a movie that involves past life regression (shades of Bridey Murphy, and every bit as boring), grave robbing, mummies, and a criminal/superhero question mark named "The Bat," Pinacate, Alvarado's delightfully cowardly, nerdy science guy, makes everything better.

reviews.text: The first film of featuring the popular Aztec Mummy from 1957 is one of the classier Mexican horror movies and not quite as campy as you would expect. It mostly has the feeling of a (B-) Universal horror movie, but with the interesting twist of including the Mexican Aztec culture instead of Egypt. There also is a kind of pulpy sub-plot about a masked criminal (who of course looks a bit like a wrestler). The film has a slow pace and takes its time, but is well made and charming enough to not get too boring. The mummy mostly shows up in the last twenty minutes, but once it's there it lifts the movie up a lot and actually makes for one of the creepier looking movie mummies I've seen.

reviews.text: The Baby takes what would otherwise be a high-camp concept-flick of the late 60's/early 70's and dyes it in the darkest hues of Family Gothic Melodrama. Similar to early John Waters vs. V.C. Andrews vs. Flannery O'Connor in a Three-Way Cage Match Of Depravity, The Baby starts off in madness and plunges deeper and deeper into its self-formed abyss. Too bananas to function allegorically, this has nothing to do with 'saying something', preferring instead to push the Creep Factor to 13. I have a hypothesis that The Wadsworth Women are the Anti-Norns, conferring stasis rather than growth and decay, but maybe I just have not taken enough medicine today. Gerald Fried's score is also a perfect slowed fire of burnt tones, strings and percussion.

Yes, it's a strange premise, but the movie takes such a silly idea pretty seriously and verges on a line between drama with elements of horror, but the movie's best aspect is the discomforting, creepy aspect of the film, and Ruth Roman, who plays Baby's mother, is a generally terrifying presence. All this strangeness, ranging from the premise to performances, makes this an entirely memorable film and definitely a product of its time, but manages to make something quietly disgusting and disturbing.

reviews.author: mike5577
reviews.text: The Bad Seed stars Patty McCormack as an amoral child who commits calculated, cold blooded murder to get what she wants. Nancy Kelly plays her terrified mother who uncovers her daughter’s secret. Eileen Heckart plays the mother of one of the murder victims. McCormack is chillingly perfect as the eight year old psychopath, Rhoda. One standout scene is when evil Rhoda calmly plays the piano as one of her victims burns to death! Of course Hollywood had to go and ruin the ending. Because of the Hays code which stipulated all wrongdoers must be punished, God strikes little Rhoda dead with a lightning bolt!!!! This may very well be the worst ending of all time. The book by William March has a much more interesting ending with a twist.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: I think any famous con artist would appreciate a treatment like this, a hagiography spinning more or less complete lies and glorifications of his actions. Notably, the real James Reavis abandoned two women in his life time (at least), including Dona Sophia, so the view of him as being redeemed by love should be galling. But then, of course, here's the thing about con men: they are the ultimate American hero, the sort that is likable only because they win (even when they don't). It's about being smarter than the rest (and luckier). Reavis' ambition is mind-blowing; the degree of his success, the almost making it, is impressive no matter what. "Oh, I'm going to steal most of Arizona." ('s some impressive cargo shorts he stuffs it into.) The audacity is why we like them, so the audacity of this film's misrepresentations just make it more likable. Well done, Fuller.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: In God We Trusted/In Arizona We Busted. Another early Samuel Fuller picture that feels like its story—a fictionalized account of the forger James Reavis and his attempt to swindle the US Government—might have been better suited to the Great American Novel rather than a 90-minute starring vehicle for Vincent Price. We also learn right from the framing device that Reavis is a fraud whose plan will come to ruin—I'm sure audiences in 1950 were likely more familiar with Reavis as a public figure, but I couldn't help but wonder if there was a way to tell this story with a little more mystery and suspense, so that the viewer wasn't already ahead of Price and merely waiting to see how his schemes fell apart. That said, Price is quite good here, and I'm sure horror buffs will appreciate a chance to see the genre icon in a more dramatic role.

reviews.text: The Bastard is, essentially, a spaghetti western, picked up and dropped into the American southwest of 1968. I mean, it's loaded with key elements of the genre: warring half-bothers (played by Klaus Kinski and Guiliano Gemma, two spaghetti western mainstays), sadistic violence, a quest for revenge and, last but not least, a mangled hand! Given those stars, and that it was co-written (along with Mario Di Nardo, who had several spaghetti westerns under his belt) and directed by Duccio Tessari, the man behind both of the Ringo films, it's no surprise that the film went the direction it did.

reviews.text: Stylish, but flimsy Eurotrash revenge crime drama that laughably strives for a Cain and Abel-like epic but has no script to back it up. Still, it has a couple of gorgeous dames, including ex-Bond girl Claudine Auger; Klaus Kinski in a surprisingly non-hammy role; and the still-amazing-at-50 Rita Hayworth who chews up the scenery while imbibing whiskey like an Irish priest just out of rehab. Her scenes are the highlight here and she proves that she still knows how to command the screen as she waxes rhapsodic about her faded beauty, kisses Kinski on the lips (not an image I ever imagined seeing), and gives the film a killer surprise ending that actually surprises. The movie is nonsense but, like all true stars, Hayworth makes the most of it.

reviews.text: The opening scenes are incredibly promising, as a dizzying array of miniatures, matte paintings, and rear-projection are cleverly integrated with traditional footage to depict a master criminal—“The Bat”—stealing a necklace from a penthouse apartment right under the nose of the police. The whole thing is somehow Fritz Lang-ier than any actual Fritz Lang movie. Unfortunately, this bravura sequence turns out to be merely a prologue—the action then shifts to an Old Dark House(tm) and the camerawork becomes much more sedate, betraying the story’s origins on the stage. The most interesting thing about the movie is the fact that it was shot in widescreen (2:1) decades before that became commonplace (a 1.33 version was shot in parallel, and is also included…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: The Bat Whispers is a truly remarkable piece of filmmaking, featuring widescreen photography (!!!) and stunning work with miniatures that’s as dynamic as anything you’d hope find decades in the future. In order to bring his vision for the film to fruition, director Roland West not only shot from 6pm-4am (thus significantly reducing the risk of studio interference), but also invented new technology like lighter camera and a new lighting rig, thus setting himself free even from physical limitations. Confirming his commitment to independence, rather than sign a long studio contract, West retired from directing the year after making The Bat Whispers and hung out with (and maybe killed?!) his wife Thelma Todd.

reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: It doesn't help that I'm smitten by the 1959 version of this story with Vincent Price, but even without the comparison, I doubt The Bat Whispers would do much for me. An innovative use of miniatures and some inspired cinematography is the only thing keeping this from a one-star, with the rest of it being flat comedy played against uncomfortable silence. I don't know if it was the copies available online, but the movie was devoid of any ambient noise and it really unsettled me... which would be fine if this were a horror movie and not a comedic mystery.

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: "The Battle of Algiers’ continued relevance is both a point of fascination and something to mourn. Thirty-five years before the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center, Pontecorvo’s film gave us a cinematic blueprint of how Western oppression in the Muslim world could lead to radicalization and terror. The United States, at least, took little heed. And even after 9/11, official policy has largely been to continue the cycle of violence. Meanwhile, American movies are still trying to keep up with The Battle of Algiers. For every Zero Dark Thirty (which, in the light of this film, looks even more like an exposé of military-employed torture), we get a handful of Lone Survivors—movies only concerned with, and largely uncritical of, the American perspective on the country’s foreign misadventures."

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: When The Beach Boys released “Surfin'” in 1961, they had no idea that they were changing the world. And by “changing the world,” I mean to say that Brian Wilson and his family made it okay for a movie called THE BEACH GIRLS AND THE MONSTER to exist. This is the world’s first (and only and best) absurdist monster-surfing movie starring a puppet named Kingsley The Lion. BEACH GIRLS takes the blueprint of HORROR OF PARTY BEACH, adds some higher production values, and rips-off the rip-off ending from MARK OF THE VAMPIRE. Basically, it's really fun—even when it’s boring. This is the taste of summer for people who live only for: 1. Monsters, and 2. Surfing. This means you. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

It's all rather quaint and camp, but it's never anywhere near as much fun as it could have been which is a shame really. The film really fails in the execution. There's not…

This isn't even in generality of things, but actually something that the film champions and wears on its shoulders, breaking the fourth wall and conversing directly with the viewership on who they think the culprit may be. The novelty element isn't long, but it's a good suggestive buy in that helps aid attention for the rest of the film's length. The overall narrative is in placed in a setting much similar to the infamous short story "The Most Dangerous Game". A similar concept of man being the most ultimate prey…

Director Barry Mahon has an extraordinary-looking filmography that must be investigated further.

reviews.text: "The Beast with Five Fingers" is a 1946 film directed by Robert Florey. A novelty of mystery and horror, the film situates itself in a small Italian old-world village. An affluent piano player lives in a large house on the outskirts of town, and with riches comes with an assortment of interesting personalities that live with him. This predominately includes an astrologist played by Peter Lorre who is a purveyor of the dark arts in a matter of scientific research. When the lead of the household dies, an ensuing fight for the inheritance begins over the estate, especially with distant relatives. The thing is the entirety of the state now seems to be cursed by a severed hand but is…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Before it becomes a conventional horror film, The Beast with Five Fingers draws its tension from the jarring selfishness of the world in which it takes place. Apart, perhaps, from J. Carrol Naish's policeman character, every other individual to whom we are introduced is seeking their own advancement at the shameless expense of others. Whether it's Hilary (Peter Lorre), who flat-out demands that Julie (Andrea King) stay in her increasingly isolating job only because it keeps their shared boss' attention off of Hilary, thus allowing him unfettered time to do the research with which he's become obsessed, Bruce (Robert Alda), who happily makes a living ripping off tourists, or Julie herself, who suddenly decides to stay in Italy when she…

reviews.author: Doctor Pretorius
reviews.text: Here’s the thing: this movie has Peter Lorre going nuts, yelling “I tell you it was the hand!” after a disembodied hand does a murder. In that sense it’s a masterpiece, and indeed, Lorre is transcendent as a sweaty, obsessive astrologer who has apparently posted up in this old dude’s library for access to some rare books, and slowly goes mad over the course of the film. There’s a scene of him all alone in the library, closeup on his giant head, ghostly rumblings in the background while a fucking hand in a box runs amok. Absolute brilliance.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: One of those old 40s thrillers that takes approximately half the running time to actually get started, but once it does it's got some real surprises. For one, the special effects are incredible - for some shots I had a very difficult time figuring out how they were accomplished. It's also much grislier than your average polite thriller from the era. And Peter Lorre deserves a special hand for yet another expert creepy performance as the gradually-unraveling resident astrology buff of the creepy gothic mansion the movie takes place in. Fun!

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: This rare example of a Warner Brothers horror from the 1940s, The Beast with Five Fingers is well made but never really fully commits to the bit. Peter Lorre plays astrologist Hilary Cummins, part of a party of relatives and friends visiting acclaimed pianist Francis Ingram in his remote manner house. Cummins becomes increasingly erratic after Ingram is killed in a fluke accident. A dispute erupts between family members over the settlement of Ingram’s will and when one of them is strangled to death the police are called in to investigate. Cummins becomes convinced that the murder was committed by Francis Ingram’s disembodied, ghostly hand.

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: Curious horror-thriller-mystery-comedy? Co-starring Peter Lorre in a more “smooth” role than one is used to but it works. Essentially a “Horror hand” movie with a killer appendage crawling around and throttling people in a castle. For the most part it works but it’s more electric when Lorre shows up and throws around his usual, unique presence. Max Steiner score is one of the best parts. What’s interesting is that it abruptly switches tones, almost like a studio exec said “wait, this is a horror picture? I wanted laughs!” But overall, has some creepy elements and REALLY well shot with some progressive camerawork and framing for a 40’s film that’s not CITIZEN KANE. Great to see it on the big screen at the New Beverly.

reviews.author: Scarecrow88
reviews.text: If you love seeing Lorre going full blown mad, his astrologer/secretary to a wheelchair-bound concert pianist with a left arm paralyzed seeing his murdered wealthy employer’s severed hand (with a distinct opal ring) playing a particular concerto of Bach or crawling around pointing at him then this manor-set little village chiller will hit the spot. Alda is a music writer selling antiques to tourists in love with the deceased pianist’s nurse (Andrea King), inheriting her patient’s estate (unless his brother-in-law and nephew can contest the will). J Carrol Naish’s inspector on the case of who murdered Francen’s pianist has a funny final scene…if you are a fan of his Columbo-like shtick, he’ll entertain you. But this is the Peter Lorre show, as his droopy-eyed, library-hermited Hilary obsessively hits the books for answers on life and death, all the while fighting it out with an active severed hand, right out of Addams Family.

If you were lured in by vague promises of Vampira reading Beat poetry, Mamie Van Doren oozing peroxide-blonde sex appeal, and Woo Woo Grabowski being...uhh....Woo Woo-esque, be advised that none of them make an appearance until well past the one-hour mark, so be prepared to suffer an inordinate amount of police procedural nonsense courtesy of hard-boiled L.A. dickhead, Steve Cochran and his partner, Jackie Coogan (sadly sans Uncle Fester…

reviews.author: Marc Kloszewski
reviews.text: Not a good movie per se, but an interesting one. It’s been a while since I’ve seen such a nonsensical, hard-to-take-serious film that nevertheless makes decisions that it will try and present challenging, serious topics while containing performances that sometimes help convince the viewer that it may rise above. The screenplay generally undermines them all along the way, though, at times ridiculous or sexist or illogical or hyperbolic. Richard Matheson’s script had to be hacked up, messed with, given what we have here. When you get periods of “should a woman keep her rapist’s baby” crossed with satirical (and extended) scenes of wacky beatniks doing their thing, you understandably have a roller coaster ride tone-wise. And if that’s not enough,…

reviews.author: David Koenig
reviews.text: The Beat Generation (1959) sometimes gets put on list as a very late period noir. It's not but I can see why due to it's very dark nature. There is a serial rapist stalking Los Angeles dubbed "The Aspirin Kid", complete with "black gloves" when the deed is going to be done. We know from the beginning who it is. A detective unknowingly picks him up and from that his wife is the next victim. The crazy thing is she becomes pregnant and the detective refuses to believe the possibility the child is "not his" but of the rapist.

reviews.author: Donald Hughes
reviews.text: [MST3K Policy: Automatic 3 stars.] Both the hosts of MST3K and many of the reviews on here accuse the film of not featuring beatniks. This is based on a misunderstanding. Our current idea of the "beatnik" is an exaggeration of a certain literary milieu, but at the time it applied more widely to an entire 'lost generation' but especially that subset that turned to vice and wandering as a way to drop out of suffocating normality after World War 2. The stars of this film are clearly within the older sense of the beatnik archetype, including their dress, speaking style, music choices and (most importantly) their cavalier attitude towards social norms and laws. The film itself is not good.

reviews.author: PTAbro
reviews.text: According to Spike Milligan, who co-wrote the original stage play, The Bed-Sitting Room is an ultra-cynical examination of man's inability to escape the past. That cynical attitude pervades the superficial absurdity on display of post-apocalyptic Londoners going about as if nothing ever happened. Men in rags step behind broken TVs to read the news to an audience of one, a man pedals a stationary bicycle to power an electrical tower to keep the now-residential tube running on schedule, and life continues on apace.

reviews.author: evilbjork
reviews.text: This is an absurdist comedy that reminded me of something Terry Gilliam would make. I don't know how much I can even really describe what happens. It's basically a bunch of people messing around while the whole world is destroyed, kind of like what's happening now.

reviews.author: Richard
reviews.text: After watching Threads a few weeks ago, and ahead of seeing The War Game the following night, I was ready for a cheerfully absurd take on the apocalypse, and The Bed Sitting Room certainly fit the bill. It is a wonderfully surrealist vision of British civility surviving even nuclear devastation. Set amid the irradiated rubble of London, I enjoyed the echoes of The Goon Show and Samuel Beckett in its stiff-upper-lipped survivors politely enduring their bizarre mutations and its paper pushers determinedly keeping the British spirit alive through relentless bureaucracy.

reviews.author: Comicbookfan
reviews.text: The bed sitting room is a British absurdist view of the end of the world due to nuclear war. It has some interesting visuals and an appropriate desolate look in its locations and it had a weird attitude that I liked but as it went on it got a bit tiring amd stale and aimless and I couldn't get into it and for all the comedians and comedic writers including dudley Moore and spike milligan it wasn't that funny.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Plunging its apocalyptic caution about a nuclear holocaust into the form of a surreal farce, The Bed Sitting Room is the type of film that could only have been put together by those who lived through WWII. Set in London on the early anniversary of the dropping of the bomb by an unnamed aggressor, the screenplay written by Charles Wood, based on a play co-written by Spike Milligan, witnesses the survivors wandering amidst the debris and having surreal exchanges with one another. The film is perhaps one of director Richard Lester's most purposeful films. Known chiefly for his Beatles movies A Hard Day's Night and Help!, it's like Monty Python's Flying Circus but without regard for punch lines.

reviews.text: Lester is a very absurdist kind of director. Very much reminds me of Swedish director Roy Andersson. However I feel This movie wants to be wackier and more noticed. I personally prefer Andersson's work of dystopic alternative present than Lester's but hat be said there are some funny moments in here and a good British cast. I wanted to like it more but it only was agreeable.
