reviews.author: MajorMajor22
reviews.text: The longest, most tedious Monty Python sketch ever. I'm all for some post-apocalyptic Beckett-inspired absurdity about the human condition but this stretches its one idea/joke way beyond the point of me giving a shit. Utterly British, and painfully of its time, this shaggy collection of vignettes wears out its welcome pretty fast and all that keeps you interested after that is the stellar cast and the impressively grotty production design. Maybe this came across better on the stage and maybe a different director could've made it work on screen, but, unfortunately, this was directed by Richard Lester, one of the most inexplicably celebrated comedic filmmakers of the late 20th century. A pretty big mess this one.

The real stars though are the locations which are some of the most putrid I've ever seen in a film. There were too many good moments to mention but I particularly liked the roaming BBC news reader and the anthem for the new Queen who was marvellously captured by Dandy…

reviews.text: Richard Lester's skewed eye locates the whoops in apocalypse. You have to admire the audacity of the absurdity of The Bed Sitting Room. It's firing off on all synapses with no regard to where it might end up. The production design and location choices are superb and it's wonderful to see a cast of this calibre plunge right in and swim in the silliness. For me, it got better as it went along, as the absurdity dug its hooks into me, so I could imagine the rating going up a notch on a rewatch.

reviews.text: Eric Finlander is like a cold war Captain Ahab, aggressively pushing his crew beyond their orders, the law and even their sanity in his single-minded, bloodthirsty pursuit of a Soviet submarine. His folly is revealed, and arguably exacerbated, by the arrival of an embedded journalist and reservist doctor, who react with increasing horror to the monomaniacal culture they find aboard ship. These three performances, from Richard Widmark, Sidney Poitier and Martin Balsam respectively, are absolutely riveting.

reviews.text: Crackerjack performance from Richard Widmark as the commanding officer of a Navy Destroyer on patrol near Greenland when it encounters a Soviet submarine outside of international waters. This is in the thick of the Cold War period, so tension is running high as the Navy ship and the sub play cat and mouse. Added to that mix is a journalist played by Sidney Poitier who is there to observe Widmark for a magazine article. One of Widmark’s best roles and he absolutely kills it. Feels like a predecessor to Jack Nicholson’s character in A FEW GOOD MEN or something. Man I love Widmark and I love to see him going all ahead full as he is here.

reviews.author: PUNQ
reviews.text: The Beginning or the End (1947) is a difficult movie to judge. Serves as a docudrama about the making, and eventual use, of the Atom Bomb. The film does it's best to justify its use, citing it's for the greater good, to finally end the dreadful war. And so it did. The film also uses the entire length focusing on the moral issues in creating such a dangerous and lethal weapon. So it's not just a celebration from the winning side, Or then again, it is. That's the double-edge sword in ending the war with a big exclamation mark like that. With that said, I feel this is an important movie.

reviews.author: SmumCounty
reviews.text: Another odd film. This is the story of the creation of the atomic bomb. It begins with the burying of a time capsule containing the film and a projector on which to play it. It’s intended to be opened in 2445, 500 years after the making of the film. I weep for the people of the 25th century who find this film. Perhaps this review will serve as a warning for future generations to not open that time capsule. Ok it wasn’t terrible just not good. It contained the portrayal of real people involved in the Manhattan project including Oppenheimer, Fermi, and Roosevelt, but all done in the classic Hollywood fashion. Oppenheimer is portrayed as a rather jovial character which I can’t believe was accurate. It would have been better if it were a documentary. The high point for me was the yummy Audrey Trotter playing a secretary.

I quite like the curious conceit of the film, which frames itself as a historical document, placed in a time capsule by (fake) Oppenheimer and company, intended specifically for an audience in the 25th century, who alone will know how the hopes and fears of this atomic age will play out.

He is given almost nothing to do except ramble about horoscopes. Even though I love me some Lugosi, I practically forgot he was in it. An okay mid-30s crime romp worth a spin on a quiet hungover Sunday afternoon.

They just knew how to make 'em back then, what can I tell you.

reviews.text: I found this film on YouTube, and if I'm being honest, it was a really well done film for the time period it was made. The premise was a bit confusing, as the black and white shots and newspaper articles kind leave certain details out. It not only took me out of the experience, but also kind of confused me. I really liked the dialogue between the two main characters, Nick and Toby. You could tell their connection was tight. Like brothers. I also really liked the ocean scenes and how they were able to get the underwater film. That was probably my favorite part of this film even though some of it was excruciatingly long. And the final underwater…

reviews.text: For me, the 60s are this incredibly vast no-man's-land for Hollywood cinema. Much like the desert locations in this film, big budget Hollywood of the 60s was stuffed with intimidating, empty spectacle. So many massive epics that time has turned into dinosaur fossils. The Bible: In the Beginning... is no exception, and in fact, it's the quintessential forgotten blockbuster. It was the number one film at the box office in 1966. Quite a bonkers year.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: Works like gangbusters right up until it doesn't: after the intermission, it spends the rest of its expansive running time slowly clicking through the story of Abraham, Sarah, and Isaac at a grueling pace, as Ava Gardner's kohl-eyed severity fails to make up for George C. Scott's ponderous earnestness.

reviews.author: Neill Shaughness
reviews.text: Had this movie just focused on the Abraham story, it would not only have been much shorter, it would have been a stronger film as well. Despite some decent photography and solid production design, this movie has the dry monotony of a book report. It is far more concerned with relating the events recorded in the Book of Genesis accurately (usually via voice over narration), than investigating the internal humanity of the characters. Most of the stories have an external classroom like quality that prevents the film from ever getting truly interesting.That is until the story of Abraham. This seems like the reason Huston wanted to make the film. It's definitely the only internalized character in the whole script.…

reviews.author: AFilmGuy
reviews.text: To be honest, nothing that special. Huston creates some beautiful images that truly feel like they could be 20th-century paintings, and the film is worthy of watching just for that. But mostly it's just a fine enough telling of stories most people know. Probably won't watch this again but I have nothing truly against it either.

reviews.text: I wish they still made films like this though it makes no sense in an age with music videos and social media. But back in the 1950s and 60s there wasn't and for most people the only chance you had to see your favorite musical groups was in films or TV. So, there were lots of films that basically had a thin plot that they hung as many different performers as they could. And that is what this is. An owner of a record company brings his son (William Reynolds) into the business and makes him a VP. The son though wants to sign artists that are a part of the contemporary scene while dad just wants to keep signing…

reviews.text: "The Big Bus" is a 1976 comedy directed by James Frawley. The film is a complete satire that is on the nose when making fun of disaster films that were prevalent within the era. Watching this film, I drew many fun comparisons between this and "Airplane!" (1980), but "The Big Bus" actually came out four years prior. Pragmatically "Airplane!" is probably the better of the two, and they are easily two very separate productions, really, I'm just speaking to point here that "The Big Bus" should be championed here a little more in the history of things than it is.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: This rather cheap and clunky 1950's police crime action thriller takes its sweet time getting to the promised titular big chase, but certainly delivers the rousing goods once said big chase finally occurs in the last third of the picture. Said big chase not only includes some great exciting stuff set in a railyard (you just can't go wrong with folks running on top of trains), but also a pretty damn kick-ass pursuit between a boat and a helicopter. Glenn Langan makes for a likeable protagonist as an eager beaver rookie cop. Adele Jergens contributes an appealing turn as Langan's pregnant wife. Jim Davis also acquits himself well as the leader of a gang of thieves who rob an armored payroll truck. Lon Chaney Jr. alas has a pretty nothing role as a brutish gang member, but fortunately still gets to really throw himself physically into his role with genuinely impressive results. A fun little B-flick.

Regardless, Hilton looked to sink his teeth into another schlock genre with his crime drama The Big Chase in 1954, where after two convicts break out of prison, they…

reviews.text: If it seems like a whole one-third of this one-hour feature is one big chase, that’s because THE BIG CHASE originally was a 26-minute short about a big chase. Written by Orville H. Hampton (THE ALLIGATOR PEOPLE) and directed in color and 3D by Robert L. Lippert Jr., 1953’s BANDIT ISLAND was later expanded to feature length with new black-and-white footage directed by Arthur D. Hilton (CAT-WOMEN OF THE MOON) from a script by Fred Freiberger (later the producer of STAR TREK and SPACE: 1999).

reviews.text: Circus flicks have been hitting the spot lately. There’s something about those colorful sets, jaw-dropping stunts, and life under the big top that keeps me coming back for more. While it’s not the grand spectacle that was DeMille’s THE GREATEST SHOW ON EARTH (1952), THE BIG CIRCUS remains a decent film in its own right. Both revolve around circus life, mixing melodrama with impressive stunt work and plenty of eye candy. Shot in glorious technicolor, THE BIG CIRCUS stars Victor Mature as the owner of a show trying to stay afloat in changing times. The dialogue ranges from witty one-liners to groan-worthy exclamations of despair. There’s always a calamity around the corner, and when something isn’t on fire or seconds…

reviews.author: DavidS60
reviews.text: Lana Turner had quite the resume. The Postman Always Rings Twice, The Bad and the Beautiful, Imitation of Life, The Big Cube…wait…The Big Cube? What the hell is The Big Cube? In a nutshell, it's a horrible movie and a sad way to start winding down your career. Turner plays a kind stepmother who is being harassed by her stepdaughter and the stepdaughter's boyfriend in order to get a share of an inheritance. And how are they harassing her? The two antagonists slip her LSD in an effort to either drive her mad or have her commit suicide. The special effects during the acid trips are laughable and the ‘actress' playing the stepdaughter (Karin Mossberg) gives one of the worst performances in the history of cinema. Other than Turner's valiant attempt to turn in a respectable performance, The Big Cube is a total disaster from beginning to end.

reviews.text: If you have been dosed with LSD, lost your memory, declared mentally incapacitated by a court, and the best treatment your friends can come up with is to write you a screenplay, then you have too many theatre people in your life. Rather than closing with a somber, final nightmare about The Dangers of Drug Use, and a happy, romantic ending for its onetime victim, the film aches to dive fully into its conspiracy, embracing a the final twist ending of the genre it ought to be, and reveal that — GASP! — the movie's upright square, Frederick Lansdale (Richard Egan well into his "my neck is too big for my shirts" era), has been the mastermind behind the plot all along.

reviews.text: A gangster movie where the gangsters are corrupt union officials, this movie capitalized on the then current US Senate McLellan Hearings on criminal activities in unions. It features an over-the-top performance by Mickey Rooney as the pint-sized Little Joe Braun, who runs the unions like a crime boss, as well as an unusual cast drawn from television and the music scene. Not a bad watch but pretty formulaic and I'm not crazy about the underlying message, which I will unpack at the end.

reviews.text: Umberto Lenzi's WWII epic obviously spent all of its budget on the overqualified cast, since its plentiful use of stock and newsreel footage and mismatched film stock give it the feeling of A BRIDGE TOO FAR if directed by Jess Franco. John Huston is so visibly inconvenienced by being in this, with an irritability that borders on acting out, that he almost literally gets up and shows himself out of the movie. Also, even though he gets out for a couple of scenes, this looks like another TENTACLES gig for Henry Fonda where he basically phones in his role from the comfort of his Beverly Hills home. Was that his thing in the late' 70s before capping his stellar career with ON GOLDEN POND? Forcing journeyman Italian directors to make house calls if they wanted him to be in their movie? And if anyone can figure out why Helmut Berger and Edwige Fenech are in this, let me know.

reviews.author: John Charles
reviews.text: The Macaroni Combat cycle was rapidly running out of gas by the time this one appeared, made presumably to cash in on the success of A BRIDGE TOO FAR. It boasts a decent cast, but a screenplay that is a tedious collection of vignettes adding up to little and actors who seem largely at sea. John Huston's final moments are remarkably dumb, though Bob Spafford fans will no doubt enjoy watching (and hearing) the veteran dubber cast as Patton! There is a lot of action that doesn't cut together very well, not too surprising considering that some is not even original (e.g. one desert tank battle is almost entirely from COMMANDOS). Umberto Lenzi had somewhat better luck the next year…

reviews.author: Jason Jeffers
reviews.text: I can’t be objective... I was 9 years old in 1979, so things like this are pure comfort food viewing for me. Even so, I can still appreciate the comedy of a guy whose hairstyle is best described as “Combover Ron Burgundy” being cast as Bondian ladykiller Robert Sands (Moneypenny and Q are combined into one character, the flirty gadget maker Miss Buttercup, and M is called “Father,” played by Ralph Bellamy.) As these things go, it could be a lot worse—it has Patrick Macnee and Keenan Wynn in supporting roles, a henchman with a bionic arm, and the print on Tubi looks brand new. I don’t know if this was a pilot or not, but it’s hard to imagine the Bond producers would be OK with it becoming a series.

reviews.text: Strategically airing two months before Moonraker was released in theaters, The Billion Dollar Threat (1979) is an Americanized version of James Bond that could be considered either an homage or a rip-off. It has the women and the innuendo, the lab and the gadgets, and a villain’s henchman with not metal teeth, but a metal arm. It might all be offensive if it weren’t so darned entertaining.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Feels weird that there's been so much agonizing over whether it's ok to like this absolutely dreadful, Sundance-approved HBO version of Twelve Years a Slave, complete with action coverage action that resembles early Game of Thrones. There's some interesting ideas here obviously, most notably the stuff about reconciling faith with unapologetically nasty violence/revenge (that given some of that psycho Mel Gibson vision of blood-soaked Christianity might have been good), but it's just all drowned out for me by Parker's completely inept, hackneyed storytelling; with sequencing so amateur and visual decisions so lazy it more often than not resembled a cheap parody of this sort of prestige moviemaking. Kind of embarrassed about how much we've discussed this one, it's not worth anyone's time.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: As a straight white man I don't honestly feel that my thoughts about this as a work of politics or progress should carry much weight. If you're interested, I found it superficially exciting despite a formal amateurishness you might find in History Channel reenactments. Much more frustrating was the absence of women's stories (or any other individual stories/perspectives beyond Parker/Turner's, for that matter, but that's a whole other thing), particularly the use of rape as a blunt catalyzer for Turner's heroism.

reviews.author: Adam Kempenaar
reviews.text: Viewers coming in predisposed against Nate Parker the person aren't likely to have their mindset challenged much by Nate Parker the director, who depicts Nat Turner - played by Nate Parker the actor - as a martyr solemnly ready to suffer through all the scorn and outrage his opposers care to heap on him. Or who portrays the aftermath of a woman's rape and beating by keeping the camera focused on his/Turner's increasingly agonized face as she speaks, rendering her mostly a prop for his emotional torment. (In fairness, Turner is our protagonist and his response to this horror is significant.)

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: Leaving aside the "this will win all the awards" hype and the really uncomfortable revelations about the director's past (and his kind of awful self-centered statements in response to that history), this prestige picture about Nat Turner's slave rebellion left me fairly mixed. The depiction of American slavery is powerful and painful, but it's also blunt and heavy-handed, and it brings in some symbolism that just seems amateurish. I believe in the writer-director-star's sincerity around it, and I'm impressed with the seven-year effort he put into funding it and bringing it to the screen, in spite of his industry's longstanding apathy about the personal stories of black historical figures. But I still wish this was a debut I was excited about because of sublime filmmaking, rather than because of the accomplishment represented in getting this to the screen at all.

reviews.text: For as important as Edgar Allan Poe is to American Gothic literature, the film adaptations of his work have not been accurate, mainly due to the brevity of his stories, but Dallas local Harold Hoffman delivers a rather faithful adaptation in his low-budget oddity, THE BLACK CAT (1966), and perhaps one of the weirder Poe films at that. It doesn't get off to a great start; in the opening credits, they misspell Edgar Allan Poe's name (Allan has an "e" before the "n") and the film starts off with some rock-n-roll, something you don't expect to hear in a Poe horror film. But if Hoffman gets something right early, it's the crazed madness of the story, thematically accurate, in Lou…

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Axe murders! Chuck Berry covers! The big screen debut of Pluto the Cat! If you want to do Edgar Allan Poe right, you unfortunately have to go to Texas. An alcoholic shitheel named Lou neglects his wife, drinks whiskey, and hates his cat. After murdering both cat and wife, Lou is plagued by unsettling visions. Is it his imagination? Or is the undead cat back for revenge? A loose adaptation of Poe’s short that was filmed in Fort Worth, THE BLACK CAT is southern-fried goth of the highest order. The shadowy black-and-white photography, psychedelic garage rock soundtrack, and disconnected narration form a time capsule from an alternate version 1966 that never existed, but should have. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

A total grimy gem -- I just wish Something Weird's DVD was anamorphic!

reviews.author: ABrungardt
reviews.text: As far as horror b-movies that were essentially just showcases of classic stars late in their careers go, The Black Sleep is one of the better ones I’ve seen. Featuring Basil Rathbone, Bela Lugosi, Lon Chaney Jr & John Carradine there’s no shortage of horror legends. There are also a couple of other fun performances as well, something you don’t always get from this tier of horror film. Essentially it’s another mad scientist conducting unethical experiments to serve his own personal agenda, and while the mood and atmosphere in the first half were more than adequate to me engaged, the second half (most notably the final 20 minutes, where Carradine goes for it in such a deliciously over the top way) help this one wrap up on a real high note. If you like classic horror, any of these stars, and a spooky almost haunted house style aesthetic, this one is very entertaining.

reviews.text: An obsessed Basil Rathbone uses whatever means he can to bring his wife out of a coma. But Rathbone cooly hides his desperation behind an unethical, snobby, exterior shroud of scientific progress while his reliance on Akim Tamiroff as his unscrupulous associate in dubious experiments with a drug that induces "Black Sleep", a deathlike condition, hints at how low he'd go to achieve his objectives to save his wife and achieve fame. The two of them make quite a pair, while the film also features Bela Lugosi as Rathbone's butler and Lon Chaney Jr. as a subject of one of his experiments. The Black Sleep plods along with the main plot but it hits a freak show vibe when Rathbone's other subjects come out of the cellar, including John Carradine and Tor Johnson in a demented ending.

reviews.text: 𝑇ℎ𝑒 𝐵𝑟𝑎𝑣𝑒 apparaît comme un objet singulier, moins parce qu’il revendiquerait un geste radical que parce qu’il semble demeurer inachevé. Le récit peine à se structurer et l’on traverse le film avec la sensation persistante de ne jamais saisir clairement ce qui se joue. Les enjeux se dérobent, les situations se mettent en place puis se dissipent avant même d’avoir trouvé leur véritable forme. Il en résulte une dramaturgie morcelée, traversée de sous intrigues esquissées puis abandonnées, qui fragilisent toute implication émotionnelle. On comprend la volonté d’installer un univers marginal, abîmé, presque spectral, mais cette intention ne se transforme jamais en véritable mouvement narratif. Le spectateur reste à distance, témoin perplexe d’un film qui lui échappe constamment.

reviews.author: SkyeRhodehouse
reviews.text: During the opening sequence of The Bridge, we are treated to various footage of the San Francisco Golden Gate Bridge. The segment is shot in voyeur cinematography from the docks below. It is a beautiful day outside as many commuters and tourists admire the breathtaking structure and its impeccable view. Then, we see a man wearing a green shirt and a baseball cap. He stands alone, looking at the tide below. He then resumes to climb over the railing and with one last deep breath, throws himself off the bridge. The camera attempts to follow him as he plummets to his death. He hits the water and is never seen again.

reviews.author: PUNQ
reviews.text: Producer Edward Small thought he'd found his next big star when he cast Anthony Dexter as Rudolph Valentino in Valentino (1951), and followed-up with a costume adventure putting him in the lead with Anthony Quinn as his screen rival. Lavish production in Technicolor and good cinematography, and solid presence from the character overall. The problem was that Dexter looked kind of goofy trying to be the handsome adventurer. He had the look of someone who'd be a good villain in B-westerns, not the hero in bigger budget pictures like this. He would find roles in adventure film for the next few years, but not exactly what would be considered a quality selection. The film tries, Dexter tires, but it never becomes more than a standard and often forgettable swashbuckler.

reviews.text: How does this film have such negative reviews? I feel like it's either incredibly misunderstood or was deeply mismarketed. Hardly a "horror" film (though scattered with homages to the horror genre), The Broken is more like an abstract psychological drama, a puzzle that never has intentions of reaching completion, a broken and irreparable mirror -- don't expect resolutions or explanations. This is borderline-non-narrative surrealism, tension folding upon itself, and itself again. All the layers fusing into nothing more than a cloud of vaguely discernible darkness; an obscure, existential exploration of identity (or lack thereof).

reviews.author: Rosie✨
reviews.text: The Broken was effectively moody horror but becomes tedious to watch midway through. Lena Headey stars as Gina, a radiologist who loses part of her memory after a car accident, questions reality, family, and friends when she caught sight of her doppelganger. Headey was good in this. The muted tone helps build the chilling ambiance. It's a slow boil, it just didn't capture the fear of losing her identity well enough. And it lacks character development and urgency. The first half was okay, I just couldn't stick with the second half.

reviews.author: Dirk Diggler
reviews.text: A deeply beautiful, humane, touching and spiritual film about suffering, loss, faith in humanity and finding purpose, set against the backdrop of war, on the blood-soaked, carcass-filled soil of Burma. Here, a soldier almost faces death and goes on a spiritual journey, and ends up finding purpose in giving proper burials and peace to the souls of the dead Japanese soldiers. I loved the simple, fable-like plot, the gentle tone, the choir singing and the beautiful music from the harp, the mis-en-scene with the use of vast mountains and bare flatlands, the powerful cinematography, and its reflective, spiritual quality and philosophy that really spoke to me. Some moments could become a bit too sentimental, but ultimately I didn't care at all. The last 20 minutes or so is so moving. It's an instant fave.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: This extraordinary anti-war film depicts the devastating consequences of World War II from the perspective of the Japanese army. Director Kon Ichikawa introduces the central themes of humility and the importance of compassion with transparency of intentions concerning the obligations to survive humanely during horrible circumstances and conditions.

reviews.author: PopcornIdeology
reviews.text: If I’m not mistaken, this is considered the first decidedly pacifist depiction of the Japanese Imperial Army. What always surprised me about these early Japanese war films is how quick they were to adopt anti-war sentiment. Perhaps it’s easier for the supposed “loser” to lean into this stance, however Japan’s complete 180-degree turn (in terms of wartime policy) is in my opinion, thanks to no small part from how the national consciousness was shifted by films like these.

reviews.author: Janus Films
reviews.text: In the last days of World War II, a Japanese platoon sustains morale through the Burma campaign by singing traditional songs, accompanied by the delicate harp-playing of Private Mizushima (Shoji Yasui). After the unit surrenders to British forces, Mizushima is tasked with convincing a holdout of cave-dwelling Japanese soldiers to lay down their arms; when his mission fails, he is counted among the dead. Mizushima survives, however, and becomes a monk who dedicates his life to providing proper burials for his fallen comrades. Meanwhile, his former platoon attempts to track him down by using music to express a shared sense of separation and longing for home. Adapted from Michio Takeyama’s classic novel, and renowned for legendary composer Akira Ifukube’s haunting score, Kon Ichikawa’s The Burmese Harp is an epic humanist masterpiece—a profound contemplation of suffering, redemption, and spiritual fortitude during the darkest periods of violence.

reviews.text: It's interesting to speculate how William Castle would have given his more mainstream films the same Ballyhoo treatment as his spook fests. Here he could have had a bunch of comedians run out into the crowd telling lame jokes and spraying people with cream pies and seltzer. The shtick here is constant and often groan worthy but Sid Caesar manages to keep the energy up, and I must say, I did laugh out loud a few times. The highlight for me was seeing Robert Ryan mocking his malevolent mobster personae, and he really seems to be relishing the opportunity. Slick 60's sitcom type stuff with Castle's usual morbid and murderous edge. The absolutely surreal Coca Cola scene is worth the price of admission alone. Just watching that made me feel sticky.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: The success of Robert Wiene's "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari" is celebrated in every film made since 1920 that has borrowed the film's look, style, or tone. From Murnau's "Nosferatu" and the American noir of the 1940s, to contemporary horror films and every piece of work where Tim Burton asks Johnny Depp to dab black around the actor's eyes, the influence of Wiene's film can be felt. While the film itself may be limited by its era, contemporary audience need only to look to other films to understand the importance of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari."

reviews.text: Legit shocked that something as blatantly homo-centric and anti-fascist as this actually made it past the Spanish censors in 1972. There's a hypnotic quality to Iglesia's focus on long takes and fluid, swooping camera movement -- a real sense of unhurriedness even as the bodies start piling up in what is essentially our protagonist's literal closet. I noticed a few images and compositions that Iglesia later reused in Los placeres ocultos -- Spain's first openly gay movie -- which seems significant, especially considering the bent that the back-half of this takes.

reviews.text: I thought the ending of this was going to be much more explicit about its homosexual undertones, but it swerved in such a way as to make it distinct but not overt. This is a film about a man who murders his fiance, then keeps murdering others to cover it up. He hides their bodies in the back room of his house, and disposes of them bit by bit in the slaughterhouse in which he works. But given the way he reacts to intimacy with women, the hesitance he has to getting engaged, the intense swimming scene he shares with another man, and the strange conversation that precedes the film's finale, this film seems to be about The Closet.

Cannibal Man begins with the accidental murder of a taxi driver by slaughterhouse worker Marcos, and continues in almost farcial fashion as the perpetrator is forced to commit more murders to cover up the initial crime. The bodies begin to pile up and the house begins to stink; the only shining light in Marcos' increasingly bleak existence is his budding relationship with the rich kid who lives in an apartment block nearby. There's no actual cannibalism in Cannibal Man, but there's plenty to hold the intetest. Powered by a score punctuated by theobbing tones and ticking clocks, the film is a real desperate descent into despair. Marcus commits his crimes with a detached determination.…

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: If there's any two films that could be asked to encompass Vincente Minnelli's entire cinema, they would be Two Weeks in Another Town and The Cobweb. If Two Weeks was his adieu to Hollywood and embrace of European modernism, then Cobweb was his horror film. The ridiculous-sounding and laughter-inducing plot — entirely predicated around an asylum trying to find the right kind of drapes — is only camp to the easily frightened. The plot becomes less something-to-be-laughed-at, and more laughing-in-discomfort: it becomes a feverish, dense, surreal exposé of the terror of American bourgeois plush. Here, the quintessential Minnelli ensemble are a group of doctors, patients, bureaucrats, wives, flower pots and China plates — so frighteningly self-absorbed — unstable atoms that…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Probably the best movie I've ever seen made by someone other than Rainer Werner Fassbinder about how little effort it takes to push the average man from their socialized notions of patriarchal authority and even mild economic stability into the realm of outright fascism. Visconti's lavish sets and pulsing color makes the demented family dynamics of incest and betrayal that much more perverse, making a microcosm of Nazi insanity that inevitably encroaches upon the Essenbecks' bubble when their own connected…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Luchino Visconti's subversive film The Damned depicts National Socialism in a microcosm; here in the form of the wealthy von Essenbeck family during the rise of the Nazi's in 1930's Germany. The family at the centre is used as a mirror to a nation in moral decline; a time where morality plays second fiddle to political power. A situation where decadance, perversion and depravity can flourish under a feeble excuse for a political ideology which favours the so-called elite echelons of society. Visconti beautifully juxtaposes the melodrama between various family members and their maneuvering for power against historical events such as Nazi book burning and The Reichstag fire. The film makes its points quietly but with a real cutting edge.…

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: Sorry, I know many consider this a great film by but I found it to be a provocative mess. Yes, there's some excellent camerawork, a star-studded international cast and a compelling score by Maurice Jarre. Also, a sumptous production with perfect 1930s period sets, costumes and details. But the characters were all so depraved and/or evil from the outset and the story so melodramatic and over-the-top that I couldn't really feel engaged in the plot except to see what outrageous development and double-cross Visconti would reveal next.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: The most savagely subversive film by the iconoclastic auteur Luchino Visconti employs the mechanics of deliriously stylized melodrama to portray Nazism’s total corruption of the soul. In the wake of Hitler’s ascent to power, the wealthy industrialist von Essenbeck family and their associates—including the scheming social climber Friedrich (Dirk Bogarde), the incestuous matriarch Sophie (Ingrid Thulin), and the perversely cruel heir Martin (Helmut Berger, memorably donning Dietrich-like drag in his breakthrough role)—descend into a self-destructive spiral of decadence, greed, perversion, and all-consuming hatred as they vie for power, over the family business and over one another.

reviews.author: Brian 🐒
reviews.text: That unique breed of brilliant, transfixing disaster that can only come about when an aristocratic, semi-repressed gay Communist madly in love with his protégé gets to make a movie about Nazism just at the beginning of a watershed moment in onscreen sexual permissiveness. Wants to be about so many things—the Faustian bargain of capitalist industrialism with fascism, the formation of sexual identity in the 1930s, the transhistorical violence of heteronormativity, Nazism’s vulgarization of the German Romantic aesthetic tradition, Helmut Berger’s thighs and shoulderblades—that it winds up completely collapsing in on itself like an overripe and particularly noxious fruit; but that advanced state of decay—aesthetic, narrative, and thematic—is mesmerizing to witness, as Visconti, a decadent at heart, well understood. Awful and…

reviews.author: Hoff Matthews
reviews.text: I tried to be a normal person and watch Wonder Woman but the HBO Max app on my Roku wasn’t working so I just watched this instead. Supposedly ghost-directed by Mario Bava (or “Mario Baja,” as he’s listed in his DP credit), this is mainly interesting as an artifact of the brief portion of the space race between Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin (note the pre-presidency JFK reference in the opening credits headlines), with an American getting to be the first man in space and then accidentally leaving behind a nuclear engine which causes a meteorite storm. Sort of a proto-Deep Impact/Armageddon, but more specifically similar to Roger Corman’s War of the Satellites from the same year, even down to the extensive use of stock footage to illustrate the natural disasters befalling the globe. And like War of the Satellites, this would’ve been vastly improved with the addition of some aliens.

reviews.text: Żuławski’s sophomore feature will leave you exhausted both mentally and physically when the end credits begin to roll. Not surprisingly, the Polish government banned it outright, though I’m not sure if this was due to the political subtext or the graphic, balls-out-sadistically blasphemous subject matter or both but either way, the Polish regime of the day were having none of this. Even now, this film is incredibly hard to find. It has never had an official release in the US and probably never will. Apart from the sacrilegious sex and violence, incest, political…

reviews.author: Rod Sedgwick
reviews.text: I reveled in every second of this maniacal masterwork from the crazy-ass Andrzej Zulawski. Set in 1793 during the Prussian invasion of Poland, our protagonist Jakub is freed from imprisonment by a mysterious character who seeks a 'list' of his co-conspirators (allegory is at play, and likely why the film was banned in Poland upon release) as the price for his rescue, and let us just say a Faustian type pact is made, turning Jakub into a crazed mass-murderer armed with a straight razor. The hysteria dial is turned up to maximum, where every character acts as if they are devil possessed - Fucking brilliant and my fave Zulawski film thus far!

Healing the former is easier: ghosts tell you exactly what they need to move on. The living? Are prone to lying. Sometimes they don't even know they're dead.

reviews.text: TMI alert. My dad suffered from MS for the last 15 years of his life. While the onset wasn't as suddenly severe as Jean-Do's affliction, it was no less frustrating for him as time went on. To have a perfectly able mind bouncing off the walls of not-so-willing body is a terror I can never come close to imagining. The loneliness, self-pity, and helplessness of wanting to communicate, of having conversations in your mind, or merely listening to a person speak, always worried that they would lose interest due to the glacially slow nature of transmission, or simply give up when sensing your frustration with yourself and imagining or projecting that the frustration was directed at them turned the mere…

reviews.author: allain♡
reviews.text: Sleep paralysis is a frightening situation everyone has experienced at least once in their life. The feeling of being conscious yet immobile at the same time is nothing short of fear-inducing, but at least it doesn’t last long–it may persist for a minute or two, but the duration won’t reach beyond an hour. The lack of body control is absolutely terrifying to come across with, let alone imagine, but some people have actually experienced this for days, weeks, months, even years. One such person is Jean-Dominique Bauby, a French editor at Elle who, at 43, suffered a stroke that resulted in a pseudocoma state known as locked-in syndrome–a condition where a person cannot move nearly all of their voluntary muscle.…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Diving Bell and the Butterfly is a beautiful movie, and in fact a beautiful consideration of the human experience. It finds an elegant and natural way to discuss disability, by focusing on what can be achieved and not what can't. Imagination and wit is not limited by physical limitations. The film finds a way to focus on memories and moments, love and regret. The unique style, bolstered by some incredible first person camerawork, captures a rare life in an abstract sense. Initially The Diving Bell and the Butterfly is focused on disability internally, the feeling of humiliation and dependency, and then later we see the perspective of carers and family. We see the inside and outside of this situation.…

Of course, it would be an insult to the memory of the man who wrote the book and inspired the film to use such an inappropriate term.

reviews.text: Curtiz é um encenador esquisito, se satisfaz observando remotamente o sensualismo solene de seu Egito alegórico. Cada cena uma ideia, de civilização, duma forma para o meio, desértico, aberto. Cada personagem um tipo, passageiro, como monumentos ressignificados pelo tempo, pelo olhar retrospectivo. Tipos que encarnam a ideia no discurso. Posturas sempre rígidas, homens estáticos perante ordens mutantes e tirânicas. O heroísmo na retórica, só a palavra assume papel de resistência. Concentrado na tangibilidade mínima que uma alegoria tão abstrata permite, seu esplendor permanece contido na imensidão do espaço, que se opõe ao movimento humano. Fleischer e Bressane me parecem os únicos que se aproximaram, posteriormente.

reviews.author: Luke McCarthy
reviews.text: In many ways feels like the most measured, literary distillation of Herzog's key preoccupations - the utter absurdity of cultured civility, the struggle to know the unknowable and to find meaning and art within struggle, all filtered through a style which is distinctly less experiential than much of his other work (especially his collaborations with Kinski). Here his camera isn't so much a journeyman as it is a Brechtian observer, more immediately inspired by other German New-Wavers such as Fassbinder in the way he wrings emotion and humour out of the somewhat stilted, artificial rhythms which he's consciously working with here. Bruno's wide-eyed, singularly odd performance works in near-perfect contrast to the satirical civility which surrounds him - the first…

Kaspar Hauser is the psychological vehicle through which the New German Cinema auteur exposes several thoughts about contemporary society as extrapolations of the universality of its themes. That is, he widely shows his concerns towards society, acceptance of social outcasts and the perspective of rare psychiatric cases as scientific research instead of humanism statements through a 19th Century biopic focused more on achieving a balance between the character under study and his surrounding material and human world. reviews.text: skilled in tapping into the human instincts of someone unbelievably castrated from the outside world, a compelling portrait of growth created slowly and steadily by the small gestures Kaspar Hauser is able to not only convey, but also learn over time. a biopic depicting the various trials of someone whose life I had previously never heard of (just knowing the name from the film's title). But, oddly, this is my mum's favourite Herzog, so I was ultimately persuaded to give it a whirl. As customary with a his work, It's first acts backed by beautiful, seemingly infinite green vistas, each contrasting with Kaspar's adolescent remoteness from the world that knows no bounds, and retreats the numerous conventions of everyday life. After reading more about him after watching, it's clear why his very existence remains a curious mystery in German folklore: hoax or lifelong victim? not nearly my favourite Werner, but an interesting watch nonetheless.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: The film isn’t a faithful adaptation of Poe’s 1839 story, it’s more like a dream version of it. Jean Epstein keeps the spirit but rewrites the body. Roderick and Madeline aren’t siblings anymore but husband and wife; the plot folds in fragments from other Poe works, sometimes a black cat, a tomb named Ligeia, a touch of The Oval Portrait, is all very much mixed. What Epstein builds feels like the essence of Poe, stripped of literalness but heavy with the same ghosts of death, beauty, and decay.

reviews.text: metastasizes poe's gothica-of-the-gaps into a psychology of the fascistic urge -- the usher family becomes an incestuous family which, once it has exhausted itself entirely via culture, then destroys said culture in a mad frenzy to purge itself of its own emotional complexity -- the books of roderick usher's house fall to pieces in the stormwind, his painting burned in order to 'restore' his 'wife' to life, meanwhile the manor erupts into a volcano around them; the anxiety to preserve a set of dilapidated traditions ends up being the final nail in the coffin of said traditions. poe's original story was a tale of the non-human's intrusion onto the human soul, with the titular home sinking into the earth which birthed it, while this surrealistic take is a political fable with cosmic implications -- i cannot help but see the reichstag fire in the stardew'd immolation of this house, freud's organism of thanatos which demarcated 20th century life.

The human spirit, trapped in a world of chaos and destruction. Obsessive thoughts that hold us back, preventing us from moving forward. Ghosts of the past haunting the empty halls of a forgotten castle. A bride in mourning attire, awakening from a deep slumber in the realm of the dead, yearning for the light once more. But time and fate conspire against those who dare to challenge the boundaries of existence. All that remains is the haunting melody of an ancient harp, echoing through the silence of the night. A mesmerizing fluid of its own kind that no words can really capture.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: Essentially a loose reimagining of Edgar Allan Poe's original, the film breaks free from the limitations of its source text—despite co-writer Luis Buñuel's fervent protests. By constructing a Gothic, Baroque world steeped in human tristesse, Jean Epstein provides a resounding commentary on mortality and rebirth, influencing a lineage of auteurs from Jean Cocteau to Manoel de Oliveira, and arguably Tim Burton.

reviews.text: The Family Secret begins with a man fleeing the scene after accidently killing his friend. He can't hide the crime from his parents, and by a twist of fate his lawyer father ends up defending the man falsely accused. It's an interesting premise, but the film largelly squanders it by proceeding down the least interesting paths it can find. reviews.text: Burdened with the handsome but somnambulistic John Derek in the lead, and further weighed down by a dreary narration (Derek again), this film loses a lot of its potential. The situation is dramatic -- a young man accidentally kills his best friend, then must watch as his father defends a man wrongly accused of the killing. With someone energetic and gifted with a variety of acting colors in the central role, this could have been a compelling story of guilt, honor, and conscience. Where it is lifted is in the subtle performance of Lee J. Cobb as the young man's father, the lawyer fighting to free an innocent man, knowing his son is the real guilty person. Cobb sheds the…

reviews.author: Silversaxophone
reviews.text: There is no secret: obnoxious, privileged white young man from a wealthy family gets away with murder. The script for this well-intentioned social conscious picture, the second John Derek did for Humphrey Bogart's Santana Pictures, after the excellent Knock on Any Door, is ill-conceived on every level. Characters' motives are wildly suspect, their actions illegal and reprehensible (including one scene where Derek's character sexually assaults the girl he is trying to romance), and their reactions to the truth are preposterous. It is no wonder Lee J. Cobb gives a defeated performance, one of the least convincing he ever committed to celluloid. The film's studio polish only makes it all worse.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: I was a little surprised not to see Humphrey Bogart in this because it was included in Indicator's Columbia Noir box set dedicated to him. Alas, he only produced the film, which makes me wonder about its inclusion. But regardless, it's an excellent film. John Derek does fine work as a young man who accidentally kills his best friend in a fight and then he and his family, including attorney Lee J. Cobb, hide it, only for Cobb to wind up defending the man it gets pinned on. Cobb, too, is exceptional in his role, desperately struggling to do the right thing but also wanting to save his son. The screenplay does lean a little bit on some unlikely coincidence…

reviews.text: This was intended to be a pastiche of cheap gothic horror movies from studios like Hammer and AIP but unfortunately it feels more like a Hollywood horror version of one of those bawdy Eastern European comedies that I never really understand. Save for a few nice moments (that climactic shot of the ballroom mirror is choice), there's only one real reason to watch this, and I'm not just saying it for cheap woke points: Sharon Tate, who burns up the screen like a true, unforgettable movie star. It's really a shame what happened to her a couple years later, widowed so young after Roman Polanski fell into a mud puddle and died.

Patrick Magee has a small but potent role as an extreme minister whose influence affects organist Ann Todd and her unstable son (Tony Beckley, warming up for When a Stranger Calls), all under the direction of the interesting Robert Hartford-Davis. Not a perfect film but definitely a memorable one, as well as a precursor to the psychologically tortured horror films that defined the early '80s like Don't Go in the House, Don't Answer the Phone, Maniac, etc. mondo-digital.com/fiend.html

reviews.author: Eltopo68
reviews.text: 70's European movies in general and British films in particular sure did not seem to hold religion in high regard. this one starts off like gangbusters with a church hymnal being superimposed over a brutal murder. It does not really reach these heights again instead focusing on Kenny and his very suspect relationship with him overprotective mother and Patrick Magee's very questionable interpretations of the Bible. This is a fairly tense psychotic case study, with plenty of early 70's sleaze sprinkled throughout, but lacks any real bite other than the issues its tackling with organized religion. Definitely for fans of fellow Brit director Pete Walker though it does not reach the heights of walker's best works.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: It's the Shaw Bros, it’s Chang Cheh, it’s the Venom Mob—you pretty much already know what you’re getting. Except, instead of nonstop hyper-choreographed action, we get a relatively decent yet hammy corruption/conspiracy thriller whodunnit mystery concealed under a silly martial arts movie cloak. Is it clunky and a little boring at times? To some, perhaps. But if your third act is just a bunch of animal-based comic book warriors who would’ve barely passed as throwaway Spider-Man villains beating the shit out of each other over a treasure map, you have me fully sold.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: I think Chang Cheh’s career at Shaw Brothers can be roughly separated into three chapters. Chapter one is his late sixties swordplay films often starring Jimmy Wang-Yu. Chapter two was his more brutal “realistic” phase (including his Shaolin-cycle) from the early to mid-seventies featuring the likes of David Chiang, Ti Lung, Chen Kuan-Tai and Alexander Fu-Sheng. And his final chapter began with this movie The Five Venoms, lasting almost until the mid-eighties when the studio closed. The “Venoms” as they came to be known where Philip Kwok, Lu Feng, Sun Chien, Lo Meng and Chiang Sheng. Another original member Wai Pak only made a couple of movies with the team before he left Shaw Brother.

reviews.text: The Flying Guillotine was another huge Shaw Brothers hit, and the title weapon became a big draw in sequels, ripoffs by other studios (Jimmy Wang Yu made his own Master of the Flying Guillotine in response), and legacy tributes like The Heroic Trio. So I didn’t expect it to be primarily a talky film, which was a surprise. The current evil Mongol emperor wants to silence anyone who questions him (sound familiar, fellow Americans?), so he tasks an advisor named Xin Kang (Feng Ku) to come up with a way to knock people off without it being traced back to him. Xin gives it some thought, and as you or I would comes up with the Flying Guillotine, which can be…

reviews.text: This is an admirably ghoulish Shaw Brothers picture that revolves solely around the creation and utilisation of the titular Flying Guillotine. The wonderfully contrived premise see's the evil Emperor order the execution (by anonymous assassin) of a couple of respected scholars. This presumably straight forward task instead results in the creation of the flying guillotine and the formation of a band of young assassins who specialise in its dubious use. Young Ma Teng (Kuan Tai Chen) is the best killer in the squad, but it doesn't take long for him to realise that they are merely tools intended to spread the Emperor's terror. Ma Teng deserts which compels the remaining members of the flying guillotine squad to hunt for his…

reviews.text: The original Flying Guillotine is not quite the classic it’s unofficial sequel, Master of the Flying Guillotine, has become of the years. It’s a solid story and Chen Kuan-tai is as good and sympathetic lead.

reviews.author: James Betsalel
reviews.text: Pleasantly surprised by how good this was. Having only seen Master of the Flying Guillotine I was expecting some wacky stuff but this is a more serious period piece that just happens to involve the most ridiculously awesome weapon ever thought of. The guillotine is used plenty and is always campy brutal fun but its presence makes the fight scenes rather short and lacking in martial arts. Combined with an attentiveness towards a dramatic and political plot makes me hesitate to even classify this as a martial arts film. Still fans of the genre will enjoy this, just go in knowing it's not your typical 70's genre flick.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Sam Peckinpah's heist gone wrong movie somehow feels less personal than his earlier westerns; but no less works on its own terms. The film is a sombre affair - building the plot slowly. The major plot points are left to simmer with no explaination - the story is told visually. Meanwhile, less relevant character interactions are emphasised. This is the sort of thing that made Tarantino famous! The film is slow to get going, but it runs at a steady pace once the plot is set in motion. It's a real seventies muscle piece, with McQueen perfect in the lead role. I love the way the abject pointlessness of the whole endeavour slowly creeps into the narrative, before the seemingly ambiguous ending really puts the tin hat on it. Not a career high for the director - but certainly a film that works on multiple levels.

reviews.text: You can tell that veteran novelist and screenwriter William Goldman had written this with aspirations of achieving a lavish, old-fashioned David Lean colonial biographical drama about a real-life 19th century bridge engineer that found himself in an African lion take on the moody adventure-horror of Jaws (pretty insane true story!), and there's certainly enough money and talent (including cinematographer Vilmos Zsigmond and composer Jerry Goldsmith) that that version of this movie might have been possible, but director Stephen Hopkins' talents are better served by something like the gnarly, stupid and deliriously stylized Predator 2 than they are the stoic handsomeness called for by this material. So despite this being perfectly sturdy it often feels a little thinly sketched and unimaginative…

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Based on the real life account of two lions that terrorized a rail road camp in late 19th century Africa, Stephen Hopkins' "The Ghost and the Darkness" is a tension-rich, old fashioned adventure. With its lovely savannah vistas, rousing score, and engaging characters, the film is fully appealing. It is a man versus nature tale where nature has the upperhand, unfolding with potent cinematic elements.

reviews.author: Waldo
reviews.text: Another underrated 90's thriller that got all kinds of shit thrown at it back in 1996 by the critics and every other asshole out there. Val Kilmer plays real life Irish engineer turned lion hunter Patterson. "His accent comes and goes" one critic complained. Boo hoo! Stop it. And Douglas plays Remington, a fictional American big game hunter that joins Patterson's hunt of a couple of man killing lions in Tsavo, Africa back in 1896. I've always felt this movie to be one hell of an adventure film with very strong and tense moments of man vs beast. Great booming score by Jerry Goldsmith. I remember it won an Oscar for sound despite all the crap thrown at it.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: For 45 minutes, this is a very boring movie about an Irish guy (played by a sedate Val Kilmer) failing to build a bridge in Africa because some man-eating lions (or, rather, some suggestive editing and very poor lion special effects) keep killing his workers. Then Michael Douglas shows up with a Southern-fried accent and a big flowing mullet and the movie at least gets a little more fun, though not enough to save it. For a much more entertaining film about big game hunting from the same director, check out Predator 2.

In other words, "The Ghost and the Darkness" is an exciting survival adventure that treats our African lions in a manner not unlike the Predator: these savage but cunning animals hunt for the pleasure of it and collect bones as trophies, and the filmmakers even give us a few 'Predator vision'-style POV shots from their black & white perspective. I'll admit my expectations were low, given this film's reputation or lack thereof, so I…

This was 1996, a year that people could invest in an historical action/drama/horror movie about man-eating lions but when it came down to depicting them on screen figured audiences would be too stupid to understand that Tsavo lions don't actually grow manes, possibly due to climate.

reviews.text: The Glass Wall is a lean, mean, earnest machine. A Hungarian refugee is on the run to avoid deportation as he seeks out the one man, an ex-parachute trooper who's life he saved during the war, who can vouch for him to stay. I found this film many shades of Deadline at Dawn, a similar thriller which takes place over one night from dusk till dawn, except this had more sincere characters which avoided the stock caricatures of the time, with even higher stakes - our man on the lamb isn't just at risk of reprisal from the law, but the ticking clock of his own mortality as well. Everything The Glass Wall stands for in regards to human decency…

Our protagonist is Peter Kuban, a Hungarian refugee and concentration camp survivor who arrives at New York without his papers in order, and threatened with deportation jumps ship. He's trying to find a local musician who can vouch for his story as helping the US war effort in Europe which would allow him to stay, but the authorities don't buy it. What's interesting is the more, at least for the movies, realistic look…

reviews.text: I do believe in the Ebertism that a movie is not what it is about, it’s how it is about it. I agree that any subject could in theory be made into a good movie with the right execution. But I also believe that like baseball players, all films have a certain floor and a certain ceiling on paper. And on paper, a superhero spoof directed by Michel Gondry, starring Seth Rogen, Cameron Diaz, David Harbour, and Christoph Waltz, written by Rogen and Evan Goldberg sounds amazing. But the The Green Hornet we got is a lot closer to that concept’s floor than its ceiling. So not only is it a nothing happening superhero story — it feels like the blandest version of this material that these people could possibly make.

reviews.text: 'The Grudge 2' has a substantially higher body count, as well as more of everything else: characters, plot-lines, locations, etc. In doing so, the ability to build up a sustained atmosphere of dread is somewhat compromised, but in upping the complexity, chaos is piled on top of chaos, and the feeling of having one of those dreams that is too byzantine to properly follow, with too many moving parts, really sets in, that impression that if you just tried a little harder, all of it would make sense, but then you wake up and you realize it was never going to cohere. 'The Grudge 2' does make sense (more or less) and does cohere (more or less) but that just-awoken, trying to put together the narrative now lost to the day is its strongest aspect.

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: I thought it would be difficult to hit a lower low than Ju-on: The Curse 2, a film that spends over thirty minutes rehashing Ju-on: The Curse, but here we are. The Grudge 2, the sequel to the first US remake (The Grudge), is actively enraging. How Takashi Shimizu's franchise took off is still beyond me, but this film showcases that the writer/director is out of ideas. I read that Shimizu felt it was important to confront Kayako's childhood and that he was excited to make a film that was decidedly different from the previous Ju-on films. Light only shows the most prominent clue to their emotional states and nothing more, leaving the viewer trapped intimately with the three men. reviews.text: The bergfilm, or mountain movie genre, was a popular trend in Weimar Germany. The Holy Mountain is probably the most well known example. There isn’t much plot to the film. Basically a dancer gets stuck in a love triangle with a couple of rugged mountain men. The artistry of The Holy Mountain is in director/cinematographer Arnold Fanck’s extremely tight control of composition, light and shadow. The film stakes its claim from the opening avant garde scene in which star Leni Riefenstahl’s abstract dancing is juxtaposed with lush and gorgeous images of crashing waves, misty clouds and rough shorelines. The location photography on the mountain itself is perfectly composed and exposed, a tricky proposition when shooting snow in difficult locations. The Holy Mountain and others in the genre must have seemed extremely exotic, like the surf/travelogue movie craze of the late 1960s and early 1970s.

reviews.text: The mountain films (Bergfilme) are a mostly forgotten subset of Weimar Germany's rich cinematic legacy, a short-lived movement spearheaded by director and keen outdoorsman Arnold Fanck whose adherence to realism and authentic outdoor photography is starkly at odds with the distorted fantasticism of his expressionist peers. The two could also be interpreted as opposite responses to the rise of fascism—the shadowy, nightmarish visions of Lang and Murnau are harbingers of psychological dread and foreboding—both would leave for America, whilst Fanck, who would go on to join the Nazi Party, whose alpine landscapes conjure up an idyllic portrait of Aryan perfection, seems to be celebrating the courage and physical excellence of the people, who are able to overcome adversity and conquer…

Entsprechend dienen besonders dem "Freund" die Berge als Projektionsfläche seiner Empfindungen - auch der destruktiven. reviews.text: Grüß Gott! It’s Oktoberfest again, which means it’s a good day for some homemade sauerbraten, some Hacker-Pschorr, and an echt-German film. It doesn’t get much more echt than this foundational Berg [mountain] film, which catapulted Leni Riefenstahl and Luis Trenker to stardom and established director Arnold Fanck’s reputation. It’s a triumph of style over substance, with the remarkable cinematography and stunt work (performed mostly by the actors themselves) outshining a fairly standard, if unexpectedly downbeat, love triangle. It also demonstrates Fanck’s influence on Riefenstahl’s later directorial style: expressionistic use of slow motion and rapid editing, commitment to difficult on-location filmmaking, etc.

Tommy Lee Jones directed, and it’s a Cormac McCarthy kind of misanthropy piece had he written it (the novel it is based on is by Glendon Swarthout who also wrote "The Shootist"). The story is initially driven by Hilary Swank as a charitable Nebraskan heroine who has volunteered to transport three women to Iowa to receive better care. It becomes one of those languidly episodic journeys, with Swank's Mary Bee Cuddy propositioning Jones' George Briggs to assist her with the…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Old codger western done with genuine care by Tommy Lee Jones. The emphasis on women do add some freshness but this is very much an old school track western with some revisionist flavor (the film I most often remember while watching it was the Walter Hill/Robert Duvall track TV western Broken Trail from a few years ago). Jones is a weird artist to wrote about today not so much because he is attracted to old fashioned material, but because he deliberate operates in a minor key. The Homesman virtues – its delicate shaped dramatic arc, many lovely performances, feel for frontier life – are discreet: a matter of fine workman like direction and commitment to drama. In an era where…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: It's been a while since I've seen a movie with as many gut-punching moments as Tommy Lee Jones' The Homesman. I've seen some grim stuff in my time, but there are moments here that truly repulsed me, and I'm sure that that was Jones' intention, bringing the harsh reality of frontier life to the screen without restraint. This is a difficult watch, a very difficult watch, but it only reaffirmed my view that Tommy lee Jones is as accomplished behind a camera as he ever was in front of it.

I can only imagine the hardships that pioneers faced trying to establish a new way of life in the untamed midwest—a life that promised very little to its intrepid settlers, destined to live out their days in a dust bowl that was devoid of essential resources, that offered little more than years of hard toil and the bare necessities for a subsistence lifestyle—an existence that must surely have been debilitating;…

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Westerns used to dominate pop culture to a degree that's probably tough to imagine nowadays, but now (in Hollywood at least) we generally see about one or two a year. So every one is kind of a throwback by default, but The Homesman isn't really anything like the kinds of westerns that used to come out all the time - it's tough and gritty, with none of the western romanticism or archetypes you used to see in stories about the west. There isn't even really much action to speak of, although this is possibly home to my favorite action scene of 2014, a knife fight between Tommy Lee Jones and Tim Blake Nelson (whoever wins gets to keep all six names). It also depends strikingly on one's affection for Jones, which for me is pretty much through the roof.

reviews.author: JakubM
reviews.text: A Brazilian western about a boy raised to be a ruthless killer, an unscrupulous landlord who enforces his will through a violent militia, and a sex worker’s son facing an uncertain future. Its sprawling narrative jumps back and forth in time, traces acts of violence as they reverberate through the community and impact new characters, and repeatedly calls back to a campfire story that serves as a frame narrative. It's sometimes too much, but the epic quality this approach to storytelling exudes is also my favourite thing about it. At these junctures, The Killer feels like a spaghetti western spiced with City of God. It's not without some surprising flourishes, either. A musical montage partway through is a highlight. That being said, some of the digital effects look like hot garbage. It also features some unfortunately homophobic characterization—it doesn't seem intentional, but that's not really an excuse at this point in time.

Se for mulher, será violentada, morta ou torturada. O homossexual é retratado como um estuprador, o negro como um capacho ou um pedófilo. O filme tenta nos mostrar um Conan do cangaço, um homem abandonado na selva, bruto, bárbaro e viril, tão selvagem que fala rosnando, mas aqui é tão mal interpretado que parece ter alguma deficiência mental.

reviews.text: The plot's simple enough, and the setting (the run-down end of the Atlantic City Boardwalk in Winter) is gloomy enough that it's easy to understand why this never quite became an audience favorite, but it's crushingly effective in the way it contrasts Nicholson's inward, seething discontent with himself and the world, and Dern's dismissal of anything that isn't him. Ellen Burstyn hits another role out of the park, and the sections that bookend the film's Atlantic City action are crushingly effective in spinning a greater tragedy out of the events that occurred.

reviews.text: Jack Nicholson is the rare actor who seems to sleepwalk through crazy performances- from chasing his wife and child round an abandoned hotel with an axe, to pulling his dick out and having a loud fake wank in an adult movie theatre, insanity comes naturally to him. When it comes to the restrained roles, where he plays characters defined by understatement, he seems to be under a deeper challenge to make the character believable. Although his character in The King of Marvin Gardens is far from a normal, respectable adult, he is nevertheless the straight man amongst a whole cast turning their crazy up to 11.

reviews.author: Jack Often
reviews.text: Lightly surrealist and full of deliberate cutting and style choices, Marvin Gardens posits itself as a meaningful look at the crumbling American dream, but I did not connect with it at all. Part of the reason is that its symbols have become dated and don't really resonate anymore, and part of it is my reaction to Jack Nicholson's excruciatingly mannered monologues. But mostly it alienated me because the poetic and significance-laden dialogue prevents the actors from ever disappearing into their roles for one second. Even in small parts.The camerawork and the views of old Atlantic City courtesy of László Kovács were a treat, at least.

So there's that, and director Tony Goldwyn's distinctly modish soundtrack choices (Snow Patrol, Coldplay), something that's by now passed the point of being merely dated and back into the realm of being rather charming. As is the preponderance of flip phones throughout proceedings. In fact this may be the…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: The Last of the Fast Guns is a sad, almost stately movie about endings. Not, as would become so common in films in the genre during next decade, about the end of the old west, but about personal endings: the end of childhood; the end of freedom; the end of a career. The end of friendship.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Jock Mahoney has been one of those B-movie actors that hasn't really set the heather on fire for me, with his films washing over me without really leaving much impression. I don't think I've seen a really bad one either, which is strange, given that he doesn't offer a whole lot of charisma as a hero or a villain. Which brings me around to The Last of the Fast Guns from director George Sherman, a guy I knew I could rely on to bring the thrills and spills from a Universal Western circa 1958, and for once Mahoney owns the film with a terrific performance that I barely knew he had in him.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A gorgeous Mexican travelogue populated by black gringo souls. One of the two or three greatest Universal International westerns.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman

reviews.author: dirtylaundri
reviews.text: The hero is a drifter turning on 30, slowly getting tired of just being a black cipher thrown into the world. The man he´s searching for left behind his old life and plenty of old money to vanish in Mexico. The bad guy was born in Europe and lived basically everywhere. Even the Mexican woman is no "flower of the land", but points out her big city past. A tale of displaced souls that starts with an open grave.

reviews.text: Another enjoyable western from Tarantino favorite George Sherman, helper by a solid script by David P. Harmon. Plays a bit like a western detective mystery.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: A kind of a lush greener looking Mexico is the setting with overgrown arched ruins and ranchos as a gunman searches for the brother of a rich Easterner. As he goes deeper into the mysteries of Mexico so do we, traveling across cactus desert and lush valleys getting closer to the mysterious man who escaped into Mexico years before. It's really like the country's beauty draws you in to its soul. Jock Mahoney plays the gunman quite stoically, and the screenplay is full of lines that seem kind of cryptic to go along with occasional gunfights. Mahoney is super fast on the draw he draws both pistols in one scene where you only see the one gun and then he's got two of them. But Mexico lindo draws him into its web in this cool af western.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: A man from another era descends into Mexican territory wearing only black if not for a red handkerchief, rides off into the sunset, and finds fading vestiges of the world he once knew. He gets a partner all dressed in white if not for the same red handkerchief, mark from the bloody world they carry, and both penetrate deeper into wild territory chasing ghosts. But what seemed as a twilight western becomes perhaps a western that is hoping for a new dawn: if one waits for the night to pass, maybe the sunrise will come in the end of the road, and the mountains that were once a place to be buried may become a place to find peace of…

reviews.author: Blake VP
reviews.text: The Last of the Fast Guns offers little that feels new for a western: young gunslingers eager to test themselves against the fastest draw, a familiar search-and-rescue plot, the dying west, and an ending borrowed straight from John Ford. A perfect B-movie Western that serves its purpose. Roland Gilbert injects some much-needed personality into the film, but his presence alone isn’t enough to elevate an otherwise bland palette.

reviews.author: Yavor Ivanov
reviews.text: Most historical epics crank up the savagery and ornamental detail only in the physical reconstruction, while maintaining their beautified and inoffensive modern sensibilities (yes, I'm looking at you, Ridley... and your Kingdoms of Heaven). But this one truly feels olden!A strange thing in a strange land, hiding under its metal shield the genuinely troubling fragility of this thing we call civilization in the midst of the sweeping chaos and hostility of the outer domains. A dying ember defiantly flickering against the hollows of Erebus. Yet it burns.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A medieval war movie with echoes of Seven Samurai and Vietnam. An intellectual convinces a mercenary leader not to pillage his village but to use it as a sanctuary, and the relationship between the soldiers and the locals affects both. Very discursive, but gorgeous shot, and consistent in being able to find good spins on the central conflict. Omar Sharif and Michael Caine are terrific as the leads, and this is very well handled by novelist James Clavell. File under offbeat big-budget movies that I'm very glad exist.

reviews.author: 🇵🇱 Steve G 🐝
reviews.text: Strange to see James Clavell adapting somebody else's novel for the screen considering he was a novelist himself.
