reviews.text: Incredible epic film about the war between Christians and Protestants with an absolutely magnetic Michael Caine. Absolutely recommend it!

reviews.author: Patrick
reviews.text: 1971 continues... A big 70mm epic ‘The Last Valley’ should be seen on a big screen. Like I said when I reviewed ‘Kingdom of Heaven’ though, there just isn’t much call for this kind of movie anymore. Everyone being stuck inside really doesn’t help the experience. Micheal Caine is excellent in ‘The Last Valley’ as a German Captain in the 30 Years War. He and his men track Omar Sharif to a small catholic village nestled in some mountains. Sharif convinces Caine that rather than ransack his army should occupy the town. This causes several clashes over religion between the protestant occupiers and Catholic villagers. There’s also a witch plot line. It’s all very well and good but I was too distracted…

reviews.author: doppelgangerdev
reviews.text: Very interesting hearing Michael Caine do a German accent. Gets quite dense at a few moments, but still impressive film. Sumptuous visuals throughout and a few nicely staged, though dry battles. We need more movies on the thirty years war. I think one reason fantasy material doesn't connect with me as much is because they tend to visualize it around this period, but since it's not historical cuts out so much of the dynamics that were in play in those characters lives. Weirdly something that maybe because I've aged is more interesting to me than the magic.

reviews.author: giant13
reviews.text: Filmed on location in Austria, The Last Valley is a beautiful looking film, especially for the 1970s. Maybe that’s the charm of the 70mm photography and work of cinematographers, John Wilcox and Norman Warwick. But even so, the film is very claustrophobic feeling—possibly the sign of an inexperienced director—which is odd for a period piece set mostly outdoors. For a historical drama it’s more than serviceable, but the leading stars Shariff and Caine cannot carry the entire film home. A one and done, another cog in the “blow, snow, or dust” filmography, for me only.

reviews.author: CC_The_Martian
reviews.text: Goddamn...Like...goddamn.How does a movie manage to take such a simple premise (a band of war weary mercenaries find a valley untouched by the war) and explore so many ideas? It's the kind of movie where different narrative threads and themes are going to stick out to different people and I love films like that. Adding to all that thematic richness is a pitch perfect cast who all work off each other well and give suitably muted performances until narrative peaks draw larger moments out of them.Did I mention the production design and costumes are literal perfection? The visuals in general are a masterstroke into themselves. There are some haunting frames in this film.Well worth your time. Check it out!!!

reviews.author: Thorkell August Ottarsson
reviews.text: As is often the case, artists are punished for making their greatest masterpieces. That was the fate of Sergei Parajanov when he made The Color of Pomegranates. He was not allowed to make another film and put in prison (on charge of homosexuality) to silence him. He would be imprisoned 3 times in his life, one of the main reasons why he died of ill health. Color of Pomegranates was published in 1968 and it was not until 1986 (18 years later) that the world got to see a new film from the master. And what does he film? A story about immurement. Was there a hidden message in this topic? I think so.

reviews.author: Luke Whittle
reviews.text: This Georgian folk tale was told in a typical Parajanov fashion with tableau like scenes, which are of course mesmerising and effective. Despite that Parajanov was disallowed to make films since The Colour of Pomegranates, I was surprised that his style was very much in tact. The beginning in particular was very captivating, and it drew me in first time watching it.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Myth and freedom. The popular imagination pushes towards sacrifice while the images conjured by the filmmaker expanda the scope. Paradjanov feel for color and movement remain stunning.

reviews.author: Div_vs_film
reviews.text: You've got to admire the career of Sergei Parajanov. Wandering across the Soviet Union and making deeply culturally rich films within and about its constituent countries. Armenia with The Color of Pomegranates, Ukraine with Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors and now Georgia. Stylistically we're somewhat in a midpoint between the two. A lot of attention has been paid to fixed camera angles and in a painterly fashion they are layered with points of cultural and aesthetic interest. People move in them but typically just performing simple actions. At the same time the camera does move, people talk and there are fragmented stories here. Unfortunately this is easily the weakest of the three and the mixing of the elements means that it…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Stylistically a clear descendant of Color of Pomegranates (a fruit I will always hesitate in the midst of spelling), this film apparently took quite some time to come about. The legendary source material is deeply rooted in historical religious conflicts, but Parajanov uses his signature style to turn poetic and folkloric stories into surreal imagery. It's a strange story that seems to condemn conversion by force while allowing that conversion by other means might not be so bad. In the end, self-sacrifice is the almost literal cornerstone.

reviews.author: Robert Beksinski
reviews.text: The Legend of Suram Fortress marks the long awaited and extremely struggled comeback of the Soviet genius Sergei Parajanov. After 15-16 years of forced absence from cinema and withstanding all of the oppressive troubles that one could take (including two lengthy prison sentences) it still was not enough to hold Parajanov down even if the effects began to slowly break him. I think the massive amount of ill fated instances that he had to suffer with during his suppressed and censored life by the higher authorities of a totalitarian government did impact his style of cinema drastically. Parajanov was only able to make four films that were completely his own, two in the 60's and two in the 80's with…

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: The Archers really were that good, huh? I never expected this to be anything less than a masterpiece, but the sheer complexity of characterization on display here really floored me. I'm particularly taken with Anton Wolbrook's Theo Kretschmar-Schuldorff and his longer section on the loss of family, home and children at the onset of the second world war. He shakes and quivers, but tries to maintain his composure when he utters sarcastically that his children are "good nazi's". He failed as a parent here, because he couldn't keep his children away from the seduction of Hitler's evil, but moreso than that he failed as a military officer because in his eyes world war II would have never happened if he…

reviews.text: one of the most sophisticated movies i've ever seen, both politically and aesthetically -- as a satire, i have a hard time thinking of an equal. a story which seems quintessentially english, but also subverts and challenges the notion of 'englishness' at every turn -- the mention of the british empire's boer concentration camps at the beginning is no accident, as candy's romanticism comes to clash with everything that the 'stately' notion of englishness carefully smooths over -- the techniques and evils of colonialism becomes the internalized logic of fascism, the hypocrisies of the english to criticize the germans when really they partake in the same disgusting philosophies -- but that's the states, not the individuals, the individual soldiers fighting…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A very beautiful and very funny movie about a fool who ages gracefully by getting forced to acknowledge the cracks in the impeccable world around him. A movie that tries such an impossible balance in how it tries to observe British early 20th century worldview from an urgent prescriptive position. It is in some ways a movie that could only be made during wartime, and that is impossible to believe someone actually manage to pull during it. Also, so affecting romantic against all logic. It is a movie that seems destined to be out of step, which is part of its allure.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The best thing about this film is still the central friendship between two men across a significant divide. Its overriding message is even more prominent the second time through, simply because, knowing it, you see it everywhere. That's fine, though. Even though it's an eloquent argument for total war, it's also a call to go against tradition and a distinct depiction of the Nazis as pure evil.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Two of the most brilliantly sophisticated visual filmmakers of all time doing both a satirical, historical wartime comedy of manners and a deeply expressive, romantic and painful portrait of the passage of time. And yet, it's all a bit... British (derogatory), innit?

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: An elegy for the old British way of life that may just have all of life (and movies) in it. An epic sweep of minute observations, of pride in good form that necessitates a certain level of obliviousness, of the military man's need for war emphasized only through the trophy heads that materialize in his rarely occupied home during peacetime, of romance revealed only in rearview as belatedly understood love sends shades of a never-aging ideal back into an older and older man's life to comfort and taunt him. A battleground's painted skies contain only the sound of birds taking their first tentative chirps at the cessation of hostilities, and low-key lighting blends with aging makeup to give further voice…

reviews.author: StephenM
reviews.text: A formative film in Japanese animation. The sixth color feature completed by Toei Animation (a company which had modeled itself on Disney), this is perhaps the first time the Japanese industry made a convincing case for what made it different from American animation. Along with the premiere of Osamu Tezuka’s Astro Boy TV series that January, 1963 was the year anime as we know it was born.

reviews.text: This was a fantastic movie. The animation was bomb, the music was groovy, and I loved every minute of the film. Different take on Susanoo than I have seen in other movies, but like Disney versions of classic tales, this makes for a great children's story while amazing the pants off of adults. Some of the sequences are so beautiful that I never wanted them to end. Felt similar to what Disney did with Sleeping Beauty and Fantasia. The message itself was sweet and I would recommend this film to anyone.

reviews.text: Because no one will explain death to Prince Susano, he goes on a quest in search for his mother who “has gone to a place you can’t find.” This brings him to multiple cool mythical locations and ultimately sets him to fight against the eight-headed dragon Yamata no Orochi. This movie is gorgeous! I love the flat art style and beautifully painted backgrounds, matched with fluid animation. All heightened by a booming Akira Ifukube score, which seems especially fitting during the dragon battle.

reviews.author: The Film Bug 🐛
reviews.text: Oh man, THESE VISUALS!! Eye-popping colors and gorgeous, jagged psychedelia. The comparisons to Disney are apt in the storytelling department, but anime came into its own in 1963 with this and Tezuka's Astroboy. It's moody, it's exciting, it's thrilling! Just a wonderful magical world and I eat it up.

reviews.author: Nathan
reviews.text: A major influence on subsequent works including Samurai Jack, The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, and the films of Cartoon Saloon, and a fascinating milestone in the evolution of Japanese animation before it fully became what we today define as anime. Mixes influences from Western animation (the rabbit sidekick is particularly Disney-esque, and a lot of the character designs have a very abstracted, European modernist look to them) with elements of traditional Japanese art and a story from Shinto mythology. As a narrative, it's a bit too episodic to hang together fully, and the English dub I watched is unfortunately pretty poor*, but the animation is absolutely beautiful throughout; well worth watching for animation fans.

reviews.author: Halcyon
reviews.text: Visually groundbreaking concepts are introduced, the sheer ambition here remains unmatched in the current industry for the most part. The film combines snippets of mythology, slightly altering them for child viewership while retaining a strict vision of Susano's character. He's temperamental and impulsive, also selfless when it comes to helping others with his bravery. Adversity's role in the script is intriguing, consistently posing a challenge for the boy, subconsciously teaching him heaven is transcendent. The production is artistically striking, inventive in its use of elementary shapes and their range of motion. Susano's gloriously dramatic battles have been influential not only for Kaiju films but animation as a whole. His final fight against the eight-headed dragon is one of the most dynamically choreographed sequences in anime history. Character designs are unique in angularity, as the background art reflects traditional Japanese hues. Wanpaku Ouji no Orochi Taiji is innovative to no end, tightly stylized, electrifying with its monaural orchestral score.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: As Katharina is dragged into interrogation and humiliated by the police, it's impossible not to consider this in light of well documented treatment of women in the wake of sex scandals and rape accusations. The investigators rip apart her apartment, question her motives and history, and make insinuations about her. They do not so much inquire as demand, so much quiz as insist. She is guilty not until proven innocent, but simply guilty. Hand-in-hand with the state's authority goes the press, sensationalizing, lying, and rumor-mongering. This is a direct metaphor for the way women are slut-shamed in private and public, and as the film progresses, it weaves into it layer upon layer.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: The Lost Honor of Katharina Blum reminded me a bit of Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion, released five years earlier, in that both detail the great pantomime of justice that is the pride of so many governments. In neither film does the police, or the media, or the justice system exist in order to right wrongs, or protect the innocent. Instead, they exist, first and foremost, to sustain themselves and, second, to present a very specific image of the state and its allies to anyone looking in from the outside.

reviews.author: St. Sebastian
reviews.text: This work serves as a brutally honest critique of the oppressive patriarchy, with its pervasive sexism, chauvinism, and the propagation of biased media that only reinforces the act of mansplaining. Despite Katharina Blum's tumultuous life, her character ultimately emerges as strong and triumphant. The final meeting scene serves as a direct challenge to a society that claims to be "correct and law-abiding," but is filled with hatred and abuse disguised as "love and care," which Katharina rightfully rejects in favor of her RAF-related Prince Charming. Both of them now stand stronger than the entire world! Furthermore, when considering the blatant disregard for individual rights exhibited by the state and society, as seen in Blum's case, it becomes evident that, even in the historical context, the entire audience supports those who defy such injustices in the distant year of 1975.

Katharina, a housekeeper, is repeatedly interrogated by the police, who scrutinize her life and expenses in detail. As the negative reports grow, Katharina begins to receive death threats and aggressive anonymous letters. reviews.text: The music lovers is a typical Ken Russel film and I mean that in a complimentary way, it’s a emotionally focused stylish biopic of famous Russian composer Tchaikovsky and is probably the furthest away from a conventional biopic but I think that’s what makes it so good. The film offers an unusual for the time look into sexual repression especially through Tchaikovsky‘s sexuality and this gives us a good dive into his torment and passion which was fuelled into his music. Richard Chamberlain who plays Tchaikovsky gives a brave bold performance who perfectly encapsulates the intensity and essence of the musician which fuels his tortured nature and just shows how underrated of an actor he was.

reviews.author: Vera Drew
reviews.text: Wow. I am so happy to be having my Ken Russell phase at this moment because I feel like I’ve fucked and unfucked my life as an artist/queer person/narcissist enough to relate to this film lol. I’ve never seen a movie so adequately portray how effectively toxic annd insatiable longing can feed creativity, commerce, and madness. The tragedy that someone can be loved for their art and despised for what they are and how it makes zero sense when art might be the purest expression of self.

Russell sets this up from the very beginning, opening the film with a near reel-long performance of the Piano Concerto No. 1 that both introduces most of the characters and the fantasies and desires that the composition and performance inspire within them. It's an exhilarating sequence, and just one of many that are all the more impressive for allowing for Russell's trademark frenzied…

reviews.text: Biopics are a genre that is often reduced to the watered down depictions of people who’s lives we are usually already very familiar with, and as such, we are able to see through the facade of most of these modern renderings. Ken Russell however, would not be content to give us this sort of glitzy, all-is-well-even-when-it-isn’t-until-the-end-or-when-it’s-convenient-to-the-picture retelling. No, The Music Lovers depicts what is furthest from the recycled, uniformly prudent biopics of today—especially those about music makers—than one could possibly imagine if their only point of reference are the recent biopics that don’t do their subjects justice.

reviews.author: Brian Formo
reviews.text: The Music Lovers elicited this response from one of the all-time great film critics, Pauline Kael: “You feel (like) you should drive a stake through the heart of the man who made it.” The man who made it is Ken Russell. Historically speaking, The Music Lovers follows the doomed heterosexual attempts by famed composer Pyotr Tchaikovsky (Richard Chamberlain) as he rises through the musical world by turning his back on his homosexuality and takes part in a sham of a marriage. It’s about the power of music but it’s also about the destructiveness of withholding sex—from one’s self and from others.

reviews.author: Ken Rudolph
reviews.text: This big budget French biopic told the story of oceanographer and documentary film maker Jacques Cousteau and his family. Lambert Wilson and Audrey Tautou played the Cousteau parents, who refitted a large boat they named the Calypso, and set off with their two young sons and a large crew to explore the ocean depths. For the next 30 years, they made films and supported save-the-oceans environmental causes. Their younger son, Philippe (another wonderful, charismatic performance by Pierre Niney) turned to aviation to abet his family's causes. The film has large scope, with beautiful underwater sequences and an extended tour of the Cousteaus' pioneering excursion to Antarctica. I'm old enough to have followed the Cousteaus' filmed adventures on television; but the family's history of triumphs and hardships were new to me; and made for a fascinating and involving true life story.

reviews.text: One of the most meticulously staged, carefully composed films of the ‘70s—much is made of Gordon Willis’ mastery of shadow and vanishing light, a tool to shade motivation and highlight a moral murkiness, but it is Alan Pakula’s patience that lifts this into rarefied territory. The recurring motif of ant-like miniaturedom—Beatty’s character trapped in the dam as water crashes through the man made valley; assassination seen from a great height; figures squeezed into airplane bathrooms or tiny apartments and offices; the tribunal at a distant remove, faceless and omniscient—underscores a theme of powerlessness and an inability to effect change, or even be seen clearly. This is the soft middle of Pakula’s famed Paranoia Trilogy, and the least celebrated of the…

Stuff like this and Chinatown and The Conversation. The scene in this where Beatty watches the indoctrination video in which the photographic signifiers of Home, Enemy, Sex, etc get mixed up... has there been anything that radical in a mainstream Hollywood movie since? Anyway anyone who worked on these movies and is still alive is probably retweeting The Lincoln Project now.

reviews.text: Even with its greedy landlords pushing black folks out of the ghetto, the class warfare element here has been a little overstated; like a lot of Craven's best stuff it's just a foundation to ground the nightmare in a recognizable headspace. Splitting the action between the decrepit mansion and the maze-like crawlspaces between walls is the clearest expression of its overlapping worlds of declining decadence and urban decay, but it also perfectly sets the stage for a supremely kooky children's-tale-turned-rancid in the scariest-ass house on the block, Hansel and Gretel spun out with a pair of incestuous siblings keeping an army of cannibal urchins in the basement. Also one of Craven's funniest movies, packed with weirdness like Everett McGill in full-on gimp bondage gear running around with a shotgun yelling his head off.

reviews.text: It's become clichéd hack shit to write, "wow, crazy to think a studio would let this fly now, let alone [x] years ago", but seriously, it's crazy to think Universal let Wes Craven cast Ed & Nadine Hurley from TWIN PEAKS as incestuous psycho greed-monger landlords (but really...is there any other kind?) who scream racist obscenities before getting dressed up in bondage gear to hunt our underage black protagonist through their suburban labyrinth estate with a shotgun. And that's BEFORE the mutant cannibals emerge from the basement of their last mansion on the left. Just an absolutely deranged studio relic that no doubt was at least one foundational blueprint for BARBARIAN (not to mention DON'T BREATHE).

The last 5 minutes of this movie after the assault sum up Erika's whole life and show us how sad it's always been for her. She's standing in the middle of the concert hall lobby with bruises on her face and tears in her eyes and yet no one cares. They just put on a fake smile, talk about themself, and wait for her to perform for them like a monkey. Her whole life has been devoted to trying to prove herself and impress others, but no one really cares. It's so sad. Erika is one of the deepest, most fleshed-out characters of any movie ever made and Isabelle Huppert absolutely delivered one of the best performances ever.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: James Glickenhaus had a major box office hit in gritty vigilante flick The Exterminator (1980), so seemed a solid choice to helm Golden Harvest's third attempt to break Jackie Chan into an international market. Only Death Wish urban gun toting sadism doesn't really blend well with the more elaborate, physical and playful action of Jackie Chan - and the uncomfortable marriage failed to live up to either man's successes. Tensions between approaches led to conflict on set, resulting in a number of theatrically released edits. Had The Protector (1985) found an audience, these animosities would have died with production, but performing well below expectations, neither man held their tongues. Coraghessan Boyle's "Road to Wellville" was published back in 1993, it immediately became a favorite read of mine, as it tied together multiple persuasions of therapeutic charlatanism into a highly entertaining tale of a young man and his wife who're drawn to John Harvey Kellogg's sanatorium in Battle Creek, Michigan. In the “yes” column, we have some pitch-perfect RKO-style musical numbers, lots of top-notch scenery chewing from the whole cast, and most importantly, Isabella Rossellini wearing a platinum blond wig, a tinsel tiara, and a pair of lager-filled glass legs. In the “no” column, we just have me not being able to connect with this film in any way that I recognize as authentically camp.

Dietrich is great as always, showing an unusual amount of range as her character develops, but I also love Sam Jaffe who hits his inbred "half-wit" out of the park.

reviews.text: A haunting, sublime, meditative masterpiece, one of those films whose every image is burned deep into my retina. A man wanders a desolate landscape, increasingly overtaken by a blizzard, his figure reduced to nothingness as the screen fills with white. He arrives, from Leningrad, at a remote Siberian village to bury his father. Nothing is easy about the process. The most painful and true and mysterious fact about life becomes reduced to a thing so grossly and emphatically there – a desiccated corpse sprawled across an unmade bed in a house gone to pieces. The spiritual act of honoring the dead, of offering tribute to life’s meaning, becomes an endless series of bureaucratic indignities and mundanities. It’s all shot in…

And this museum in question is one that consists of memories that help you with coming to terms with death. Granted, it's exactly what this narrative we're watching in here is built around, but there's also a point in which one wonders what's set in store for us after death. Sokurov leaves you thinking deeply about this, should we find ourselves facing death, as we know it's set to…

reviews.text: Als ich 2016 zu Bud Spencers Tod eine kleine Werkschau von etwa 30 seiner Filme machte, war "Der Große mit seinem außerirdischen Kleinen" zusammen mit seinem Nachfolger "Buddy haut den Lukas" (Lupo 1980) einer der Tiefpunkte, diesmal gelang es dem Film jedoch durchaus, gute Laune zu erzeugen. Den 6jährigen Co-Star Cary Guffey kennt man bereits aus "Unheimliche Begegnung der 3. Art" (Spielberg 1977, hier noch 4 Jahre alt) und wurde aufgrund des SF-Themas dieser Komödie sicher nicht zufällig ausgewählt. Interessant ist auch, dass der Film vieles aus Spielbergs später entstandenem Film "E. T." (1982) vorwegnimmt. Der Film richtet sich an eine sehr junge Zielgruppe, die sich noch mit dem "außerirdischen Kleinen" identifizieren kann und von slapstickhaften Prügelszenen, sprechenden Tieren und eingängigen, teils von Kindern gesungenen Songs von Oliver Onions begeistert sein dürfte. 1979 war der Film entsprechend auch einer der größten Kassenerfolge in den deutschen Kinos.

reviews.text: Super-Harmloser Kinderspaß, für den ich 1979, als ich ihn im Kino sah, eigentlich schon zu alt war, obwohl ich noch gar nicht so alt war. Aber die Kombi Bud Spencer/Außerirdischenbezug war Pflicht für einen Kinogang 1979, denn genau diese beiden Aspekte beherrschten damals die Leinwände. So war DER GROSSE MIT SEINEM AUSSERIRDISCHEN KLEINEN auch Platz 7 der Kinocharts. Man könnte annehmen, dass mit solcher Art Filmen, also Komödien bzw. Verarschen die SF-Welle langsam wieder abebbte (denn das waren mehr oder weniger auch die in den Charts noch davorliegenden LOUIS UNHEIMLICHE BEGEGNUNG MIT DEN AUSSERIRDISCHEN (Platz 1) und MOONRAKER (Platz 3)), aber ALIEN (den ich nur 2 Monate später im Kino sah) stand schon in den Startlöchern und revolutionierte das alles nochmal. DER GROSSE MIT SEINEM AUSSERIRDISCHEN KLEINEN ist primär nix mehr für einen alten Sack wie mich, hat aber das Herz am rechten Fleck, ist supersympathisch und werde ich mir irgendwann in 20 Jahren nochmal mit meinen Enkel*innen ansehen.

The main difference between the earlier type of film and The Snapper is the latter’s lack of overt sentimentality and its openness about sex. Adapted by Roddy Doyle from his novel, The Snapper deals with characters from an earlier Doyle novel and the 1991 film The Commitments. Because the producers of the earlier film own the rights to the characters’ names, however, the Rabbitte family has become the Curleys. reviews.author: animebachelor btw
reviews.text: A beautiful forgotten classic of animation, and apparently the reason Miyazaki got into the animation business. Stylistically, it resembles a hybrid of Fleischer school of animation with pre-Snow White Disney. The Snow Queen herself is one of the most fascinating characters I've seen in animation. She is a personified force of nature, practically a Russian variation on a Greek goddess. She does not passionately lash out at the trite insults of little Kay because she is literally animated ice [no meta-pun intended]. Instead, her reaction is matter-of-fact, which makes it all the more intriguing. You respect her because she is all-powerful, like the deities of ancient Greece. If you haven't seen this, it's on YouTube for free, but only subtitled. Besides, it's only 60 minutes long. What's to lose? See it for the beautiful animation and the joyous adaptation of a classic tale.

reviews.text: Wow, wasn't expecting this to hit so hard! This dark crime/noir film was based on the same real life story that Fritz Lang based his 1936 "Fury" on - a heavily publicized kidnapping/murder that led to the mob lynching of the suspect. It's also about how societal circumstances can turn an ostensibly good man to criminal behavior to survive. As with "Fury", it was extremely powerful.

reviews.author: mike_sabathia
reviews.text: Almost certainly one of the darkest noirs I've seen. Even darker than Fritz Lang's Fury, its closest companion as it was based on the same incident. There isn't a single facet of postwar American society the film doesn't condemn. The underlying desperation, loneliness and spiritual and financial despair and thoroughly brought out in the open. And the mob mentality depicted in the final scenes is truly harrowing. Frank Lovejoy stars as a family man, living in California, who is having much trouble financially. He meets up with a small-time hood Jerry (Lloyd Bridges) who convinces him into participating in crimes that slowly escalate into something serious. It's a shame that this film isn't better known.

reviews.text: The aural elements of the film are introduced by the score, whimsical and mostly comprised of woodwinds, emerging over a series of children’s drawings that gradually make up the opening credit sequence. Abruptly being dropped into such a fantastical and “innocent” audiovisual experience definitely contributes to the idea of a childlike perspective, which will be the point-of-view of the audience for most of the film (Ana’s POV). The score of The Spirit of the Beehive also contains strings, and possibly even an organ, but the introductory sequence is enveloped in a fairytale-esque tone mostly due to the recurring flute motif.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Spiritual death, spirit death; the loss of childhood innocence brings with it the loss of divinity. Where everyone else sees inevitability in the material world the child is the only who sees the possibility of change through the spiritual one, the grace of God in this case being that of the power of cinema (non-reality, reverie) but more-so a grace that is conveyed through cinema. It is this divinity that imparts itself on six-year old Ana and gives her the spirit to change the world, to revolutionize the world, and it is also this divinity that appears before her in the form of spirits only she can see. The death of one means the death of the other.

reviews.author: Scott Anderson
reviews.text: As a child, seeing a film was the spark that lit my imagination on fire, from my first journey through a galaxy far, far away to the nights I couldn't sleep because a Xenomorph might be lurking in the darkness. In The Spirit of the Beehive, a traveling cinema brings Frankenstein to a small Spanish village and people of all ages line their chairs up in excitement to catch a glimpse of the picture. Included in this group are two sisters, six year old Ana and the elder Isabel, and Ana is fascinated by the film, in particular a specific scene in which Frankenstein plays with a little girl only to accidentally kill her.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: This is one of the most beautiful films I've ever seen. It put me in mind of Malick's Days of Heaven, with its amber fields and stunning vistas. This film is an allegory of class and politics, decoded when a (Spanish) Republican soldier flees, wounded, into a nearby shack. In here is a message of hope to the people of Spain, at the time still living under a repressive regime (albeit not quite as much so as it had once been). The spirit has no body, but it can appear to you if you close your eyes and call to it.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Haunting, impressionistic slice of Spanish magical realism where a young girl learns about the concept of death and war and slips into a dreamlike fable to make sense of it, or simply a movie about what it's like to watch Frankenstein for the first time and become obsessed with Boris Karloff? A gorgeous, meditative film regardless.

This is the point of inspiration for several future moviemakers around the world, especially Guillermo del Toro.

reviews.author: SilentDawn
reviews.text: An expertly layered tale of emotional maturation and family termoil; The Spirit of the Beehive is also a creepy and understated ghost story. Yet it isn't a ghost story in a traditional sense; the film mostly focuses on the human ghosts in our lives: Secrets, our troubled past, long-kept family heirlooms, and the brushed-aside comfort of the truth.

reviews.author: Lowe McKee
reviews.text: Can you remember when it was that you first really thought about death? When you first recognized that you and everyone you love will go away some day... Was it the loss of a grandparent? It's hard for me to remember, really. For so many of us, it isn't just one moment. It happens through the osmosis of being alive. Attending a funeral as a young kid, watching movies or tv shows where characters are killed off, overhearing adults talk about the death of a loved one, listening to bigger kids joke about it at school.

It’s the kind of movie that gently opens a door in your mind to a different kind of cinema, one that lives in metaphor, and trusts you to lean in and listen closely.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Spirit of the Beehive is a beautifully subtle film, a work made so calmly and yet filled with unstated conflict. It is primarily a film of children, taking us to their view of the world. Explanations and context are not provided, because none are fully understood by children. The Spirit of the Beehive is about Francoist Spain and an innocence set to be raised under a dictatorship. The film depicts the barren landscapes of a dying country, where stories thrive because reality is painful. The narrative centres on a family who are never seen all together, representing the divisions of a disintegrating Spain. reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: For Hollywood studios for much of the 20th century, war movies were about depicting the heroism of Americans and/or their allies. During WWI and, far more extensively, WWII, the American government was directly involved in film production, going so far as to issue detailed guidelines during the early 1940s about how to treat subjects from American allies, to domestic conflicts, in ways that would best suit the war effort. (Films that weren't submitted for approval were unable to get export certificates, so while approval wasn't technically required, it may as well have been.)

reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: Discussed with Marsha Gordon on the latest podcast, and a textbook example of how a writer-director can make a war movie about a contemporary moment that is political without having a stated politics. Both the DOD and the communist papers interpreted Fuller's politics as against their own position. It's of course humanizing (or enraging?) to think that even 60 years ago, the confusion between depiction and endorsement has been brewing. But what's most important is how Fuller could even make this film work neither as a diatribe nor as propaganda, but simply and brutally showing the life of a soldier.

reviews.text: Director Sam Fuller is justly renowned for really knowing how to open a motion picture, and his first war feature THE STEEL HELMET is no exception. It earns enough good will in its first minutes to more than compensate for what it loses due to extreme budgetary constraints. Made for nearly nothing, the film leans into its extraordinary screenplay rather than relying on action. Like Kubrick's later PATHS OF GLORY it's a war film whose foundation is built on ideas. There are any number of remarkable dialogue exchanges here: politically risky and poetic in equal measure.

Naturally, Disney never released this doc, but it wasn't hard to find on YouTube. And boy, for someone who knows the movie, this is fascinating. Zatoichi arrives in his first movie fully formed, a blind masseuse who recently spent years mastering a sword because, in his words, "As far as I'm concerned, whether you call me blind or crippled, I won't object because it's the truth. reviews.text: Andrzej Żuławski set the bar high with his debut feature. The Third Part of the Night is a mash-up of dreamscapes and Gestapo war-crimes set in Nazi-occupied Poland. After a man’s wife and young son are murdered by a group of German soldiers, he decides to join the resistance effort in the nearby town of Lwow. As he wanders the streets of this war-torn city, he witnesses a man being shot who looks eerily like him. He goes to inform the man’s wife, but low and behold, the woman he sees looks exactly like his recently deceased wife. This sets off a cerebral chain of events that turn more bizarre and violent as the film progresses. Doppelgängers, feeding lice, hallucinatory and…

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: The material is much more disturbing when read between lines. There is an asphyxiating aura of war claustrophobia like almost anything seen in the history of world cinema; tension abounds; the underground operations may disturb the characters' motivations permanently if revealed clearly. Exceptional Polish masterpiece about the simultaneous disintegration of nations caused by war, of social relations and the inner struggle of individuals to come to just terms with themselves. Too bad that the Biblical references of the Book of Revelations are included quite preposterously, absolutely out of the Polish context given, when their meaning are actually something entirely different. That minor flaw substracts a point from this damn near perfect film.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Seen through the eyes of its young protagonist, Oskar Matzerath, The Tin Drum communicates the circumstances which foreshadowed the period of National Socialism in Germany along with its widespread injustices and brutal discriminations. David Bennent provides an extraordinary portrayal as Matzerath, and his achievement accelerates this stimulating film. It's an enterprising portrayal of someone who unequivocally advances to the pounding of his own drum and offers up an artistic representation of an individual who prefers not to connect with others. There's a generous sophistication in its direction by Volker Schlöndorff as he employs an extraordinary figurative language.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: Ah, little Oskar, we meet again. Oskar, like a malevolent Peter Pan or a demonic cherub, your star seems to have faded over the years but not to me, you still shine as brightly as ever.Oskar doesn't like the look of the adult world so he refuses to grow up as he lives through the rise of Hitler and WWII. And he inadvertently, or perhaps purposely, causes mayhem and death to those around him, as he uses his tin drum and piercing, glass-shattering scream to get his own way.This was the first film I saw that really made me realise there was a different way of telling stories, that you could make the horrible and grotesque funny, that took me to a place of blackly comic magical realism which I was very comfortable in.I still love it.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: A clever but unformed hunk of speculative science-fiction, Lennart Ruff’s “The Titan” is essentially two parallel stories of survival that are being told at the same time. One is physical and intimate; the other is abstract and infinite. Strangely, they’re both far more interesting on their own than they are cut together, but each of them poses a handful of intriguing questions about our instinct for self-preservation, asking us to locate the point at which trauma might change the basic foundation of who (or what) we are. If only these questions were posed intriguingly, and not just churned through the machinations of genre shlock that doesn’t have the courage to be as smart as either of its stories require it to be.

reviews.text: Despite its exceptional quality and the presence of genre hero Richard Widmark, "The Trap" has mostly eluded noir enthusiasts. It's hard to see why: coming in at barely 85 minutes, the script is taut as a piano wire and immediately hits you with its vitality and tension. Widmark plays a mafia lawyer forced to use family law enforcement connections to help mob boss Lee J. Cobb escape from an oppressively hot desert town. reviews.text: Football features in many of Kiarostami’s films, but none perhaps, as centrally as it does in his full length debut, The Traveler. The focus is on the 10-year old boy Hassan, who is obsessed with the beautiful game. The rest of his life is a frustration interfering with his obsession, and there’s enough of his social backdrop shown to suggest football is his only real outlet of pleasure. His aim is to skip school - and skip home for that matter - by raising enough money to catch a bus to Tehran to watch his team play at the stadium. The first half of the film follows his attempts to raise the money, by hook or by crook, and then…

reviews.author: #im’s
reviews.text: Abbas Kiarostami’s The Traveler is a short, realist gem rich in emotions. It centers on Qassem, a clever but neglected boy who goes lengths; lies, cons his friends, even steals to catch a bus to Tehran to watch his favorite football team play. Along with Kiarostami’s charming narration and beautiful b&w frames, the film is carried by the performace of the boy, Hassan Darabi. Just brilliant. Even if Qassem lies and steals, the writing gives him our sympathy. We fear for Qassem, roots for his dream even it’s flawed and feels the loneliness he suffers. I wish the film continued but the anticlimax is so well placed leaving the emptiness and disappointments of life.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Much like Hot Blood, The True Story of Jesse James feels like a throwback to Ray's RKO potboilers, but the earlier film gypsy setting genuine intrigued him, while Jesse James seems don't. There's two opposite ideas at play here, the script plays up the mythmaking qualities while Ray's direction tries to sell a tormented Jesse (an idea torpedoed by Robert Wagner characteristically non-descript performance). The two are supposed to meet in some form of folk ballad, but the idea remains distant more suggested than lived. Ray's direction has enough dynamic framing, this is far from a total loss, but is hard to imagine anyone but the more hardcore mise en scene afficionados getting taken by it.

reviews.text: Relatively late-career western from Nicolas Ray about the notorious farmhand-turned-outlaw who so perfectly encapsulated that "curious mixture" of good and evil characteristic of the Wild West. How did he become the legend we all know today? Was he turned to violence by the Civil War? Or did he become a Robin Hood figure because of his upbringing? (Two options conveniently offered by a newspaper obituary writer.) The film attempts to answer this question by engaging in some historiography and examining a few key points of his life.

reviews.text: the key innovation in les vampires -- an innovation that has been largely forgotten in the grander tradition of cinema -- is the disruption of post-renaissance western existential assumptions. many reviews of this, at the time and even today, focus on les vampires' status as disposable pulp, a prologue to hitchcock and lang and other myopic purveyors of sinister kill-a-reel entertainment, but that analysis is to mistake the surface content for the form itself; les vampires is not a film about the hunt for a criminal gang, but an ontological rift in visual storytelling that only filmmaking itself can achieve.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Feuillade's static frames and lack of clutter mask an absurd complexity of movement and reversals, the matter-of-factness of the image only making the endless twists all that more bewildering. This reminded me so much of the Resident Evil franchise, in which you can physically see characters die, only to watch them return minutes later, often in some new guise. And even when someone does stay down, it takes seconds for someone to assume their role. Alternating its pioneering procedural with moments of genuine shock and even more of outright hilarity (all the way to the finale which plays equally well as manic farce as it does violent catharsis), this is one of the most outrageously fun works in the history of cinema. I could have watched another 10 episodes of this.

reviews.author: Gylfi
reviews.text: Irma Vep, Satanas, Moréno, Mazamette, such a wonderful set of characters. Watching the film today, you notice Mazamette's constant awareness that he is in a film, looking straight into the camera and winking or giving a sly smile (even funnier when you see that his kid is also aware of the audience), it feels very postmodern and fresh. The action is fast-paced and often suprisingly gripping. The influence it had on Rivette's Out 1, Noli me tangere is evident. A real treasure of a film, I see great replay value here! I recommend the brilliant Kino Blu-Ray version, the almost 100 year old images truly came alive on the screen. Next up, Fantomas and Tih Minh.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: Learning to love. Every gesture exchanged by Granger and O’Donnell’s bodies, be it a gaze, a touch or a phrase, is among the most precious of all cinema. One of those rare spoken films where the human face achieves a paroxysmal point of beauty and bleakness only matched by Griffith. The way the camera sticks to them with a remarkably poetic and pungent patience, cherishing each second, each breath, as if knowing that what they had couldn’t last for much time, is simply too heartbreaking to even comment on. The mix of formal dryness and intense romanticism in the form of economic storytelling has rarely been this rewarding, and the way the short-lived utopia lived by the couple contrasts harshly to the film’s acid takes on capitalism and structural injustice remains very effective and desolating. Out of place, living the impossible as long as they are together, their watches always running out of time, until the lights to go out.

reviews.author: Jaemart
reviews.text: This footage shows Jafar Panahi’s almost stupidly deep passion for an imaginary job that might not seem to matter with the state of the world and with gunshots and sirens polluting the background of Iran. But his exposed love for film, and the heartbreak of being banned from the one thing he cares about, and the presence of his friend who is putting his life and family at risk simply by holding a camera around Panahi, shows the importance of movie-making. This self-aware, charming, and gentle documentary reassures me of my own passions, and that might be the greatest thing a piece of art can do.

reviews.author: Jonathan White
reviews.text: My inspiration for watching this was a recent viewing of Mohammad Rasoulof’s masterpiece The White Meadows. Jafar Panahi, the subject of this quasi documentary, is a well known and respected Iranian filmmaker who recently lent his hand to Rasoulof’s film as an editor. Rasoulof’s film was released in late 2009, and both Rasoulof and Panahi were arrested, tried, sentenced, and jailed in late 2010 for film related activities, specifically propaganda against the Iranian government. Moreover, aside from their six year sentences, they were both banned from any filmmaking activity for 20 years.

reviews.text: This Sporting Life is one of these early 60s dramas coined under the term kitchen sink, part of the British New Wave that propelled a new generation of directors such as Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz, and John Schlesinger — figures who elevated the “angry young man” archetype, crystallizing the angst of post-war British youth into poignant and harrowing portrayals of dreamers whose goals were wasted under the weight of reality and social pressure. Films like Room at the Top and Saturday Night and Sunday Morning depicted young lads pressured into fitting in with society at the expense of their own sense of self-accomplishment — figures who were more antiheroes than heroes, embodying a kind of anti-existentialism that shaped the new…

reviews.text: The best way to watch This Sporting Life is with the mindset of Downhill Racer. In a nutshell, quote: “Like all of the best sports movies, the film is not about the record of the team or the success of the character as an athlete, but rather about the qualities of the person who exists as a result of the game.” Redford & Harris differ in temperament, but the probing is the same. Being a successful athlete—especially at peak—takes a toll. Psychologically. Emotionally. How does that cost affect human relationships? Day-to-day living? Ordinary conversation?

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Lindsay Anderson's 1963 British kitchen sink drama, This Sporting Life, is a remarkable adaptation of the 1960 novel of the same name by David Storey. The novel was a critical success, winning the 1960 Macmillan Fiction Award, and Storey's screenplay captures the essence of the work. The film tells the story of Frank Machin, a talented rugby league player in Wakefield, a mining city in Yorkshire. Despite his success in sports, his romantic life is less successful. Storey, a former professional rugby league player himself, brings a unique insight to the story. It is a vivid and powerful depiction of the struggles and joys of working-class life in the 1960s.

reviews.author: Bruno Youn
reviews.text: What a superb finale for one of the best trilogies ever made. Krzysztof Kieślowski now turns his attention to fraternity and mainly explores the difficulty of making lasting connections in Red. Interestingly, the most developed relationship in the film is the one Valentine forms with the lonely judge instead of her family and boyfriend. One recurring moment in the trilogy is an old woman recycling a glass bottle and Valentine is the only person who helps her, being the kindest one and reinforcing the ideal of fraternity. Irène Jacob’s second collaboration with the director rendered us with another delicate and remarkable performance. Red has a very powerful ending, showing the union of all the symbols and emotions that these characters represent. It’s unfortunate Kieślowski passed away so soon but his legacy will last for eternity.

reviews.text: Red is about the beauty of serendipity, and about the sometimes cruel, constantly mysterious, yet ultimately hopeful ways of fate. In this spontaneous tale, two broken souls connect as a result of a run over dog, and ultimately change each other's life path forever. It's a delicate story that requires tremendous visions and styles to pull off, and director Krzysztof Kieślowski was more than capable to present such a deceivingly mundane story as a visually and thematically memorable statement on life that's equal parts shattering and heartfelt.

reviews.author: autocinephilia
reviews.text: Definitely the most subversive rape-revenge film I've seen. The sound design was especially amazing, with the irregular synth patterns and the whirring discomfort that accompanied the most disturbing moments of the film. The squibs were very pleasing, especially in slow motion. The slow motion sequences were the highlights of the film, with some magnificent camerawork (those slow zooms were tremendous) and great gore splatter. Only disappointment was the lack of penis mutilation, and I also loved how the film teased me with the possibility of an awesome car chase and then made fun of me for wanting one. The structure was tremendously subversive and succeeded in making me feel uncomfortable, especially with those extreme close-ups of penetration. All around, it's the most subversive and artistic its genre has to offer, and I was floored by it's fascination with unflinching and realistic brutality.

reviews.text: Power systems within power systems, oppression subjugated by the oppressed. Even within the trio who seek to break out of late-capitalist confines is systematic oppression still exerted, the realm of boxing a hyper-masculine domain which welcomes the men but not the woman. Radicalism when without structure turns to an animalism that, while still seeking to disrupt power structures, can create its own by taking root in already-existing learned intolerance: Tsuda rebels against his soulless corporate rat-race by "manning up" to feel like he has any power in his life while Kojima works towards radicalizing Tsuda; both deny Hizuru any agency of her own even while she must exist in relation to these two and their life-altering influence. Boxing offers a…

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: I really liked the 2 acts of this movie... then act 3 came along and totally eviscerated me. Explosive gore and chaotic boxing mayhem intertwined with Tsukamoto’s very specific Tetsuo-esque body horror and it’s pretty damn unforgettable. Tokyo Fist may very well be the closest thing to a Boxing horror film? Perhaps, but however you look at it this is most definitely another fucking face-melter from Shinya Tsukamoto.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: tsukamoto's expressionist lighting, gonzo editing and jolting, untethered handheld style applied to an ostensible masculine boxing drama where feelings of inadequacy and rage about relationships and a modern, dilapidated tokyo is expressed through pounding on each others bodies. only tsukamoto being tsukamoto takes that to its logical horror extreme and films this idiosyncratic love triangle as a mass of sweat and blood surrounded by concrete and steel in claustrophobic, delirious frames that eventually explode into what feels like a euphoric montage of mutilation and gushing blood. a tangible emotional release from the structures and bodies we're trapped in.

reviews.author: Juan Castillo
reviews.text: Tras ver Toro, he llegado a la conclusión de que Kike Maillo deseaba anclar su "Torremolinoir" a nuestra realidad social, siguiendo el ilustre ejemplo de Urbizu o Alberto Rodríguez, a la vez que pretendía construir cierta poética a partir del relato criminal y la tragedia con apuntes mitológicos genuinamente meridionales, como un Vermut emparentado con Bigas Luna.Casi todos esos elementos se concentran en el personaje de Romano, interpretado por un hierático José Sacristán, fascinante por sus contradicciones, típicamente hispanas: es una figura paterna que devora a sus hijos, un empresario de hostelería que dirige una organización criminal y un fervoroso adorador de la imaginería católica que conduce su vida en base a supersticiones. Lo mejor de la función.Lo demás, diría yo, no pasa de ser ruido de fondo que intenta dotar de densidad a una partida de ajedrez con demasiada gente jugando a las damas.

reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: One of the better films out there to examine bi-polar disorder, as it does not exploit the condition for laughs (like Silver Linings Playbook), while at the same time it transcends its trappings as propaganda (famed author of the source novel Kay Redfield Jamison actually has a cameo) through pure respect for its subject matter and actors who truly surrender to their roles. Luke Kirby and Katie Holmes are fantastic as two lovers who meet during hospital stays, and rage against the system that tries to keep them apart and medicated, and director Paul Dalio keeps things interesting and unpredictable by adopting their perspective - an inside looking out approach, rather than outside looking in - which makes this more than just Lifetime fodder.

reviews.author: marisa
reviews.text: An unsettling portrayal of two poets with bipolar disorder falling in love while in a mental hospital. As much as I wanted to love this movie (due to my own diagnosis of and time spent in a hospital because of bipolar disorder), I hated it. I was shocked to read that the writer/director wrote it based on his own experience with bipolar disorder because so much of it just seemed to reenforce the horribly stigmatizing caricatures of people with mental illness, especially those who have "the crazy" illnesses. Add to that Katie Holmes's bad acting, and it's just an unfortunate mess. However, it gets two stars for the ending instead of the one star I wanted to give.

reviews.author: Sylvia
reviews.text: One of the most underrated movies ever. It’s visually beautiful and emotionally compelling with a well-constructed story and amazing acting, music, and editing. The writer/director/musical composer/co-editor derived this film from his experiences with his own bipolar disorder; the accuracy and the fact that Touched With Fire was a labor of love shines through in every moment.

reviews.author: Dietcoke4breakfast
reviews.text: This movie means A LOT to me cuz, well... I've lived it. Bipolar is a disease *and* a gift. And it's so damn hard to make things work in a bipolar coupling. Luke Kirby, Griffin Dunne and especially Katie Holmes all give incredibly authentic performances, true to experiences I've witnessed, as well as my own.The cherry on top of everything I love about this movie is the scene of Katie Holmes' mom bathing and shaving her during a depressive episode. Very Splendor in the Grass.

reviews.author: Carlo Vanstiphout
reviews.text: Imagine Tommy Wiseau wrote a spec script for Twin Peaks, someone only cleaned up the language to sound like actual English, but changed nothing else; then Golan & Globus got like, Vampire's Kiss Nic Cage to be an acting coach; and finally put everyone on a strict diet of cocaine. I'm 100% convinced that every ounce shown in the movie is the real deal, and NONE of it went to waste. Everyone in this movie is certifiable, and the grandiose garbage that comes out of their mouths is mind boggling. Not even kidding when I say Wings Hauser is the most nuanced part of this ludicrous equation. Well, he does slur the words "I made you come 16 times in one night" after he just had a stroke, but still.

reviews.author: Evan “Raymond Gun-Virus” Pincus
reviews.text: The devil made this picture. A fever dream of pulp fiction losing control of itself- like Lost Highway, but on accident. People always talk about "oh god, oh man," but that's not even close to scraping the top 20 most baffling lines of diologue here. The opening credits alone exude an unrivaled cocaine energy, but "a Golan-Globus production... of a film by Norman Mailer" might be the greatest one-two punch of all time (although the later "music composed by Angelo Badalamenti... visual consultant: John Bailey" is up there as well).

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: Norman Mailer takes southern gothic and transplants it to coastal New England and fills it with a cast of cartoon noir characters that wouldn't be out of place in Cool World - and it works! Hard to put into words what Tough Guys Don't Dance is - and words are its strong suit - but any world where a film that combines the talents of Mailer, Golan & Globus, Francis Ford Coppola, Angelo Badalamenti, Wings Hauser and Isabella Rosselini is considered "bad" or "so bad it's good", is not a world I want to be a part of. A near perfect movie experience in every way and one of the rare cinema instances of an author being given complete reign to adapt their own novel and do just about anything in the process, regardless of taste or good sense.

reviews.author: Will Menaker

reviews.text: I still think this is a clear case of someone who isn't primarily a filmmaker having zero control over tone, performances, or final edit, but on what has to be my 3rd or 4th viewing I'm starting to think that this is more like Showgirls than Blue Velvet in its aim: a deliberately gaudy, overwrought funhouse mirror of American values, American drive, American sexuality, and American masculinity (with its nasty dovetails of misogyny and homophobia). I dunno, Mailer is kinda full of shit, and Ryan O'Neal is such a dry white turd in a punch bowl. Parsing what's intentional or not takes some of the fun out of just deep-sixing your head in the choppy waters of Helltown and letting it float off into the mist.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: This is uniquely powerful in its choice to barely acknowledge the gunman who on August 1st, 1966 took the University of Texas hostage by climbing the campus tower and firing at civilians below, and instead allow the brave survivors to dictate the way this event is told and remembered. It's harrowing to watch as they recall specific memories of the event (like a savior's hair color, or a part of the body that still remembers being preemptively ready to have a bullet penetrate it) and see them complimented by deeply expressive rotoscope animation reenactments that beautifully capture all the detailed, human moments and feelings that swirled around such a tragic day. In the end, it's those brief moments of humanity and bravery that are going to get us through events like these.

reviews.text: An inventive exercise in artistic journalism, Tower revisits the 1966 University of Texas mass shooting by dramatizing the memories of those who were there via rotoscoping animation (in which live action is layered with animated effects). reviews.text: I don't say this about a lot of things on a first viewing, but I believe this may be a masterpiece of documentary storytelling. I've never seen anything quite like it and it is moving, often horrifying, emotional, intense, artistic, and downright profound. I couldn't take my eyes off of this film. It is such a beautifully made film and while it may seem like the art style could take away from the subject or diminish the message of courage that was on display, it really only adds to what makes this documentary truly special. I had no idea what I was in store for with this film, but I couldn't be happier that I gave it a chance. This truly is a masterwork of cinema and a wonderful documentary.

reviews.text: Tower is a perfect documentary. It’s based on the 2006 Texas Monthly article 96 Minutes by Pamela Colloff about the 1966 shootings at the University of Texas at Austin. I knew next to nothing beforehand regarding this tragic event, but director Keith Maitland excels at putting us present tense center of the action; we feel we are there, though more importantly, we feel we get to know the people who were. Incredibly moving, uniquely captured, and poignant in every sense. Very few films restore my faith in humanity. Tower is one of ‘em.

reviews.author: Jaime Rebanal 🇵🇸
reviews.text: There's almost no acknowledgement whatsoever of the gunman in this scenario but I feel like that's also what makes Tower feel so visceral, because it works best as a representation of the memories being recreated. It's unlike most other narrative feature films about similar subject matter in that it's not an approach that feels exploitative, but knowing what the people went through it also feels like the best way for this story to be told to its viewers and it's all the more compelling for that reason alone.

reviews.author: Michael James
reviews.text: An ambitious and powerful crime drama from Steven Soderbergh which explores the illegal drug trade via three interconnected stories from various tangible perspectives in users, traffickers, enforcers and politicians. With an ensemble cast, the well written narrative and characters are given the much needed amplification. Their grayness and untrustworthiness keeps the guessing game live throughout. The lightings, highly saturated visuals, hand held cinematography and documentary style treatment makes it all the more absorbing and gripping. Though it gets draggy and melodramatic at places, it’s a solid drama with both style and substance. Recommended.

reviews.text: Despite reflexively buying the Criterion of this when it came out, I've had no interest in revisiting this as the prospect of returning to a 2.5-hour network narrative about the drug war as an adult and not a budding cinephile teen felt doomed. reviews.text: Sums up as a boiler room episode type film. One setting for the most part. Gotta say I liked this for what it is. Very 90s style thriller with lost treasure, gangs, Ice Cube doing his thing, and underappreciated Bill Paxton. Very weirdly mixed soundtrack. Lots happen but due to the one location it doesn't quite feel eventful. Still it was pretty entertaining. Surprised this one doesn't have a bit more love on here (sadly besides the few famous ones a lot of the 90s urban film subgenre is kind of lost to the modern audience). Pretty solid just not great. Still if you like Bill Paxton you gotta watch it just for him.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This is a classic nineties thriller that isn't great but it is thrilling in all the right places and a thoroughly enjoyable watch all the way through. The plot follows a couple of firefighters who come a cropper of a local drug gang while on the hunt of gold in an old tenement building. Director Walter HIll constantly injects the film with tension which helps to keep things interesting even when the film takes a turn for the ridiculous. The characters are all set up early doors and the audience knows the stakes right from the start. While the story does err towards the predicable side; it remains interesting for the duration and Trespass is an entertaining thriller all the way through. Bill Paxton is great, along with the rest of the cast and theres a real sense of black humour running throughout the film. Good watch with a few beers!

reviews.author: Matheus Fiore
reviews.text: Everett recebe o trabalho de produzir uma reportagem sobre as últimas horas de Frank, homem condenado à morte pelo assassinato de uma jovem. Nas muitas viagens de carro que faz durante sua investigação, ouve sempre um noticiário pelo rádio sobre o caso. Mas o noticiário nunca discute o crime, nunca ressalta a ausência de provas, nunca questiona o processo legal que levou Frank à pena capital. O que se ouve são detalhes sobre a injeção legal, minúcias do processo de execução. É um ritual, com aval do estado, da imprensa e da sociedade. O trabalho de Everett, então, é desnudar o quão distorcidos são esse estado, essa imprensa e essa sociedade.

reviews.text: An emotional rollercoaster, monumentally moving, sacrificing your entire life for a belief in order that another man can live happily with his family - that's where true heroism lies, martyrdom is the only means towards actually arriving somewhere meaningful. It gets a bit rushed towards the ending and that heart chain was way too much emphasized, to an extent where we all already knew where the narrative was going half an hour before its time, but who cares when we have so many strikingly beautiful moments with the inmate and his wife and daughter? Or Eastwood's character in a madly, miraculously pulp ride bumping into everything he needed in order to save a life. Santa Claus rides alone.

reviews.text: 'Twixt' is a film aptly named, one hard to tease or puzzle out, but easy to love. Probably the most Francis Ford Coppola movie in the history of Francis Ford Coppola movies, this movie has nearly everything in it but belongs to no one set genre or style. The film it is closest to in FFC's catalog is 'Rumble Fish', which was a smaller, more personal and experimental take on the kind of story told in 'The Outsiders', so maybe it is possible to think of this as a greatly delayed 'Rumble Vampire', as thematically and even visually, it takes many cues from 'Bram Stoker's Dracula', and, like 'Rumble Fish', frequently operates in black and white with highlights and aspects…

reviews.text: Watched the new B'Twixt Now and Sunrise version - billed as "The Authentic Cut" - which is nine minutes shorter than the original. Justin helpfully explains that Coppola has cut the conclusion of the mystery plot to instead end on the reveal Kilmer's daughter's death. The ending is really abrupt now, like when you think there's one more step in a staircase but there isn't, but there's a certain power to that.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Coppola's digital poverty row movie about the dangerous allure of fictions. It exists somewhere between Carpenter's In The Mouth of Madness and late Resnais resurrections of archaic theatre. As a Brazilian underground filmmaker once said, if you can't make a movie, you can always make movies about movies. Val Kilmer and Bruce Dern are delicious on the joke, Ben Chaplin as Poe is not, which might make him even funnier. Some haunting images, a feeling that it is all laid bare, a little too much as a lecture. There are lots of embarrassing moments and a few very touching ones. Deeply personal, the moment Kilmer's writer is turned into a film spectator, and it becomes clear what the movie is about hits as hard as anything on Coppola's body of work. If Megalopolis never happens, this silly mad movie is not a bad career summation to go out on.

On their trip back from this town to the airport the get into the biggest storm for 25 years and they have to make a 3-day-break in a hut. After this they find some beautiful surf spots and in the last 10 minutes there are some fantastic scenes about these guys surfing in the polar lights!!!These guys are pretty likeable, so this was ok to. reviews.author: Dustin Baker
reviews.text: Tarnation was a wonderful movie, showcasing a family that still had the patience and love to help each other even with all of the sickness around them. It was especially touching to someone like me who's completely given up on maintaining familial relationships and in fact tried moving 3,000 miles away to help get away from this shit. So I consider Jonathan here on the level of sainthood. And while this film may not have a lot to add to the other, for those of us who cared, it serves as a great follow up, keeping us in touch with these people in the decade after. The footage speaks for itself, while also allowing the editing to create a film with a voice all of its own, avoiding anything resembling cliche. It creates an artist's voice when other documentaries barely try to do so.

reviews.text: Nicolas Roeg is fast becoming one of my favorite directors. Granted, I've only digested three of his films so far, and I understand that his quality declines quite drastically later in his career (otherwise, I would have expected him to be one of the all-time greats instead of just respected yet rarely talked about), but he has yet to take a misstep in my book. Not only are the films of his I've watched commendable, they are truly excellent. From his mastery of the thriller/horror in Don't Look Now to the daring experimental sci-fi of The Man Who Fell To Earth, I've now been lucky enough to catch the beautiful, perhaps even 'Malickian' nature odyssey of Walkabout.

He also consistently succeeds in pushing the boundaries of the cinematic medium, contrasting images and forcing us to draw our own conclusions from them.

An early scene involves protecting a wagon being chased by bandits – handled with a flourish that could be a climax for any other film; Wanted is not short for set pieces. Gemma consistently relies on the kindness of strangers - who more often than not become collateral damage - with the question soon becoming, what price freedom? Despite being a paragon of virtue, Gemma doesn’t spend a lot of time mourning the dead – though this could be related to how action packed the film is.

I am usually very indulgent of dubbing, especially in Italian films of this period when dubbing was very much the norm. I can live with Klaus Kinski's voice veering between Paul L. Smith and Paul Lynde depending on which movie he's in. Inappropriate voicing is something I am used to. But this voice cast takes expressionlessness to new levels. It sounds like... I don't know how to describe…

reviews.text: The scale of this series is very nearly incomprehensible. In fact, it's even challenging to wrap one's head around just this small portion of it, given the thousands of extras, the attention-seeking camera movement, and the glorious, spectacular sound design. It's the kind of movie that you watch, awestruck, as it passes before you; the kind of movie that indulges every fanciful filmmaking whim anyone has ever had; the kind of movie that not only attempts the impossible, but which achieves it — over, and over, and over again.

By the time one notices the protagonists of the film are Price Andrei Bolkonsky and the idealistic Pierre Besukhov instead of Natasha Rostova, one can just speculate the sociopolitical and historical agenda intended by Tolstoy will be given the utmost respect by Bondarchuk, whose massive work is the spiritual (and even chronological successor) of Abel Gance’s 1927 unsurpassable epic. The delicacy for framing a time in history and dissecting psychology like onion layers is worthy of mentioning along the best European political auteurs of the…

reviews.text: Potentially the best part of the series, Bondarchuk closes the war arc with the delusional power of politics and Napoleon’s insatiable thirst of power and blood stepping into Russian territory, with his insane military strategy being a foreshadowing of Hitler’s same equivocal decision. A whole population flees its mother city while they see it burst in flames in the distance. This is arguably the basis for what war represents for defenseless civilians, as Come and See (1985) would capture later. This part also opens new storytelling possibilities within the literary genre of historical fiction through revisionist history and this is where Pierre’s focus acquires a greater significance: now that all your five senses have tasted war to its fullest like…

reviews.text: Even after watching the previous three parts, I can not wrap my head around how insane it is to see this many extras and the gigantic sets in this film. Then watching actors run in and out of burning builds becomes even more shocking. It's complete and utter madness and a perfect end to an amazing four-part film.

The special effects are actually rather good aswell - a scene in a bathtub is the standout. The clown ice cream man doing the revenge is creepy as hell, as is the little jingle that plays everytime another death is close. It is all rather simple stuff and a long way from great but it's well executed and obviously very tongue in cheek. Entertaining enough and one of the better season two episodes.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Werckmeister Harmonies is a film of constant symbolism and allegory. It is the greatest philosophical and political allegory since Sátántangó, another film by master auteur Béla Tarr. Werckmeister Harmonies is Tarr's most exciting film (although Sátántangó remains his best) because it's the most brimming with ideas. Adapting the novel The Melancholy of Resistance by László Krasznahorkai, Werckmeister Harmonies more than matches the quality of the masterful original text. The film is more implicit in some ways, taking the dense metaphorical nature of the novel but removing the clarity of the book's multi-viewpoint narrative. What remains though is the unfolding of a Mitteleuropean tragedy, which is hypnotically enchanting and slow, and on an intimate scale with cosmic flourishes.

reviews.author: Ronan Doyle
reviews.text: Why do I hold Werckmeister Harmonies aloft as the greatest film I have ever seen? A huge part of it, admittedly, and the thing that makes me think it will remain my favourite film to the day I die, is its profound personal relevance. I first saw the film about 5 years ago now, at a time when my interest in cinema was in the very very earliest stages of blossoming. It blew me away. Takes that long, images that symbolic, music that intoxicating, scenes that spellbinding, meanings that elusive... it was far too much for my uninitiated mind to deal with, but I knew that it was changing me. What's funny is that I encountered it entirely by mistake:…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: The original title "The Melancholy of Resistance" is apt. A weary, hunched-shouldered, and hypnotic funeral march of the highest order. Wandering the ruins of a world so broken and immiserated you can't even remember what the foundations were supposed to look like before they crumbled. The only thing left to do is stew in your desperation and rage and sadness.

Rather, I am going to rattle off some of my initial reactions (as I frequently do after viewing the films of Andrei Tarkovsky) with the hope that at least one of them will hit you on a personal level, and you will make the decision to SEE THIS FILM, if you haven't already;

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: life-affirming cinema; hope out of the deepest despair. bela tarr's camera is the most tender and ethical i have ever seen -- the end of this world is given a dignity and sadness, but also a love that these things are what they must be, that collapse clears away decay and rust -- the whale carcasses of history do not define us, but we must live within them with a boldness and an unflinching eye towards the eternal capacity of the human spirit -- the smallest tonality is the universal truth, and all the grand circuses of politics and chaos cannot ever drown out its beauty; there is life after every apocalypse, there must be. we have always been in these ruins, but we are not of them -- the shapes of the past are guideposts, sagely markers of hubris and wonder -- the dream goes on, fade into morning mist, see you tomorrow.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: This is the first Béla Tarr film I’ve seen, and I'm completely shaken. The film did not just impress me, but it dismantled something in me, quietly, methodically. I really expected austerity, perhaps some formal difficulty, but what I witnessed was something closer to a metaphysical event. It’s a film that arrests time itself. I found myself suspended in its rhythm, in its shadows, in its terrifying calm. From its first image to its final stillness, I felt as though I had entered the final movement of a symphony, a lament for the failure of both utopia and reality. And to help others enjoy as much as I did, I'll try to shed some light on some subjects.
