reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: This knowing and affectionate sendup of Wagnerian opera is one of Chuck Jones’ masterpieces and a lot of animation buffs’ choice for the greatest one-reel cartoon ever made. Jones famously had his animators churn out a Road Runner cartoon in about half the usual time so that they could surreptitiously devote extra time to this. The trick paid off. The animation is extremely pleasing, invoking the theatricality of opera performed on stage — albeit on a much grander and more surreal scale. I’m a fan of opera, though not a hardcore one, and I think this parody evinces a much better understanding of how opera actually works (and what its appeal is) than some more reverential film adaptations I’ve seen. But I don’t think you have to appreciate “high culture” to enjoy this. It’s utterly delightful!

reviews.text: Zusammen mit seinem Vorgänger "Der Große mit seinem außerirdischen Kleinen" (Lupo 1979) ist "Buddy haut den Lukas" der wohl kindgerechteste Bud-Spencer-Film. Spencer tritt in den beiden Filmen nicht als gleichberechtigter Partner z. B. eines Terence Hill auf, sondern als starker Papa eines sechs- bzw. achtjährigen Kindes, der aufgrund seiner außerirdischen Herkunft die ein oder andere Superkraft, mit der er wiederum Spencer überlegen ist, gegen Feinde einsetzen kann. Regisseur Lupo verzichtet diesmal auf sprechende Tiere - eine der Superkräfte des Keinen ist, Tiere sprechen zu lassen - und leider auch weitgehend auf Songs von Guido & Maurizio De Angelis, nur einen, den man als Hauptthema schon häufiger während des Films gehört hat, gibt es im Abspann zu hören. Stattdessen gibt es eine Geschichte um eine Außerirdischeninvasion, die vielleicht für Kinder spannend sein kann, erwachsenen Zuschauern aber durch ihre nur auf Sparflamme kochende Spannung und zu wenig Humor Längen beschert.

reviews.text: a film of extraction and extermination. the underlining thread that ray draws between ecological catastrophe and the nazi holocaust amounts to a full-on suspicion of the enlightenment project, as we see the miami settlers' prosperity made at the cost of both the rural locals and their avian prey, yet ray doesn't paint burl ives' hunter as anything but a natural consequence of a system that rewards cruelty and demands heedless profits for scarcer resources -- the assembly-line wiping-out of a whole species is simply that logic taken to its extreme, a fashion made out of fascistic means.

reviews.author: cult_vegetables
reviews.text: Its turbulent production is now legendary, and Nicholas Ray's contribution has been sliced & diced, but there's still the beat of an adventure inside this technicolor patchwork. If the promise of a Floridian 'Heart of Darkness' evaporates (Burl Ives' swamp-king is fine, but he lacks the enigma), it settles into an odd, and much safer, Pirate/Western hybrid. Yet in its uneven and painterly way, the film addresses the still-relevant exploitation vs. ecosystem conundrum, and even resolves it in a classic showdown.

reviews.text: Based on what was happening on set while it was being made, it's a wonder that Wind Across the Everglades exists at all. Not only was director Nicholas Ray aggressively not interested in the story (at one point during a location tour, he refused to leave his cabin, proclaiming "you've seen one glade you've seen them all!"), but he was also drinking so heavily and using enough unspecified drugs that writer-producer Budd Schulberg described him as "in a way a distortion of the Nick that we had known."

reviews.author: Seer
reviews.text: With the benefit of hindsight, I might have called this film South of Heaven's Gate. This film was killed by the studios, therefore by the public of its time (who then and now rarely see how bound up they are in the paradigm set by the studios), and even today it does not quite get its due. It was up to those like Serge Daney, looked at like madmen and terrorists, to defend the refugees of the American cinema against the Hollywood rule. Therefore, Wind Across the Everglades is newer than the New Hollywood, and today more than ever.

reviews.text: A radical achievement within the Hollywood system, lambasted by hacks far and wide. Surprisingly similar to Aguirre, The Wrath of God—a mythical descent into the abyss, and comparable also to Ray's own Bitter Victory (released a year earlier—these are his two best films imo) only transposed to Florida’s Everglades. All three films reach similar conclusions regarding man’s place within nature, the imperialism of the western soul being exposed under harsh conditions. The dissonant violin strings are boundary-pushing and turn this into a horror film in its final act, as our two dueling protagonists—who each represent one half of the proletarian psyche vying for dominion (that is, the half that is conscious of class/ecology and the half that is not)—reach the…

reviews.author: Avalyn Wu
reviews.text: Makes perfect sense as a follow-up to Bitter Victory. In spite of the evident incongruities, Ray is able to preserve a kind of coherence through sound bridges, which map the screaming and gunfire of our characters onto the landscapes themselves. It sets the groundwork for a film that lunges further and further into the feverish, quasi-mystical terrain of nature, functioning as a stage for the conflict between these two conceptions of power. Contrary to what one might except, nature sides with the state against vulgar individualism. True to their word, the wind and the snakes don’t heed to anyone, especially those who pretend to be their ruler.

reviews.text: It just doesn’t get any more absorbing, provocative, existential and beautifully shot than this! Woman in the Dunes is only my first Hiroshi Teshigahara film and it absolutely floored me with the excellent performances, claustrophobic atmosphere, introspective look into the human condition and isolation, visual allegories, memorable dialogue and an unnerving musical score which reminded me of Mica Levi’s work in Under the Skin to some degree. There are many impressive shots of sand slithering downward, having a constant menacing aspect to them. After all, our protagonists are forced to live in this pit because of sand and they end up finding purpose in living on those circumstances. You also get a strong sense of fellowship throughout the film, emphasizing traditional Japanese family and community values. Overall, Woman in the Dunes is a remarkable gem and a must-see for every film enthusiast!

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Fassbinder gets the jump on decades of philosophical sci-fi with this miniseries. His penchant for reflective surfaces and obscuring glass is taken to an early extreme here, with countless shots incorporating reflections into blocking or framing characters through glass that often warps dimensions and even at its least intrusive makes it clear that everyone is being watched. (The adjective "cinematic" is used freely and almost always emptily in current discussions of TV, but Fassbinder, like the other European auteurs who experimented on the small-screen, comes closest to cinema by expressly foregrounding the format of their television productions with an aesthetic that shows them adapting to its different demands and even the implications of its alternate screen.)

reviews.text: Trying to indicate the scale of a movie so immense and full of life that it can’t possibly be described (only experienced), the British critic Nigel Andrews wrote that calling “‘Yi Yi’ a three-hour Taiwanese family drama is like calling ‘Citizen Kane’ a film about a newspaper.” It’s a clever line, but those who haven’t seen Edward Yang’s final masterpiece could easily mistake it for a cop-out. At a passing glance, it seems like the kind of thing someone in Andrews’ position might say when they’re too awed to do their job well. And yet, to watch “Yi Yi” is to know where the critic was coming from, and to recognize that he wasn’t surrendering to a great work of…

reviews.text: “I’m sorry Grandma. It wasn't that I didn't want to talk to you. I think about all the stuff I could tell you... You must already know. Otherwise, you wouldn't always tell me to 'Listen!' They all say you've gone away. But you didn't tell me where you went. I guess it's someplace you think I should know. But, Grandma, I know so little. Do you know what I want to do when I grow up? I want to tell people things they don't know. Show them stuff they haven't seen. It'll be so much fun. Perhaps one day... I'll find out where you've gone. If I do, can I tell everyone, and bring them to visit you? Grandma, I miss you. Especially when I see my newborn cousin who still doesn't have a name. He reminds me that you always said you felt old. I want to tell him that I feel old, too.“

reviews.text: Edward Yang's original intention with this film upon conceptualizing the idea for it was to make a work which traced a persons life from birth to death. Quite an ambitious prospect! Yet the film as is can be described as exactly that - the film opens with a wedding and ends with a funeral. What Yang does is make a very narrative film, probably his most accessible, but this is for the purpose of breaking down the stages of life into specific characters at specific times in their lives. Rather than necessarily making these ideas accessible (though the film does, which is not a problem) it also allows one stage of life to cross paths with another, and maybe this…

reviews.text: "Yongary, Monster from the Deep" is a 1967 film directed by Kim Kee-duk. The film follows the all too familiar scenario of a nuclear blast unearthing a giant reptilian monster that wrecks havoc to civilization within its somewhat close proximity. This time blasts in the middle east have the creature attacking South Korea, to which majority of the film houses an all out war to take the monster out. The film was created in connection with the South Korean film system and Toei, notably a rival film studio to the "Godzilla" (1954) film studio of Toho.

reviews.text: Sometimes a movie is exactly what it looks like. This dirt-cheap Korean Godzilla knock-off plays like a dirt-cheap Korean Godzilla knock-off, but minus most of the goofy charm that might imply. Points for actually keeping the monster onscreen for a lot of the run time, demerits for giving said monster precious little to do with all of that screen time. Yongary spends more time scratching himself than he does smashing up the various sets and miniatures, and the usual gang of boring humans doesn't do much to pick up the slack. This does feature a surprisingly gruesome monster death scene, if that's what does it for you. (And if you're following me on Letterboxd, there's a solid chance that's exactly what does it for you.)

reviews.author: Stephen Gillespie
reviews.text: There are two films in Zebraman, two films that are independently interesting and show the different sides of Miike’s sensibilities. The issue is, when placed together, these films undercut each other and spoil the whole equation. So, while the first act is fascinating (and explores potent - and timely - themes) and while the back two thirds go full Miike, the balance is off.

reviews.author: Aleheez
reviews.text: Miike's shot at a superhero project left me extremely underwhelmed. I was expecting Zebraman to be nuts, maybe at times a bit controversial given the director's track record. But no it's surprisingly dull throughout its whole runtime for a concept like this. I was locked in as to not click away. If I'm gonna watch a superhero movie about just some regular loser in over his head, I'll just stick with James Gunn's Super instead. Or even Kick-Ass.

reviews.author: Jaime Rebanal 🇵🇸
reviews.text: I feel like we just need more superhero movies quite like this one; made outside the Hollywood studio system and being more than willing to embrace the wacky and chaotic nature of their origins, because they translate better to the screen than most of your typically overtly gritty and dour entries that you'll see from most modern superhero film franchises now. And better yet, considering this is a film by Takashi Miike, you know he wouldn't be one to let down on how ridiculous it is - because no matter the sort of film he would make, whether it's something super violent like Ichi the Killer or as demented as Visitor Q, you always saw a style you can attribute to him.
